title: The live-work registry: agent workers and long-running processes
description:
Build the live-work registry: one store holding agent workers and long-running processes.

Both are things this repo started that are still alive, so they share one registry rather than
two. Each entry carries a state (running, waiting on input, done, failed), a line saying what
it is doing right now, and a handle to the pane it runs in. "Waiting on input" must be
distinguishable from "still working" without attaching to anything.

Entries can be attached to, killed and retried. Attaching focuses that entry's pane.

NOT a tab. The prototype settled that live work is not a separate surface: admin-3rgp.20's Work
tab renders this registry alongside the commands, in one list under one cursor. This ticket is
the half that knows what is alive; .20 is the half that draws it, and it blocks on this.

Reference for how entries render: docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/swarm.txt shows the cursor on a
worker, including the detail-pane shape a worker gets.
acceptance_criteria:
- A dev server started from the Work tab is registered and appears in the list.
- An agent worker dispatched by a workflow appears in the same registry.
- Each entry exposes its state, a current-activity line, and a pane handle.
- An entry waiting for input is distinguishable from one still working without attaching.
- Attaching focuses the entry's pane; killing stops it; retrying restarts a failed entry.
- The registry is queryable programmatically, so the Work tab renders it rather than owning it.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at 962d1d0. .28 (a26ed8c): internal/livework extended — Entry gains an optional *WorkerInfo (branch/worktree; nil for a bare process, so one struct is NOT forced to cover both kinds, per the epic's amendment), an Activity line, StateWaiting, and Attach/Kill/Retry via a per-entry Ops struct both real producers now wire (pane.go's recordLiveWork and workflowdispatch.go's dispatchOne). Entry.ID redefined as a producer-chosen stable slot identity so Retry replaces its row rather than appending. .38 (5bc9362): glyph-based icon generation — apple.generate_icons / apple.generate_tv_icons, text glyphs via x/image + embedded Go Regular, SVG via oksvg+rasterx, full tvOS brandassets layer stack. This was .38's last named remaining item. Orchestrator independently verified the new dependencies against the stated bar: CGO_ENABLED=0 builds clean and internal/luahost cross-compiles to linux and windows with cgo disabled.

title: Worktree per target under a concurrency ceiling
description:
Dispatch a workflow: one git worktree per target, under a concurrency ceiling.

Each target gets its own worktree, seeded with the configured populate files, and runs the
configured agent there. The ceiling caps how many run at once; targets beyond it queue and start
as slots free. Each running target registers as live work with a handle to its pane.

Per-workflow agent overrides win over the project default.

A worker never removes its own worktree — a process cannot outlive its working directory.
Retirement is done from outside.

Out of scope: the two invocation paths, which are their own tickets, and the Swarm tab.
acceptance_criteria:
- Dispatching over N targets creates N worktrees, each seeded with the populate files.
- No more than the ceiling run at once; the remainder queue and start as slots free.
- Each running target appears in the live registry with its pane handle.
- A per-workflow agent override is used in preference to the default.
- No worker deletes its own worktree.
close_reason: Landed as 0891e61 on feat/one-tool-go-merge. internal/kinds/workflowdispatch.go: DispatchTargets creates every target's worktree up front via internal/create.Worktree (seeded with populate files), re-verifies each worktree still exists immediately before its agent starts, runs targets under a semaphore-bounded ceiling so a slot frees only when a target settles, and registers each running target in internal/livework with its pane handle. Per-workflow agent override beats the config default. New [workflow] config table (agent, ceiling) with repo-overrides-global merge. Three mutations run and reverted, including one proving the ceiling actually binds (observed max concurrency 5, want <= 2). NOTE: the worker's first test draft omitted t.Chdir and leaked six branches (t0-t4, vanish-me) plus six worktree registrations into the PRIMARY repo's shared ref store; it self-disclosed, fixed the tests, and the orchestrator pruned and deleted all twelve. A full suite run after the fix leaks nothing.

title: The workflow kind and its target source
description:
Add the workflow kind and its target source.

A workflow expresses "run this same thing over many targets". It declares where its targets come
from, and that declaration decides how it can be invoked:

- `over = "selection"` — the user picks targets on a row. Never appears in the Commands tab,
  because a command that cannot say what it will act on should not be offered.
- `over = { query = "…" }` — the tool resolves its own targets. Appears in the Commands tab and
  can be run bare.

A workflow declaring neither is a validation error. That ambiguity is the whole reason the key
exists, so it is caught at `check` rather than at dispatch.

Out of scope: dispatch, worktrees and concurrency. This ticket is the definition, the merge and
the rejection.
acceptance_criteria:
- A workflow with a selection source parses, merges and validates, and does not appear in the
  command list.
- A workflow with a query source parses, merges, validates and does appear.
- A workflow with no target source fails `check` with an error naming the missing key.
- Workflows merge from archetypes the same way commands and actions do.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at 58de9de. .24 (58e1a9f): the workflow kind — WorkflowSource/WorkflowTarget, ParseWorkflowOver for over='selection' (row-only) vs over={query=...} (runnable bare after confirming the resolved set), ValidateWorkflows wired into admin check; TUI wiring stays with .26/.27 so makeWorkflow's Runner is deliberately not-implemented for now. .18: internal/logbridge (0.0.0.0 bind, /health + /log, UnwrapInnerPrefix, console-level mapping, timestamp-ordered batches, host-only logging, dead-PID sweep) and internal/keybindings, both built on internal/streams.OutputPump rather than a new pump; interactive-shell and bridge-listen factories replace their stubs. One additive conflict in factories.go resolved by the orchestrator as the union — three distinct kind names, each registered once. Verified integrated: go build, go vet, go test ./... all green.

title: Config tab and the explicit manifest keys
description:
Build the Config tab, and add the manifest keys it renders.

Every value the dashboard infers today becomes a declared key: which tracker the project uses,
whether it uses pull requests, the identity login and email list that decides whether a branch is
yours, the worktree root, the populate patterns, the default agent, and the concurrency ceiling.

The tab renders resolved values, showing which are declared and which are defaulted.

Ownership stays a configured question, not an inferred one: a branch is yours when its PR author
matches the configured login, or when the first non-merge commit's author email is in the
configured list. No third rule, and no default.

Out of scope: editing values from the tab. It is read-only.
acceptance_criteria:
- Every key above is readable from the manifest and rendered on the tab.
- A key not declared shows its default and is marked as defaulted.
- Branch ownership resolves through the two configured rules only; a branch matching neither is
  reported as unknown rather than guessed.
- A project declaring no tracker renders that fact rather than guessing one.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at fdf5941. .21 (91ea7ee): tracker and uses_pull_requests are now DECLARED top-level admin.toml keys, merged manifest-wins over archetypes, and the Config tab was rewritten from a raw dotfile viewer with an $EDITOR escape hatch into a read-only resolved readout of seven keys, each naming its origin (archetype name, (manifest), global config, local config, or defaulted); an undeclared tracker renders 'no tracker declared' rather than a guess. Three executed mutations. .50 (5e16558): cmd/check.go checkUnknownKinds validates every resolved action's kind against the catalog via kinds.Declared. Orchestrator re-verified .50 directly with a fresh binary and a manifest declaring kind='nosuchkind' beside a valid shell action: 'action "build": unknown kind "nosuchkind"', exit 1, no false positive on the valid action.

title: The Work tab: commands and live work in one list
description:
Build the Work tab and make it the landing tab.

The Work tab holds commands and live work as ONE list under ONE cursor, with a detail pane on
the right third. This replaces the earlier split of a Commands tab plus a separate live-work
tab — the prototype settled that they were never two objects.

Layout:

- Left two thirds: the rows. Commands first, then any worker with no command behind it. One
  cursor traverses both; the order is stable so it does not jump when something starts or stops.
- A row's second column answers one question: the command's DESCRIPTION when idle, the LIVE
  STATUS and its pane when running. Last run is NOT in the list — it is a detail-pane field.
  The earlier column said "last run 2h ago" for an idle row and a live status for a running
  one, so it meant two different things and the useful half only appeared once work had
  already started.
- Right third: a POLYMORPHIC detail pane. It changes shape with the row's kind, not just its
  values. A command shows kind, archetype, last run, log path and its steps with each step's
  contributing archetype. A worker shows state, what it is doing right now, branch, worktree,
  elapsed, and its attach/kill/retry actions. They share almost no fields; squeezing both into
  one field set is exactly what made the earlier two-tab split necessary.

Tabs are Work, Repo, the tracker tab, Config. Four, not five.

Query-sourced workflows appear in the list; a selection-sourced one does not (it is offered on
a row instead).

A repo with no manifest has no Work tab at all. Absent, not disabled.

Reference frames in docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/: commands.txt (idle),
commands-workflow-selected.txt (a query-sourced workflow selected), running.txt (a command
mid-run), swarm.txt (the cursor on a worker, showing the other pane shape), no-manifest.txt.

Out of scope: dispatching a workflow (its own ticket), and the live-work registry itself
(admin-3rgp.28) — this ticket renders that registry, it does not build it.
acceptance_criteria:
- The dashboard opens on the Work tab when the project has a manifest.
- Commands and workers appear in one list under one cursor; moving the cursor across the boundary works.
- A row shows its description when idle and its live status plus pane when running. Last run does not appear in the list.
- The detail pane changes shape with the row kind: a command shows kind/archetype/last run/log/steps-with-archetype; a worker shows state/current activity/branch/worktree/elapsed/actions.
- Running a command from the tab dispatches it, and the row switches to its live status.
- A directory with no admin.toml opens on the Repo tab and shows no Work tab.
- The tab is fully operable from the keyboard.
close_reason: Landed as 5fadaba on feat/one-tool-go-merge (worker commit ca1ab6f). internal/tui/work.go + workview.go: ONE list under ONE cursor holding both commands and live work, with a detail pane on the right third whose shape follows the row's kind — a command shows kind/archetype/steps, a worker shows state/activity/branch/worktree/elapsed and the a/k/r actions bound to internal/livework's Attach/Kill/Retry. Work is now the first tab; the prototype's key indices were bumped to match. Verified with real --dump-frame runs of the compiled binary against this repo's own admin.toml, plus 12 unit tests and two executed mutations.

title: Rebuild the reference frames for the settled design
description:
Rebuild the dashboard reference frames to match the settled design, and commit them.

The prototype built during design settled the layout question by comparing three fan-out models.
The design that was chosen is a synthesis of all three, so none of the three variants is the
design — citing one would mislead. Rebuild it as a single-variant artifact of the settled shape
and dump one text frame per named state.

Text frames rather than screenshots: the artifact is a character grid, and a dumped text frame is
already how a UI change is checked at the surface in this codebase.

States to capture, one file each: `commands`, `commands-workflow-selected`, `repo`, `issues`,
`issues-selected`, `dispatch-sheet`, `swarm`, `config`, `running`, `no-manifest`.

Commit to `docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/` — the build and the frames together.
acceptance_criteria:
- `docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/` contains the prototype and one text frame per state above.
- Each frame shows the settled design: Commands landing tab with the resolved-action reader,
  Swarm tab, Config tab, and workflows appearing in the Commands list only when query-sourced.
- Every ticket citing a reference frame names a file that exists.
close_reason: Rebuilt and committed as d7d90d7 to docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/ — a single-variant Go renderer plus ten 96x30 text frames (commands, commands-workflow-selected, repo, issues, issues-selected, dispatch-sheet, swarm, config, running, no-manifest). The original Claude Design prototype was never in git and is unrecoverable; the frames are rebuilt from docs/PRD.md and the assertions in internal/tui/design_parity_test.go. The citations in .20 and .28 now resolve. Live-work tab renders as a placeholder 'Live'; its final name stays open per PRD.md:110.

title: Kinds carry a lifetime; long-running dispatches to a Herdr pane
description:
Give each kind a lifetime, and dispatch long-running ones into their own Herdr pane.

The kind catalog gains a third flag beside the existing ones: whether a kind is long-running. A
transient kind runs inline in the frame, as now. A long-running kind spawns a Herdr pane, returns
immediately, and registers itself as live work with a handle to that pane.

With Herdr unavailable, a long-running kind falls back to running inline with the pinned footer —
exactly today's behaviour — so the tool stays usable over SSH and in a bare terminal.

The registry this creates is what the Swarm tab reads and what the orchestrator epic will need.

Out of scope: the Swarm tab itself, and agent workers.
acceptance_criteria:
- A long-running kind returns control immediately and appears in the live registry with its pane
  handle.
- A transient kind runs inline and does not appear in the registry.
- With Herdr unavailable, a long-running kind runs inline with the footer and the command still
  works.
- The registry survives for the life of the process and reports each entry's state.
close_reason: Landed as 189e9e9 on feat/one-tool-go-merge. internal/kinds.Kind gains Lifetime (Transient/LongRunning), every catalog entry classified; RunActionRouted splits a Herdr pane for long-running kinds and re-invokes via a hidden 'admin __run-action', recording a handle in the new internal/livework registry (which admin-3rgp.28 extends). Orchestrator verified the fallback specifically, since it is the path almost every run takes: dispatchToPane gates on shim.Available() (HERDR_ENV != 1 or herdr not on PATH) and returns ErrHerdrUnavailable, which RunActionRouted falls through to inline RunAction; any other error stays a real error. Test suites pass with HERDR_ENV unset AND with HERDR_ENV=1, and the Herdr pane count was unchanged across the run (12 -> 12), so tests do not spawn real panes. interactive-shell deliberately stays Transient because detaching it would break its own keystroke handling.

title: Frame, output pump and log rendering
description:
Port the framed-action surface: the pinned footer, the output pump and log line rendering.

The footer pins to the bottom of a scroll region while output scrolls above it — a status row,
the absolute log path, then one row per URL, each a hyperlink. It activates on the presence of
`urls`, and `footer` overrides that in both directions. It declines when stdout is not a
terminal.

**One pump, one place.** Every caller that reads a child's output writes through a single pump
which is the only thing that touches the terminal, because the footer has to be repainted after
each chunk. This was five separate copies in the Python and must not become two here.

Log rendering strips whatever timestamp the source printed, stamps one clock column, colours the
four severity levels by hand, and colours scope tags by a hash of the label so a tag is the same
colour in every project and every run. Unwrap an app's own logger prefix when the message
carries one.
acceptance_criteria:
- A framed action pins its footer while output scrolls above it, and the footer survives a child
  that positions its own cursor.
- Exactly one code path writes child output to the terminal.
- `footer = true` raises a frame for an action with no URLs; `footer = false` suppresses one the
  URLs would have raised.
- Piped output raises no frame.
- A log line carrying its own timestamp is restamped, not double-stamped.
- The same scope tag gets the same colour across two separate runs.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge: .11 as 0c15e42 (internal/frame with DECSTBM pinned footer + OSC 8 links, internal/streams.OutputPump as the single terminal-writing path, internal/logformat with crc32 scope colors, wired into shell/shell-passthrough/multi-target), .40 as 44c3bf0 (19 tests mutation-tested, 4 blind ones strengthened). Re-verified integrated: go build, go vet green; luahost stable across 2 runs. .40's strengthened TestRunCmd passes against .11's rewritten RunCmd.

title: Validation and the check verb
description:
Implement schema validation and the `check` verb.

Validation covers command and action shape, the command-is-pure-routing rule, `requires` shape,
`urls` shape and reference resolution, and `footer` being a real boolean. Errors share one
umbrella type, as ADR-0008 established, so a caller can distinguish a validation failure from
any other error.

`admin check [DIR]` parses, merges archetypes and validates, reporting every problem it finds
rather than only the first.

Out of scope: the anti-pattern reporting from ADR-0009, which is its own ticket.
acceptance_criteria:
- `check` on a valid manifest exits zero and says so.
- `check` on a manifest with several distinct errors reports all of them, each naming the key.
- A `urls` entry that is neither a key of the URL table nor a real URL is rejected.
- A command containing `kind`, `run` or `targets` is rejected.
- Every validation failure is distinguishable as a validation error rather than a generic one.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at 1d65eb2. .8 (9944cba): new internal/validate with the ADR-0008 Error umbrella, ADR-0003 command-routing check, footer-bool shape check, ValidateURLRefs now accumulating every bad entry, admin check [DIR] running all four via errors.Join. .16 (a30ae54): split branch (in-place checkout) from a new worktree verb, both with --prune, plus internal/git.ClassifyDead ported from admin_lib/gitwt. .15 (1d65eb2): kill-port, nuke-dev, dev-precheck, raylib, fixtures — internal/ports EXTENDED not duplicated. Verified integrated: go build, go vet, go test ./... all green; exactly one OutputPump and one RunWithReload per build tag. .15 is closed for its real scope; the rust/launchd remainder is split out because it is a design question, not a port.

title: Decide how admin <command> reaches the CLI, and wire it
description:
Decide the Go binary's command-line identity, then wire manifest commands into it.

NEEDS A HUMAN DECISION BEFORE IT CAN BE IMPLEMENTED. This ticket halted at the AFK gate on 2026-08-28 and the reason stands: nothing in the epic, the ADRs, docs/architecture/design.md or the spec says how a manifest command becomes a CLI verb on this binary.

What makes it undecided, concretely:

- `cmd/root.go` came in with repo-dash (040461c) and its `rootCmd.Use` is "repo". The binary's own name and root identity are unsettled.
- `dispatchArgs()` already claims any unrecognized bare first argument as branch shorthand: `repo <name>` becomes `repo branch --yes <name>`. An arbitrary manifest command name would be swallowed by that path.
- `cmd/` already owns `branch`, `prs` and `populate`. The five reserved tool verbs are `new`, `check`, `compile`, `branch`, `worktree`. A manifest may define a command with any name at all, and nothing says how the three sets are kept from colliding.
- The spec's user stories run Commands from the Dashboard TUI. There is no stated bare `admin <command>` CLI story; its only CLI mention is a test-seam aside.

Questions to answer: does the root command's Use become "admin"? Does the branch shorthand survive, and if so does it lose to manifest commands or beat them? Are manifest commands reached bare, or under a subcommand? What happens when a manifest names a command that collides with a tool verb or an existing cmd/ verb?

The answer belongs in an ADR, since it is a user-facing interface decision that later tickets cite.

The nine kind factories were SPLIT OUT to admin-3rgp.35 and are unaffected by any of this — that half was always settled. .10 through .15 now depend on .35 rather than this ticket. What still waits here is .8 (the check verb) and .16 (the branch and worktree verbs), both of which are argv-shape questions themselves.
acceptance_criteria:
- An ADR records the binary's root identity, how manifest commands are reached, and the collision rule between manifest command names, the five reserved tool verbs, and cmd/'s existing verbs.
- A manifest command dispatches through the built binary per that decision.
- The branch shorthand behaves as the ADR specifies rather than by accident.
- A manifest command whose name collides is rejected with an error naming the rule.
notes:
DECIDED 2026-08-31 by docs/adr/0011-the-binary-is-admin-and-manifest-commands-are-bare-verbs.md.

The "NEEDS A HUMAN DECISION" block in the description is RESOLVED and no longer applies.
Answers to the four questions it posed:

- rootCmd.Use becomes "admin"; "repo" survives as a cobra alias, because
  `repo completion zsh` is wired into the user's .zshrc and would fail silently at
  shell-startup time otherwise. The alias may be deleted once nothing invokes it.
- Manifest commands are reached BARE (`admin <command>`), not under a subcommand.
- The branch shorthand SURVIVES but moves to last place. Resolution order for a bare
  first argument: (1) tool verb or cmd/ verb, (2) manifest command, (3) branch shorthand.
  Rationale: a manifest command swallowed by the shorthand fails silently (`admin deploy`
  quietly makes a branch called "deploy"); a branch name shadowed by a command fails
  loudly. Prefer the visible failure.
- Tool verbs and cmd/'s verbs WIN collisions. `admin check` rejects a manifest that
  declares a colliding command name, with an error naming the rule and the name.

What remains here is implementation only: wire dispatchArgs, rename the root, add the
alias, and add the collision check to `check`.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at c308510. .7 (ada1b28): rootCmd.Use='admin' with 'repo' as a cobra alias, dispatchArgs resolves tool/cmd verb -> manifest command -> branch shorthand per ADR-0011, cmd/manifest.go + cmd/check.go enforce the reserved-name collision rule; first real caller of kinds.RunCommand. .39 (4b7b08d): pruneRetain in internal/luahost/host.go, retain=0 disables pruning per the Python reference. .13 (c308510): docker-dev, docker-reload-loop, server-reload, install-template, plus new internal/reload and internal/remotehost packages. Re-verified integrated: build, vet green; Windows cross-compile of internal/reload and internal/kinds clean; only the known admin-3rgp.44 flake fails.

title: Kind catalog and factory registry
description:
Build the kind catalog and the factory registry.

The catalog is the closed single source of truth for valid kinds, carrying per-kind metadata.
The registry maps a kind to the closure that executes it. Two invariants must hold and must be
enforced, not documented:

1. Registering a factory for a kind not declared in the catalog is an error.
2. A declared kind with no registered factory fails at startup, not at dispatch.

`python` and `python-script` are declared kinds and stay declared.

Out of scope: implementing any kind's behaviour. This ticket is the catalog, the registry and
the two invariants.
acceptance_criteria:
- Every kind the Python `KINDS` catalog declared is declared here.
- Registering a factory under an undeclared name fails loudly.
- Removing a factory for a declared kind makes the binary fail at startup with a message naming
  the kind.
- The derived views (known kinds, configless kinds, kind-to-module) are computed from the
  catalog rather than maintained separately.
close_reason: Landed 2fb576c: internal/kinds catalog + factory registry, both invariants enforced structurally with tests (undeclared registration fails; a declared kind with no factory fails at startup naming the kind). python and python-script stay declared. Stub factories registered so the startup invariant holds ahead of the porting tickets.

title: Convert the 14 archetypes to archetype.toml plus script files
description:
Convert the fourteen existing archetypes from Python modules to the directory format the loader
reads.

Each archetype's `ARCHETYPE` dict becomes `archetype.toml`. Eleven of the fourteen have no
embedded logic and are pure transcription. Three — `apple`, `forge-engine`, `react-native` —
carry Python payloads as string literals (`_BUILD_PY`, `_DEV_PY` and similar); those strings move
verbatim into files under the archetype's `scripts/` directory, and the action's `run` points at
the script path.

**The Python is not rewritten.** It moves out of string literals into real files, byte for byte.
`kind = "python"` and `kind = "python-script"` remain in the kind catalog and are not removed —
they are how an archetype or a project runs Python, the same way `kind = "docker"` runs Docker.

Out of scope: changing what any script does, and porting any payload to Go.
acceptance_criteria:
- All fourteen archetypes exist as directories with an `archetype.toml`.
- For each archetype, the merged result of loading it equals what the Python loader produced for
  the same input.
- The three payload-carrying archetypes have their scripts as files that run standalone under
  `python3`.
- No archetype's script content differs from the string literal it replaced.
- `admin.toml` files across existing projects resolve to the same command and action set as
  before.
notes: SUPERSEDED IN PART 2026-08-28 by ADR-0010. The archetype.toml conversion stands; the Python script payloads it created (archetypes/*/scripts/*.py, and the archetype.toml run values naming them) are replaced by Lua and Bash under admin-3rgp.37. The Go/Python equivalence harness this ticket added loses its counterpart when the Python side is deleted.
close_reason: Landed fac7fc0: all 14 archetypes now exist as archetypes/<name>/archetype.toml directories beside the untouched .py modules. apple, forge-engine and react-native have their Python payloads extracted byte-for-byte into scripts/. Parity proven by tools/archetype_parity.py + internal/archetypeparity/parity_test.go — 28 subtests comparing the Go and Python loaders across all 14, kept as a checked-in harness for admin-3rgp.30.

title: Archetype loader, search path and merge semantics
description:
Load archetypes from disk and merge them into a parsed Manifest.

Merge semantics are unchanged from ADR-0002: archetypes contribute partial manifests, merged in
list order, last wins on conflict. No inheritance, no override blocks.

The loader reads from a filesystem abstraction and searches, later winning by name:

    (embedded set — empty for now, reserved so archetypes can be promoted into the binary later)
    ~/.admin/archetypes/
    <repo>/.admin/archetypes/

An archetype is a directory containing `archetype.toml` and optionally a `scripts/` directory.
The embed slot exists but ships empty: the binary has no built-in archetypes, and archetypes are
installed by a separate deployment path.

Out of scope: converting the existing archetypes to that format, and the detectors.
acceptance_criteria:
- An archetype directory placed in `~/.admin/archetypes/` is found, parsed and merged.
- The same name in `<repo>/.admin/archetypes/` overrides the one in `~/.admin/archetypes/`.
- `archetypes = ["a", "b"]` merges both with b winning on conflict, per ADR-0002.
- Loading an archetype requires no interpreter and no subprocess.
- A binary with no archetype directories present runs and reports no archetypes, rather than
  failing.
close_reason: Landed a08a4f3 + 7cd4ed8 on feat/one-tool-go-merge: internal/archetype loader with the three-slot search path (empty embed slot, ~/.admin/archetypes, <repo>/.admin/archetypes), ADR-0002 last-wins merge, no interpreter or subprocess. The first pass's blocking review finding was fixed before landing: manifest [commands.X] overrides now fall back per field to the archetype command (desc, steps, group, priority, log_file, log_retain, log, env) instead of replacing the whole value, matching admin_lib/archetypes.py:155-185, and an override naming a command no archetype provides with no steps is now an error.

title: Parse admin.toml into a Manifest in Go
description:
Parse a project's `admin.toml` into a normalized Manifest in Go: project metadata, commands,
actions, the archetype list, log config and URLs.

Preserve the `${VAR}` scanning behaviour the Python parser has, including which values are
expanded at dispatch time versus parse time.

Out of scope: archetype merging, validation, and executing anything. This ticket parses one
file into a data structure.
acceptance_criteria:
- Writing a temporary `admin.toml` and parsing it yields a Manifest whose commands, actions,
  archetype list and URLs match the file.
- `${VAR}` references survive parsing unexpanded, in the same fields the Python parser leaves
  them in.
- A malformed manifest produces an error naming the offending key, not a panic.
close_reason: Landed 925e99c on feat/one-tool-go-merge: internal/manifest parses admin.toml into a Manifest (manifest.go, logs.go, envrefs.go) with table tests. Mutation check ran and discriminates.

title: Go module foundation: move repo-dash source in
description:
Establish the Go module and bring repo-dash's source in as first-class source of this
repository.

repo-dash is a Go/Bubble Tea dashboard living in a separate repo. Its source moves here and is
edited in place from now on. This is a move, not a dependency: no import of
`github.com/McBrideMusings/repo` may exist at any point, now or later.

The Python implementation is untouched by this ticket. Both live side by side until the
contract ticket removes the Python.

Out of scope: porting any Python, changing any TUI behaviour, deleting anything.
acceptance_criteria:
- `go build ./...` succeeds and produces a binary that opens the existing dashboard unchanged.
- Every test that passed in the repo-dash repository passes here.
- `grep -r "McBrideMusings/repo" .` returns nothing outside historical docs.
- `admin-run` and the Python test suite still work exactly as before.
close_reason: Landed 040461c on feat/one-tool-go-merge: repo-dash's Go source moved in as first-class source (81 files, 23550 insertions). Module renamed to github.com/McBrideMusings/admin-project-tool, 42-file import rewrite, no reference to McBrideMusings/repo remains. Python side untouched.

title: One tool: merge repo-dash into admin as a single Go binary
description:
`admin` and `repo-dash` become one Go binary installed with `go install`. The binary is both
the manifest interpreter and the repo dashboard.

Settled decisions this epic implements:

- **One Go binary.** `admin_lib/` is ported from Python to Go. ADR-0001 (stdlib-only) is
  superseded — its purpose was a dependency-free artifact, which a static binary achieves more
  completely. Third-party Go dependencies are fine.
- **One repo.** repo-dash's Go source moves into this repository as first-class source and is
  edited in place. repo-dash is archived. Nothing here ever imports
  `github.com/McBrideMusings/repo` — the merge is a move, not a dependency.
- **Command Tab layout.** The dashboard lands on the Commands tab, a two-column split with a
  resolved-action reader beside the list. Then Repo, the tracker tab, Swarm, Config.
- **Kinds carry a lifetime.** Long-running kinds dispatch into a Herdr pane; transient kinds run
  inline in the existing frame. No Herdr available falls back to inline, which is today's
  behaviour.
- **Workflows declare a target source.** `over = "selection"` is row-only; `over = { query = … }`
  appears in the Commands tab and runs bare after confirming the resolved set.
- **Archetypes are plugins.** Their manifests become TOML, their scripts stay as they are, and
  they install to `~/.admin/archetypes/` by a deployment path separate from the binary. Nothing
  is embedded in the binary for now.

Spec: `/private/tmp/claude/Projects-admin-project-tool/spec.md` (transitory).
Principle governing manifest content: `docs/adr/0009-manifests-reference-archetypes-carry-implementation.md`.
notes:
AMENDED 2026-08-30 by the admin-tui-desktop prototype (docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/).

The dashboard's tab set is Work, Repo, the tracker tab, Config — four, not five. Commands and
live work are ONE list under ONE cursor on the Work tab, with a detail pane on the right third
whose shape follows the row's kind: a command shows kind/archetype/last run/log/steps, a worker
shows state/current activity/branch/worktree/elapsed/actions. They share almost no fields,
which is why one field set could not hold both and why the earlier two-tab split existed.

Consequences: .20 is now the Work tab and renders the registry; .28 is the registry alone and
blocks .20; the live-work tab naming question is retired rather than answered (docs/PRD.md).

Three findings from inventorying repo-dash, each contradicting an assumption:
- "The tracker tab" is three conditional tabs. visibleTabs (internal/tui/model.go:352) derives
  them, and usesPRs() is len(remote.PRs) > 0 (model.go:333) — the PRs tab exists only while the
  repo has open PRs. tracker and uses_pull_requests are separate keys; .22 says so now.
- paneCleanup draws nothing of its own (internal/tui/local.go:701) and Stashes is skipped when
  empty (local.go:708), so the Repo tab has two focusable panes, not four.
- internal/tui.Frames landed: load once, snapshot many key sequences. Settle is a deadline, not
  a quiescence check, so one Frame per view paid the full wait every time.

title: a bound row key dispatches a second run over an already-live command
description:
internal/tui/rowkeys.go:139 — rowKeyDispatch fires a HIT without checking whether the target command already has a live pty entry.

The Commands-tab path it otherwise reuses (activateCommand) does check: when an entry is already live it attaches to it rather than starting a second run. The row-key path skips that branch, so pressing a bound key twice on a row starts a second process against a command whose first run still owns the log file.

That is the same failure recordHostedPTYWork's own comment describes and guards against by keying the live-work entry on the step name rather than the command name — the guard exists, this path just does not consult it.

Fix: route the HIT through the same already-live check activateCommand uses, so a bound key attaches to a running command instead of racing it.

Found by the review stage of the admin-l6kb.2 implement pass (landed as 5308c1f); reported non-blocking, so it landed as-is.

title: verify-project covers no Go surface
description: The repo's .claude/skills/verify-project/SKILL.md documents only the Python admin-run and pytest surface. It says nothing about the Go binary, the TUI, or the hosted-pty path, so the admin-3rgp.61 worker had no verification route and fell back to verifying at the code surface it inferred from the ticket. That worker also reported the bundled verify skill refusing invocation (disable-model-invocation), leaving verify-project as the only route. CLAUDE.local.md requires this skill be kept current as features land. Every remaining slice in admin-3rgp (.62 through .66) is Go TUI work and will hit the same gap.
acceptance_criteria: verify-project names the Go build and test commands, how to drive the dashboard headlessly, and how to verify a hosted-pty run end to end.

title: Test the hosted-pty log file and pinned footer
description: Two of admin-3rgp.61's seven acceptance criteria landed without a test and rest on code reading alone: (1) a Command dispatched onto the hosted pty writes its log file at the same path and in the same format — timestamping and ANSI stripping — as a plain-CLI run of the same Command; (2) a Command declaring urls or footer still produces its pinned footer, written into the pty. The other five are covered by TestFrameDuringHostedRunShowsTheDashboard, TestStartHostedPTYRegistersALiveEntry, TestStartHostedPTYEntryReportsExited, TestActivateCommandAttachesWhenLive and TestHostedReentryArgsUsesTheHostedVerb. Both gaps are regressions waiting to happen as admin-3rgp.62 through .66 build on the same path.
acceptance_criteria: A test asserts the hosted run's log file bytes match a plain-CLI run of the same Command. A test asserts an action declaring urls or footer emits its scroll region and footer rows into the pty.

title: Synchronize reads of livework.Entry.State
description: go test -race on internal/kinds.TestStartHostedPTYEntryReportsExited reports a data race on livework.Entry.State. Registry.SetState writes the field while holding the registry mutex, but Get and List return a live *Entry and every caller in internal/kinds and internal/tui reads e.State directly with no lock. The drain goroutine started by StartHostedPTY calls SetState concurrently with those reads, so the race is reachable in the dashboard, not only in tests. Predates admin-3rgp.61 — the pre-branch version of the same test polls the same unsynchronized field — so it did not block that item. Fix is a synchronized State accessor on Registry with every caller in kinds/ and tui/ moved onto it, rather than a lock at each read site.
acceptance_criteria: go test -race ./internal/kinds/... ./internal/livework/... ./internal/tui/... is clean. No caller reads Entry.State off a Get/List result directly.

title: needs human input: where the (row kind, key) shadow table lives
description:
admin-l6kb.1 halted at the AFK gate on its shadow-detection acceptance criterion:
"a binding whose key already carries a built-in meaning for that row kind passes,
and check prints a shadow line naming what it displaces."

The table that criterion needs does exist, but in the wrong package. Model.keymap()
at internal/tui/view.go:634-663 already maps every built-in key to a human-readable
label, and it is keyed by tab/pane, which corresponds 1:1 to the six bindable row
kinds: tabBeads->bead, tabIssues->issue, tabPRs->pr, tabLocal/default->branch,
tabLocal/paneCommits->commit, tabLocal/paneStashes->stash. The ADR's worked example
resolves exactly against it: tabBeads carries {"d","detail"}, so keys.bead.d shadows
"detail".

The blocker is layering, not missing information. internal/validate imports no other
internal package today (it is a leaf, per internal/validate/validate.go). The shadow
check must read a table that currently lives in internal/tui, the heaviest package in
the repo. The slice's own scope note -- "Nothing in internal/tui changes here" --
forbids extracting that table into a shared package, which is the move that would
make the check possible without inverting the dependency direction.

So the slice as written cannot be implemented: it requires reading a tui-owned table
while forbidding any change to tui.

The decision needed: where the shadow table lives, and whether admin-l6kb.1's scope
note moves to permit the extraction. Until that is settled, admin-l6kb.1 is not AFK-able
and the whole epic is stalled behind it.
close_reason: Decided: the built-in key label table moves to a new leaf package internal/keymap, re-keyed by row kind, and Model.keymap() reads it back. Recorded as a Consequence in ADR-0018 (commit 136a6be) and folded into admin-l6kb.1's scope, which now implements the extraction. Duplicating the table into internal/validate was rejected — two tables with nothing checking they agree.

title: The footer keybar shows the effective binding
description:
The footer keybar merges the bindings for the row kind under the cursor, so what it advertises is what the key actually does:

- A bound key's label becomes the named command's description, falling back to the command's name when it has none.
- A bound key with no built-in meaning for that row is added to the bar.
- Moving the cursor onto a row of an unbound kind restores the built-in labels.

The footer is where every key in this TUI is learned. A rebound `enter` that still renders its built-in label is worse than no footer at all — this slice is what stops the feature from lying on screen.

The bar is already under width pressure: it drops pairs from the middle when the keymap outgrows the line, keeping the first pair and the last two throughout. Bindings add to that pressure and must not break the invariant — `q quit` and `←→ tab` stay visible however long a project's keymap gets. See [ADR-0018](../docs/adr/0018-row-scoped-key-bindings.md).

Out of scope: a `?` help overlay listing every effective binding with its shadows. `admin check` already reports shadows at config time, which is where that question is answered.
acceptance_criteria:
- With `enter` bound on beads, the footer on the Beads tab labels `enter` with that command's description rather than the built-in label.
- With `o` bound on beads and no built-in `o` behavior for that row, `o` appears in the bar with the command's description.
- A command with no description falls back to labelling the key with the command's name.
- Moving the cursor from a bound row kind to an unbound one restores the built-in labels.
- With no `[keys]` table in the manifest, the footer renders byte-identically to today's.
- A keymap made long by several bindings still shows `q quit` and `←→ tab` — pairs are dropped from the middle, and the first pair and the last two survive.

title: A bound workflow dispatches over the row, or over the selection
description:
A binding whose command resolves to a single-step `kind="workflow"` action declaring `over = "selection"` dispatches over targets instead of running as a plain command. Two paths, decided by whether anything is selected:

- **Rows selected** — the binding runs over the whole selection, through the confirm overlay that already exists for the `space`-then-`w` picker. Nothing about that overlay changes.
- **Nothing selected** — the binding runs over the row under the cursor, immediately, with no overlay. The status line reports what was dispatched over what.

Selection-wins-with-cursor-fallback is the rule `x` on the Branches pane already established, so the dashboard keeps one selection semantic rather than two.

The overlay is skipped for a single row on purpose. Its stated reason to exist is that a *query* can match more than the user expects; the row under the cursor cannot. A confirm step on the most-used key is the kind of friction that gets a feature turned off. The cost is that the misconfigurations the overlay reports as a field — chiefly "no agent configured" — need somewhere else to go on the immediate path, and that is a red status line with nothing dispatched. See [ADR-0018](../docs/adr/0018-row-scoped-key-bindings.md).

Out of scope: any change to the confirm overlay itself, and to the `space`/`w` picker, both of which must keep working exactly as they do today.
acceptance_criteria:
- With `enter` on beads bound to a selection-sourced workflow, cursor on a bead and nothing selected: one target is dispatched, no overlay appears, and the status line names the command and the bead id.
- The same binding with three beads selected opens the confirm overlay naming three targets; confirming dispatches all three.
- With no agent configured, the immediate (cursor-row) path reports it as a red status line and dispatches nothing.
- A binding that names a command which is not a selection-sourced workflow still runs as a plain command, unchanged from the previous slice.
- `space` then `w` still opens the workflow picker and behaves exactly as it does today, selection semantics included.
- Dispatch goes through the same path the picker already uses — no second dispatch path is added.

title: A bound key runs its command with the row in the environment
description:
With the table parsed and validated, make it do something: the dashboard consults it before its own key switch, keyed on the pair (key pressed, row kind of the row under the cursor).

- **A hit** runs the named command through the existing command-activation path — the same one a Commands-tab row uses — with the row's identity exported to the dispatched process.
- **A miss** falls through to the built-in behavior, completely unchanged. This is what keeps every existing project behaving exactly as it does today: with no `[keys]` table, no key in the dashboard changes meaning, `enter` on a bead included.

The row reaches the command through the environment rather than as an argument, so it flows through every step of a multi-step command and every action kind without any of them knowing about it — and so it cannot be invalidated by whatever `admin-1qte` decides about args forwarding:

- `ADMIN_ROW_KIND` — `bead`, `issue`, `branch`, `pr`, `commit`, `stash`
- `ADMIN_ROW_ID` — the bead id, the issue or PR number, the branch name, the commit sha, the stash ref
- `ADMIN_ROW_URL` — set only when the row carries a URL

Scoping the lookup to the row kind is what makes this safe on an already-full keymap: nearly every letter is taken, so a binding lands on top of a built-in rather than in free space, and row-kind scoping makes that collision local. See [ADR-0018](../docs/adr/0018-row-scoped-key-bindings.md).

Out of scope: bindings that resolve to a `kind="workflow"` action, which dispatch instead of running as a plain command — that is the next slice. The footer keybar is a separate slice too, so a bound key is not yet advertised anywhere.
acceptance_criteria:
- With `[keys.bead] o = "<some command>"`, pressing `o` on a bead row runs that command.
- The dispatched process sees `ADMIN_ROW_KIND` set to `bead` and `ADMIN_ROW_ID` set to that bead's id.
- `ADMIN_ROW_URL` is set when the row carries a URL and unset when it does not.
- The same key pressed on a row of any other kind still does exactly what it did before.
- With no `[keys]` table in the manifest, every key in the dashboard behaves as it does today — including `enter` on a bead, which still opens a worktree.
- Binding `enter` for one row kind leaves `enter` on every other row kind untouched.
- A key bound for a row kind does nothing on the Work tab's own rows (`command`, `commandTarget`, `worker`), which keep their existing behavior.
close_reason: Landed as 5308c1f (merge of row-key-dispatch, commit 0f1e23f). internal/tui/rowkeys.go consults the [keys.<row-kind>] lookup (validate.RowKeys over Manifest.Keys and the new Manifest.CommandNames) before the dashboard's own key switch; a hit dispatches through the existing command-activation path with ADMIN_ROW_KIND/ADMIN_ROW_ID/ADMIN_ROW_URL, a miss falls through unchanged. StartHostedPTY gained an env parameter to carry them. Verdict PASS, verified_parent 89dfd2a matching the commit's parent, mutation check discriminates. Merge conflicted against 247dd1f in internal/kinds/hostedpty.go and was resolved by keeping both statements (Setsid SysProcAttr plus the env append); go vet also caught three stale 5-arg StartHostedPTY call sites in hostedpty_test.go that the textual auto-merge left behind, fixed with a nil env argument. go build, go vet and go test clean; ./admin-run test 1126 passed with only the pre-existing tests/test_sign.py signing-identity failure.

title: [keys.<row-kind>] parses and validates
description:
admin.toml may carry a top-level [keys.<row-kind>] table per bindable row kind — bead, issue, branch, pr, commit, stash — whose entries map a key name to the name of a command declared in the same manifest:

    [keys.bead]
    enter = "implement"
    o     = "open-bead"

This slice is the manifest frontend: parse the table into a lookup keyed by (row kind, key), validate it, and run the validator from `admin check` alongside the existing workflow validation. Report every problem found in one pass rather than stopping at the first, matching how the workflow and URL validators already behave.

Three rules the validator enforces, all settled in ADR-0018 (docs/adr/0018-row-scoped-key-bindings.md):

- Reserved keys are never bindable: q, ctrl+c, esc, tab, shift+tab, the arrow keys, j, k, 1-4, /.
- The Work tab's own row kinds are not bindable — command, commandTarget, worker.
- Shadowing a built-in is allowed and reported, not blocked.

## The built-in key table moves to internal/keymap (decided; see admin-l6kb.5 and ADR-0018)

Shadow detection needs a (row kind, key) -> human-readable label table. It exists today as Model.keymap() at internal/tui/view.go:634-663, keyed by tab and pane, which corresponds 1:1 to the six bindable row kinds: tabBeads->bead, tabIssues->issue, tabPRs->pr, tabLocal default pane->branch, paneCommits->commit, paneStashes->stash.

internal/validate imports no other internal package today (it is a leaf). Importing internal/tui into it would invert the dependency direction. So this slice extracts that data into a new leaf package internal/keymap, re-keyed by row kind, and rewires Model.keymap() to read it back. Both consumers — this slice's shadow check and the footer merge in admin-l6kb.4 — then import one table.

Do not duplicate the table into internal/validate. Two tables with nothing checking that they agree is the failure this extraction prevents.

Constraint: Model.keymap() must keep returning exactly the pairs it returns today, in the same order, for every tab and pane. internal/tui/model_test.go and design_parity_test.go assert the footer contents and drop behavior and must pass unchanged.

Out of scope: the dashboard reading or acting on the parsed [keys] table (that is admin-l6kb.2). No behavior change in internal/tui — only the rewire of where keymap()'s data comes from.

Repo orientation: the Go binary is the live tool. Manifest parsing lives in internal/manifest, validation in internal/validate, key-name vocabulary in internal/keybindings. `admin check` runs validation.
acceptance_criteria:
- A manifest with `[keys.bead] enter = "implement"`, where `[commands.implement]` exists, passes `admin check`.
- Naming a command that does not exist fails check, and the message names both the binding and the missing command.
- A reserved key fails check, and the message says the key is reserved.
- A row kind that is not bindable — `command`, `commandTarget`, `worker`, or an unknown word — fails check, and the message lists the kinds that are.
- A binding whose key already carries a built-in meaning for that row kind passes, and check prints a shadow line naming what it displaces (e.g. `keys.bead.d shadows the bead detail overlay`).
- Two distinct problems in one manifest are both reported by a single `admin check` run.
- A manifest with no `[keys]` table at all is unaffected in every respect.
close_reason: Landed as 89dfd2a (merge of keys-table-validate, commit 185f08f). Adds internal/keymap as a leaf package holding the built-in key labels keyed by row kind, internal/validate/keys.go for the [keys.<row-kind>] validator, and wires it into admin check; internal/tui/view.go's Model.keymap() now reads the extracted table. Verdict PASS, verified_parent 136a6be matching the commit's parent, mutation check discriminates. go build and go test clean in the worktree and again on the merged result; ./admin-run test 1126 passed with one pre-existing unrelated failure (tests/test_sign.py signing-identity ambiguity, reproduced at 6c8ff7f before the merge).

title: Row-scoped key bindings
description: Let a project declare, in admin.toml, which key does what on a dashboard row — enter included. Design and rejected alternatives in docs/adr/0018-row-scoped-key-bindings.md.

title: The Work tab tick runs the sweep, off by default
description:
Wire the sweep into the running dashboard, off unless a project asks for it.

The `workTickMsg` case in the Work tab's update path calls `Sweep` on each tick — that tick
already exists as the Work tab's only wake source for state changed by goroutines this
process never otherwise hears from, so no new timer is introduced.

`internal/config` gains an `[orchestrator]` table with `enabled` (default **false**) and
`stuck_after`.

The default matters more than the wiring. This feature types text into a running agent with
nobody watching it, so a project that has not asked for it must never get it. `[workflow]`
and its `ceiling` key are the existing precedent for an opt-in table in this config.

## Out of scope

Showing anything about a nudge on screen.
acceptance_criteria:
- With `enabled = false`, or with no `[orchestrator]` table at all, no sweep runs and no
  prompt is ever sent.
- With `enabled = true`, an entry stuck past the threshold is nudged within one tick.
- `stuck_after` overrides the default threshold; an absent value falls back to it.
- `admin check` accepts a well-formed `[orchestrator]` table and reports a malformed one
  (wrong type, unknown key) rather than ignoring it.
- The sweep never blocks the tick: a slow or hanging send cannot freeze the dashboard.

title: internal/orchestrate decides who is stuck and what to send
description:
A new `internal/orchestrate` package holds the whole supervision policy: which entries are
stuck, what gets sent to them, and the bookkeeping that stops one blocked state producing a
stream of prompts.

Shape:

```text
Sweep(registry, memo, send)
  for entry in registry.List()
    if entry.State is not StateWaiting                      -> skip
    if now - entry.StateChangedAt < StuckAfter              -> skip
    if memo already nudged (entry.ID, entry.StateChangedAt) -> skip
    if entry.PaneID is empty                                -> skip
    send(entry.ID, NudgeText)
    memo.record(entry.ID, entry.StateChangedAt)
```

The memo keys on `(ID, StateChangedAt)` rather than ID alone, so one blocked state gets
exactly one nudge while an agent that answers, works, and blocks again gets a fresh one.

`Sweep` takes the registry and the send function as parameters so the package is testable
with neither a TUI nor herdr present.

`NudgeText` is a single canned continuation line — the orchestrator has not read the
question it is answering, so the text has to be safe against every question an agent might
have asked.

A pty-addressed entry (`PTYID` set, `PaneID` empty) is skipped: the send addresses a herdr
agent by name and a pty-hosted entry has none. That gap is tracked separately.

## Out of scope

The TUI wiring, the config table, and anything rendered on screen.
acceptance_criteria:
- An entry that has been `StateWaiting` longer than the threshold is sent exactly one nudge.
- The same entry is not nudged again on the next sweep.
- The same entry, after transitioning away and back into `StateWaiting`, is nudged again.
- Entries in `running`, `exited`, or `failed` are never nudged, however old.
- An entry addressed by `PTYID` is never nudged.
- A send that returns an error does not abort the sweep of the remaining entries.
- Every test runs without a herdr binary and without a TUI.

title: shim.PromptAgent sends a prompt and returns
description:
`internal/shim/agent.go` gains `PromptAgent(name, prompt string) error`, running
`herdr agent prompt <name> <prompt>` with no `--wait`, beside the existing
`PromptAndWait`.

The distinction is the whole point. `PromptAndWait` blocks on purpose — it is the workflow
dispatch's concurrency-ceiling mechanism, and a goroutine holding a ceiling slot must not
return until its agent has actually settled. The orchestrator runs on the Work tab's
1-second UI tick and must never block, so it needs a send that returns as soon as herdr has
accepted the prompt.

## Out of scope

Anything that calls it. This slice adds the capability only.
acceptance_criteria:
- The argv is exactly `herdr agent prompt <name> <prompt>` — no `--wait`.
- Covered by a test using the existing fake-herdr harness, not a real herdr binary.
- A non-zero herdr exit is returned as an error, never swallowed.
- `PromptAndWait`'s behavior is unchanged.

title: livework.Entry records when its state last changed
description:
`livework.Entry` gains a `StateChangedAt time.Time` field recording when the entry last
transitioned. `Add` defaults it alongside `StartedAt`; `SetState` stamps it on every
transition.

This is the orchestrator's only stuck signal (see the resolved interview answers on
admin-16ju.1): a worker is stuck when it has been `StateWaiting` — herdr's "blocked", the
agent settled on a question or an approval prompt — longer than a threshold. Reading
registry state rather than output means the signal works identically for a pane-hosted and
a pty-hosted entry, and does not gate on the unmerged ring buffer in admin-3rgp.61.

It must be correct before anything reads it, which is why it is its own slice.

## Out of scope

Any reader of the field. Nothing consumes `StateChangedAt` in this slice.
acceptance_criteria:
- A `SetState` transition advances `StateChangedAt`.
- A second transition on the same entry advances it again.
- A re-`Add` under an existing ID (the `Retry` path) resets `StateChangedAt` rather than
  carrying the previous entry's stamp forward.
- Every existing `internal/livework` test stays green.

title: beads auto-export intermittently stops firing, so the committed issues.jsonl diverges from the DB
description:
## Category

bug

## Summary

`bd`'s auto-export to `.beads/issues.jsonl` stops firing partway through a session. The Dolt DB stays correct; the committed export silently goes stale.

## Observed

2026-08-31, during an orchestrate run. `bd close admin-3rgp.60` printed `Exported 570 issues to .../issues.jsonl` and the export was current. Later in the same session `bd update admin-3rgp.61 --add-label hitl` and `bd comment admin-3rgp.61` both reported success, but printed no export line and left `issues.jsonl` untouched.

The divergence: `bd show admin-3rgp.61` reported `LABELS: hitl` while the committed `issues.jsonl` still carried `["afk"]` for the same issue. Committing at that moment would have published — and did, until caught — a label set that contradicted the tracker.

Once earlier in the same session an export was also skipped with a visible cause: `Error: auto-export: git add failed: git index is locked at .../.git/index.lock; skipping auto-stage`. That one at least announced itself. The later skips announced nothing.

## Why it matters

`.beads/issues.jsonl` is the passive export, but it is the committed artifact — a fresh clone, and anyone reading the repo without a Dolt DB, sees only the jsonl. A silent divergence means the tracker state in git is wrong with no signal, and the next commit bakes it in.

It also defeats review: a bead edit that produces no diff looks like a no-op change rather than a failed export.

## Workaround in use

`bd export > /tmp/fresh.jsonl && cp /tmp/fresh.jsonl .beads/issues.jsonl`, then diff before committing. `bd export` writes to stdout, not to the file, so it cannot be used as a plain refresh command.

## Desired behavior

Either the auto-export runs for every mutation, or a mutation whose export was skipped says so on stderr the way the index-lock case does. A silent skip is the failure.

Separately, a first-class "rewrite the export file now" command would make the workaround unnecessary — `bd export` writing to stdout means every caller reinvents the redirect.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A mutation whose auto-export does not run reports that on stderr, naming the reason.
- [ ] After any sequence of mutations, `.beads/issues.jsonl` matches the DB, or the divergence was announced.
- [ ] There is a documented single command that refreshes the export file in place.
acceptance_criteria: A mutation whose auto-export does not run says so on stderr with the reason. After any sequence of mutations the committed issues.jsonl matches the DB or the divergence was announced. A documented single command refreshes the export in place.

title: Work tab detail pane shows a running command's log, elapsed and pinned URLs
description:
## Category

enhancement

## Summary

The Work tab's detail pane shows a running command's log path, how long it has been running, and its configured pinned URLs with a reachability indicator.

## Current behavior

The pinned-footer feature is documented in CLAUDE.md and implemented in `internal/frame`: a framed action runs inside a DECSTBM scroll region with a status row (action label + elapsed), the absolute log path, then one row per URL, every row an OSC 8 hyperlink. `[urls]` in `admin.toml` names them; `frame.validate_url_refs` (called from archetype resolve) rejects an entry that is neither a key of `[urls]` nor a real URL. Per-target overrides ride on `meta["target_urls"]`, and `footer = true` raises a frame for an action with no URL at all.

That is the footer. The Work tab's detail pane is a different surface and carries almost none of it. `internal/tui/workview.go:233-234` renders `wd.logPath` and nothing else from this family — no elapsed, no URLs.

So the information exists, is configured per project, and is visible only while you are looking at the framed action's own terminal. Selecting that command in the dashboard tells you much less than the footer does.

## Why it matters

Many projects configure these. The dashboard is meant to be the place you look at what is running; a detail pane that omits the URLs and the elapsed time sends you back to the framed terminal to read what the dashboard already knows.

## Desired behavior

With a running command highlighted on the Work tab, the detail pane shows:

- **log** — the absolute log path, as it does today, and it is the path actually being written rather than a glob result.
- **elapsed** — how long the command has been running, updating while the pane is open.
- **urls** — one row per configured URL for that command, resolved through the same `[urls]` table and per-target inheritance the footer uses, each with an indicator of whether it is currently reachable.

An idle command shows whatever of these is meaningful and omits the rest; it does not show a stale elapsed or a reachability state for a URL nothing is serving.

URL resolution reuses the footer's existing path — the same table, the same `${VAR}` expansion through `resolve_computed` then `resolve_env`, the same per-target inheritance rules. No second URL resolver is introduced.

## Key interfaces

- `internal/tui/workview.go:233` — the detail pane's body, which gains the elapsed and URL rows.
- `internal/frame` — the existing URL resolution and label handling, reused rather than reimplemented.
- The live-work entry, which carries the start time the elapsed value is computed from and the real log path.
- Whatever performs the reachability probe, which must not block the render.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A running command's detail pane shows its absolute log path, taken from the live entry rather than a filesystem glob.
- [ ] It shows elapsed time, which advances while the pane stays open.
- [ ] It shows one row per URL configured for that command, with the label from `[urls]` where the entry names a key and the bare URL where it does not.
- [ ] Per-target URL inheritance matches the footer's: `None` inherits the parent, an explicit list replaces it, and an empty list shows no URL rows.
- [ ] `${VAR}` in a URL is expanded, so a computed value such as `${LAN_IP}` renders resolved.
- [ ] Each URL row carries a reachability indicator, and an unreachable or unprobed URL is visually distinct from a reachable one.
- [ ] The reachability probe never blocks rendering — a hung host leaves the pane responsive and the row in its unprobed state.
- [ ] An idle command shows no elapsed and no reachability state.
- [ ] Asserted through the dashboard's headless frame renderer.

## Out of scope

- Changing the pinned footer itself, which stays exactly as it is. This slice reads the same configuration onto a second surface.
- The where-column and per-row live status, which is admin-3rgp.64.
- Making URLs clickable in the detail pane. OSC 8 in the footer is unaffected either way.
acceptance_criteria: A running command's detail pane shows its absolute log path from the live entry, an advancing elapsed time, and one row per configured URL with label and reachability indicator. Per-target URL inheritance matches the footer's. ${VAR} is expanded. The probe never blocks rendering. An idle command shows no elapsed and no reachability. Asserted through the headless frame renderer.

title: Announce the log file path at the start of every command, not only at the end
description:
## Category

enhancement

## Summary

Announce the log file path at the start of every command as well as at the end, so it can be copied and handed to an agent while the command is still running.

## Current behavior

The log path is printed when a command finishes. A framed action also pins it in the footer for its duration (`internal/frame`), but a command that is not framed — no `urls`, no `footer = true` — prints nothing until it exits.

## Why it matters

The stated use is: start a long command, immediately point an agent at its log, and let both proceed. That requires the path on screen at the beginning. Waiting for the end inverts it — by the time the path appears, the run whose output you wanted watched is over.

It also matters for a command that never terminates cleanly. A dev loop killed with ctrl-c may never reach its closing announcement, so the only place its path was ever printed is a line that never ran.

## Desired behavior

Every command prints its log file path once when it starts, before any step output, and once when it finishes, as it does today.

The path is absolute, on its own line, and unprefixed by any level word or scope tag, so it can be selected and pasted without editing.

Printing the path at the start is also what materializes it, matching the Python contract that asking for the path settles the name (`admin_lib/core.py:214`).

## Key interfaces

- The command dispatch entry point, where the opening announcement goes.
- The existing closing announcement, unchanged.
- `internal/frame`'s pinned log-path row, which stays as it is — the opening line is for the unframed case and for scrollback.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Running any command prints its absolute log path once before the first step's output.
- [ ] The same path is printed at the end, as today.
- [ ] The opening line is the path alone — no level word, no scope tag, no surrounding punctuation.
- [ ] The announced path is the file actually written, asserted by stat-ing it after the run.
- [ ] A framed command still pins the path in its footer, and the opening line does not duplicate into the footer region.
- [ ] A command interrupted before completion has still printed its path.
- [ ] Piped (non-TTY) output includes the opening line.

## Out of scope

- The footer's own log-path row.
- `admin logs`, which reads a path rather than announcing one.

## Blocked by

The log file being created for every command in the first place.
acceptance_criteria: Every command prints its absolute log path once before the first step's output and once at the end. The opening line is the path alone, no level word or scope tag. The announced path is the file actually written. A framed command still pins the path in its footer without duplicating it. An interrupted command has still printed its path. Non-TTY output includes the opening line.
