title: verify-project covers only the Python interpreter, not the Go binary that ships
description:
## Current behavior

`.claude/skills/verify-project/SKILL.md` is 124 lines and mentions `kinds`, `dispatch`, `pane` and `herdr` zero times. It exercises the Python interpreter from source without disturbing `~/.admin`.

But `admin` on PATH is the Go binary (CLAUDE.md: "admin-py is the outgoing Python one"). Everything a change to `internal/` affects is outside what the skill knows how to verify.

## Why it matters

CLAUDE.md's Finishing work section says every project keeps a `verify-project` skill and to "keep editing it as features land so each one's verification path and surface is in there." Go features have been landing into a skill that describes the Python half.

The concrete gap this was filed from: after admin-3rgp.59 there are two command-dispatch entry points that deliberately land on different surfaces — `RunCommand` opens a herdr pane for a LongRunning kind, `RunCommandHosted` never can. Nothing in the skill tells the next session how to check which surface a dispatch took, or that checking is required.

## Desired behavior

The skill covers both halves, and names the Go surface explicitly:

- How to build and exercise the Go binary from source without overwriting `~/.admin/admin` (or that `bash install.sh` is the intended path and the installed copy IS what to verify — CLAUDE.local.md says reinstall after every tool edit).
- Which entry point a given producer uses, and how to observe the surface a dispatch landed on.
- That `go test ./...` plus `./admin-run test` are both required, and that the shell suite chains after pytest.

## Out of scope

Rewriting the Python half. It is still accurate for what it covers.
acceptance_criteria: verify-project names the Go binary as the shipping surface, gives a build-and-exercise path for it that does not silently verify a stale ~/.admin copy, and tells a session how to confirm which dispatch surface a command landed on.

title: currentSurface is a process-wide singleton — two overlapping dispatches clobber each other
description:
## Parent

admin-3rgp

## Category

bug

## Summary

The nested-dispatch surface lives in a package-level var, so two overlapping dispatches in one process clobber each other. Thread it through `Factory` as an explicit parameter and delete the var.

## Current behavior

`internal/kinds/dispatch.go:126` parks the nested-dispatch surface in a package-level var:

    var currentSurface *dispatchSurface

`RunAction` sets it at `internal/kinds/dispatch.go:225-230`, after the Runner is built, and restores the previous value in a `defer`. A Runner reaches it through `dispatchNested` (`dispatch.go:134`) and `dispatchNestedCommand` (`dispatch.go:146`), and `internal/kinds/multitarget.go:293-299` reads it directly.

Five call sites depend on it today:

- `internal/kinds/interactiveshell.go:119` and `:190` — the keybinding hooks
- `internal/kinds/docker.go:89`, `internal/kinds/vitedev.go:453`, `internal/kinds/cleandev.go:268` — the pre-kill hop

This is safe today because one process runs one dev loop at a time — the same assumption `admin_lib/reload.py` and `frame.activate` already make.

## Why it stops being safe

admin-3rgp.61 breaks that assumption on purpose: the dashboard stays up and hosts commands on its own pty. Two hosted commands can then overlap in one process. The second command's `RunAction` overwrites `currentSurface` for the remainder of the first command's run, so the first's nested delegation dispatches against the second's manifest and registry — and the save/restore is LIFO, so whichever finishes first restores a surface the other is still using.

Nothing errors. A multi-target target delegating to `action = "other"` simply runs the wrong project's action, or fails with "not declared in [actions]" naming an action the user never invoked.

## Desired behavior

The surface travels with the call. Two concurrent dispatches cannot see each other's, because neither reads shared state.

**Decided: thread a dispatch handle through `Factory`. `Runner`'s signature does not change.**

This is possible because the surface is fully determined before the Runner is built. `dispatch.go:226-229` constructs it from `m`, `r` and `nested`, all of which are in scope at `dispatch.go:220` where `factory(...)` is called. So it is built one line earlier and passed in, and each Runner closes over the surface belonging to its own dispatch.

### The signature change

```diff
-type Factory func(name string, action manifest.Action, m *manifest.Manifest) (Runner, error)
+type Factory func(name string, action manifest.Action, m *manifest.Manifest, surf *Surface) (Runner, error)

 type Runner func(args []string) error
```

`dispatchSurface` is exported as `Surface` because it now crosses the factory boundary. Its two fields keep their meaning and stay unexported.

### The dispatch path

```diff
 RunAction(m, r, name, action, args)
   guards.Register / RunRequires
   factory, ok := r.Lookup(kind)
+  surf := &Surface{
+    action:  func(n, a) { return nested(m, r, n, a) },
+    command: func(n, a) { return runSteps(m, r, n, a, nested) },
+  }
-  runner, err := factory(name, action, m)
+  runner, err := factory(name, action, m, surf)
-  prev := currentSurface
-  currentSurface = &dispatchSurface{...}
-  defer func() { currentSurface = prev }()
   return runner(args)
```

The save/restore pair disappears with the var — there is nothing global to restore.

### The nested helpers become methods

```diff
-func dispatchNested(name string, args []string) error {
-  if currentSurface == nil { return fmt.Errorf(...) }
-  return currentSurface.action(name, args)
-}
+func (s *Surface) Action(name string, args []string) error {
+  if s == nil { return fmt.Errorf(...) }
+  return s.action(name, args)
+}
```

`dispatchNestedCommand` becomes `(*Surface).Command` the same way. Both keep their existing error text verbatim — a Runner invoked outside any dispatch still gets a nil surface, and the message that names `kinds.RunAction/RunCommand` is still the right one.

## Key interfaces

- `internal/kinds/registry.go:39` — `Factory` gains the `surf *Surface` parameter.
- `internal/kinds/registry.go:13` — `Runner` is unchanged. Nothing that calls a Runner changes.
- `internal/kinds/dispatch.go:119` — `dispatchSurface` is exported as `Surface`; its fields stay unexported.
- `internal/kinds/dispatch.go:126` — the var is deleted.
- All 32 factory constructions in `internal/kinds/` gain the parameter. Most ignore it as `_`; the five call sites listed above and `multitarget.go:293` use it.

## Rejected, with reasons

- **Key the var per goroutine.** Trades one global for a different one — the condition that lets two dispatches collide still exists, it is only harder to hit. It also breaks the moment a Runner delegates from a goroutine it spawned itself.
- **Thread `context.Context` through `Runner` as well.** Would change all 32 Runner signatures and every Runner call site, and buys nothing here: the surface is fixed for the whole life of a Runner and is already known when the Runner is built, so it is a construction-time dependency rather than a per-call one. If cancellation is wanted later, that is its own change with its own reason.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `internal/kinds` contains no package-level mutable dispatch state; `var currentSurface` is gone.
- [ ] Two `RunAction` calls running concurrently in one process each resolve nested delegation against their own manifest and registry, asserted with two manifests declaring the same action name with different bodies and a barrier holding both mid-run.
- [ ] A multi-target target delegating with `action = "other"` under one of those two concurrent dispatches resolves against its own command's manifest, with the other still mid-run.
- [ ] Invoking a factory's Runner directly, outside any dispatch, still returns the existing error naming `kinds.RunAction/RunCommand`, with its text unchanged.
- [ ] `Runner`'s signature is unchanged, asserted by the absence of any edit to Runner call sites in the diff.
- [ ] `go build ./...` and `go test ./...` pass.

## Out of scope

- Cancellation or deadline propagation through dispatch. Separate concern, separate ticket.
- Any change to `admin_lib/reload.py` or `frame.activate`, which make the same one-loop-per-process assumption for their own reasons.
- The hosted-pty dashboard itself — that is admin-3rgp.61.

## Blocked by

Nothing. It only *matters* once admin-3rgp.61 lands, but doing it first is cheaper than doing it after the dashboard depends on the current shape.
acceptance_criteria: internal/kinds contains no package-level mutable dispatch state; var currentSurface is gone. Two RunAction calls running concurrently in one process each resolve nested delegation against their own manifest and registry, asserted with two manifests declaring the same action name with different bodies and a barrier holding both mid-run. A multi-target target delegating with action = "other" under one of them resolves against its own command's manifest with the other mid-run. Invoking a factory's Runner directly outside any dispatch still returns the existing error naming kinds.RunAction/RunCommand, text unchanged. Runner's signature is unchanged. go build ./... and go test ./... pass.
close_reason: Factory now takes an explicit *Surface; var currentSurface deleted. Runner's signature unchanged. Merged as f72af0d (commit 8df2663), verdict PASS with a discriminating mutation check and two new concurrency tests.

comments.author: pierce
comments.text:
Failed the /orchestrate dispatch gate on 2026-08-31 and was not dispatched. The body's "Design options (not settled)" section offers two paths — thread a context/dispatch handle through Factory/Runner, or key the var per goroutine — with no pick, and states plainly that "changing that is the design question, not a patch." That is an objectivity-test failure: an agent would have to invent the answer.

Labelled hitl. Needs an iron-out pass to settle the Factory/Runner signature before it can be dispatched.

title: Sort the tracker list with a cycle key on s
description:
## Category

enhancement

## Summary

Sort the tracker list (Beads + Issues tabs) with a single cycle key bound to `s`.

## Current behavior

The tracker tab renders its issues in one fixed order — whatever `bd` returned. `internal/tui/beads.go` never sorts. No key in `internal/tui/` binds a sort. With a backlog in the hundreds, finding the thing you touched this morning, or the oldest thing still open, means reading the whole list.

## Desired behavior

`s` cycles the tracker list through the orders, wrapping at the end. The active order is named in the header so it is readable without opening anything. Orders:

- last modified
- oldest first
- newest first
- most dependencies first — the closest thing to "what unblocks the most"
- by type (task, bug, feature, epic)

The chosen order persists while the dashboard is open and resets on restart.

## Decided design — cycle key, not a spike

The three-design comparison this ticket originally called for is dropped. One key, no permanent row: the tracker footer at `internal/tui/view.go:645` and `:648` already drops hints at narrow widths (see `internal/tui/design_parity_test.go:108`), so a persistent sort bar would make that worse. `s` joins the existing footer hint list.

## Key interfaces

- A comparator per order, selected by the current sort state.
- The tracker tab's row-building path, which applies it before windowing.
- Session-scoped state on `Model` holding the active order.

## Acceptance criteria

[ ] `s` on the Beads tab and on the Issues tab cycles the orders and wraps.
[ ] Each of the five orders produces the documented ordering, asserted on a fixture with known dates, dependency counts and types.
[ ] Sorting is stable: two items equal under the active order keep their relative order.
[ ] The active order is named in the rendered header without opening anything.
[ ] The order persists while the dashboard is open and resets on restart.
[ ] An empty list and a single-item list render correctly under every order.
[ ] `s` appears in the tracker footer hints.
[ ] Asserted through the dashboard's headless frame renderer.

## Out of scope

- Persisting the chosen order across restarts.
- Text search or filtering by anything other than type — filtering already exists (`/`).
- Sorting any list other than the tracker's. The Repo tab groups by section on purpose (`internal/tui/branchespane.go:106`).
- A sort bar or an overlay picker.
acceptance_criteria: `s` cycles the tracker list through five orders and wraps. Each order produces the documented ordering on a fixture with known dates, dependency counts and types. Sorting is stable. The active order is named in the rendered header. The order persists while the dashboard is open and resets on restart. Empty and single-item lists render under every order. `s` appears in the tracker footer hints. Asserted through the headless frame renderer.
close_reason: s cycles the Beads/Issues tracker through five stable orders, named in the header; merged and pushed to main

title: No collapse key for an open Work-tab submenu — only enter on the parent
description:
## Summary

A multi-target command's submenu on the Work tab opens and closes only with enter on the parent row. From a target row there is no way to close it, and there is no way to open one with an arrow key at all. The prototype specifies both.

## Current behavior

`internal/tui/work.go:642-649` toggles the submenu on enter on the parent row, and that is the only binding that touches it. `internal/tui/model.go:1657` routes `rowCommandTarget` for enter only.

The reason a collapse key is missing is not an oversight in the row handler — it is a collision with tab navigation. `internal/tui/model.go:1405-1411`:

    case "right", "l":
        m.filter = ""
        m.stepTab(1)
    case "left", "h":
        m.filter = ""
        m.stepTab(-1)

Left and right switch the top-level tab unconditionally, before any row-kind routing. So pressing left with the cursor on a target row does not do nothing — it leaves the Work tab entirely. Any fix has to carve the Work tab's collapsible rows out of that path without breaking tab navigation everywhere else.

## Reference frame

`docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/commands-targets-open.txt` — the settled Work tab with `build`'s submenu open and the cursor on the `ios` target row. Two things it fixes:

- The keybar reads `↑↓ move · ↵ run or open · →← submenu · k kill · q/esc quit`. Arrows own the submenu, and the hint says so.
- The detail pane for the selected target row reads `↵ run   ← collapse`.

The parent row renders `▾` when expanded (`◇ ▾ build`) and target rows render `├`/`└`.

## Desired behavior — decided

On the Work tab, left and right act on the submenu when the cursor is on a row that has one, and fall through to tab-switching otherwise. Precisely:

- **right** on a collapsed parent row (a command with targets) expands it. On any other row, it switches tab as it does today.
- **left** on an expanded parent row collapses it. On a target row it collapses the parent and moves the cursor to that parent row, so the cursor never lands on a row that no longer exists. On any other row it switches tab as it does today.
- **esc** collapses from the parent row or any of its target rows, cursor to the parent, same as left.
- enter keeps its current meaning everywhere: toggle on the parent, run on a target.

`h` and `l` stay pure tab-switching on every row. Only the arrow keys and esc gain the submenu meaning, so a user who navigates tabs with `h`/`l` is unaffected.

## Key interfaces

- `internal/tui/model.go:1405-1411` — the left/right case gains a Work-tab check before `stepTab`.
- `internal/tui/model.go:1657` — `rowCommandTarget` routing gains left and esc.
- `internal/tui/work.go` — the collapse helper that clears `Model.expandedCmd` and repositions the cursor onto the parent row.
- `internal/tui/view.go` — the Work tab keybar gains the `→←  submenu` hint, matching the prototype.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Right on a collapsed command row with targets expands its submenu and does not change tab.
- [ ] Left on an expanded parent row collapses it and does not change tab.
- [ ] Left on a target row collapses the submenu and leaves the cursor on the parent row.
- [ ] Esc from a target row does the same as left.
- [ ] Left or right on a row with no submenu — a plain command, a worker row, a section header — still switches tab exactly as today.
- [ ] Left or right on every other tab still switches tab exactly as today.
- [ ] `h` and `l` still switch tab on every row, including target rows.
- [ ] The Work tab keybar shows the submenu hint.
- [ ] Enter behaviour is unchanged: toggle on the parent, run on a target.
- [ ] Asserted through the dashboard's headless frame renderer.

## Out of scope

- The running-command shortcircuit that prevents opening a submenu at all once one target is live. That is admin-3rlr.
- The badge count changing when a submenu opens. That is admin-4s8d.
acceptance_criteria: Right on a collapsed command row with targets expands its submenu without changing tab. Left on an expanded parent collapses it without changing tab. Left on a target row collapses and leaves the cursor on the parent. Esc from a target row behaves as left. Left/right on a row with no submenu, and on every other tab, still switches tab as today. h and l still switch tab on every row. The Work tab keybar shows the submenu hint. Enter is unchanged. Asserted through the headless frame renderer.
close_reason: landed fe3322b: arrow-key open/close for the Work-tab submenu

Observed: with 'dev mac' running, enter on the 'dev' row attaches to the mac pane; 'dev ios' is unreachable from the TUI. internal/tui/work.go:639 — 'if wd.live != nil { return m.attachEntry(wd.live) }' sits above the 'len(wd.targets) > 0' toggle added in f11c4ae.

title: Terminal view over a hosted pty
description:
## Parent

admin-3rgp

## Category

enhancement

## Summary

Read and drive a hosted process's output inside the dashboard, via a terminal emulator over its pseudo-terminal.

## Current behavior

A command dispatched from the dashboard runs on a pty the dashboard owns, and its output goes to a log file. There is no way to see that output without leaving the dashboard and opening the log, and no way to answer a process that is prompting — which is the state a multi-target command reaches immediately.

The live-work registry can already address a pty-backed entry and route its attach operation here, but the destination does not exist.

## Desired behavior

Attaching to a live command row opens a terminal view over that process's pty, occupying the whole tab.

The view renders the child's bytes through a terminal emulator, so everything the child emits works: colour, cursor positioning, and the pinned footer the child writes into its own pty. That footer is why no second footer implementation is introduced — from the child's point of view the pty is its terminal, and the emulator interprets what it writes there.

Keystrokes reach the child, so a prompt can be answered and a reload keybinding can be pressed.

Detaching returns to the list with the process still running. `q` and `esc` both detach; from the list, either raises the quit confirm. Two presses to leave a process you are watching, whichever key you reach for.

Before the child writes anything the view says so rather than showing an empty rectangle.

Output produced before attaching is not replayed — the log file holds it.

## Key interfaces

- A terminal-emulator dependency interpreting the child's byte stream into a renderable grid. Choosing it is part of this slice; at least two candidates resolve as Go modules, one in a module family this repo already vendors.
- The view is entered from a live row's attach operation and exited by a key, with the process's lifetime unaffected by either.
- Key events route to the child while attached, and to the dashboard otherwise.
- The pty is sized to the view's own area, and resized with it.

## Visual acceptance

See the design field.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Attaching to a running command shows its output; detaching returns to the list with the process still running.
- [ ] A keystroke typed while attached reaches the child — verified by answering a process that is prompting and observing it proceed.
- [ ] A command declaring `urls` or `footer` shows its pinned footer inside the view.
- [ ] The footer is never pushed off the bottom by output volume.
- [ ] Before any output arrives the view renders the copy `waiting for output…`.
- [ ] `q` and `esc` both detach while attached, and both raise the quit confirm from the list.
- [ ] Resizing the terminal resizes the child's pty.
- [ ] Log lines keep the level colouring the existing formatter produces.
- [ ] Asserted through the dashboard's headless frame renderer.

## Out of scope

- Replaying output produced before attaching. The log file holds it.
- Retry. Removed from the design deliberately.
- Attaching to a detached pane-backed entry — that focuses its pane, unchanged.
- Scrollback beyond what the emulator holds.

## Blocked by

The live-work registry's pty address, and the dashboard's hosted-pty dispatch.
design:
**Reference frames:**

- docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/hosted.txt — attached, output streaming.
- docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/hosted-empty.txt — attached, nothing written yet.
- docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/commands.txt — the list this is entered from and returns to.

**States**, by name:

- attached-empty — attached before the child has written anything. Header, rule, then the copy waiting for output… and nothing else.
- attached — header, rule, output, then the child's own pinned footer.

**Full width is the decision, not a default.** The terminal view takes the whole tab, not the right-hand detail pane. At a third of the screen every log line dies at 14:22:09 [INFO] test: ======…, which is unreadable — that was measured in the spike, not assumed.

**Header** — one line: the state glyph, the command name, the state word, elapsed, then the current activity. It must agree with the output below it; a header reading running above output that ends on a prompt is a bug.

**Output** — the child's bytes, rendered by a terminal emulator. Log lines keep the level colouring the log formatter already uses: [ERROR] red, [WARN] yellow, [INFO] cyan, [DEBUG] dim, the scope tag its own hue, the clock dim.

**The emulator is github.com/charmbracelet/x/vt, added as a direct dependency.** Decided 2026-08-31. Pin the pseudo-version at the time of implementation; `v0.0.0-20260830003929-9f48cc723c1c` was latest when this was decided.

- It is the same family as bubbletea, lipgloss, x/ansi and x/term, all already direct deps in go.mod, and it builds on x/cellbuf which is already in the tree as an indirect dep.
- It supplies the screen model this ticket's acceptance criteria require: a scrollback for the ↑↓ scroll binding, and reserved rows so the pinned footer cannot be pushed off by output volume.
- ADR-0001 (stdlib only) does not apply. It governs the Python generator and the generated ./admin script; the Go binary already carries 13 direct dependencies. No ADR is needed for this.
- Accepted cost: the module is untagged, so it moves by pseudo-version and its API can change between updates.

**Rejected, with reasons** — recorded so this is not re-litigated:

- github.com/hinshun/vt10x — independent of the Charm stack, so a Charm API break would not reach it, but its latest is v0.0.0-20220301184237 (2022-03-01) and it is untagged too. It would add a second, stale dependency family alongside the one this repo already maintains.
- No emulator, writing the child's bytes straight through the way internal/tui/frame.go already does — the pty is already sized to the scroll region for cursor-positioning children (wrangler, vite, metro). Rejected because it fails this ticket's own acceptance: with no screen model there is nothing to scroll, so ↑↓ scroll has no backing, and "the footer is never pushed off by output volume" cannot be asserted. Taking it would mean rewriting those two criteria, not just swapping a library.

**The child's pinned footer renders inside this view.** It is the child's own output written into the pty, not dashboard chrome — that is what keeps one footer implementation instead of two. It must never be pushed off the bottom by output: reserve its rows and let the output scroll.

**Keys** — q and esc are the same key at two depths. Attached, either detaches and the process keeps running. In the list, either raises the quit confirm. So leaving a process you are watching is two presses of whichever key your hands reach for, and neither can kill a dev loop by reflex from inside its own output.

**Copy** — verbatim: waiting for output…, and the footer q/esc detach · ↑↓ scroll · k kill · typing goes to the process.

**No retry.** Removed deliberately: restarting a live thing under the same identity is not something every producer can honour or every kind of work can survive.
acceptance_criteria: Attaching shows output; detaching returns to the list with the process still running. A keystroke reaches the child, verified by answering a prompting process. A command declaring urls or footer shows its pinned footer inside the view. The footer is never pushed off by output volume. Before output the view renders 'waiting for output…'. q and esc both detach while attached and both raise the quit confirm from the list. Resizing the terminal resizes the child's pty. Log lines keep the existing level colouring. Asserted through the headless frame renderer.

title: Live status and where-column on every command row
description:
## Parent

admin-3rgp

## Category

enhancement

## Summary

Show each live command's state, activity and where it is running on its own row, so the Commands list reads as a lightweight orchestration view.

## Current behavior

A command row with a live entry already folds that entry in and shows its state and activity. But the location column prints the entry's pane id unconditionally — and once the dashboard hosts processes on its own pseudo-terminals, most live rows have no pane at all. The column then either prints an empty string or, worse, a pane id belonging to something else.

There is no way to tell from the list whether a running thing is a child of this dashboard (dies on quit, output readable in-app) or a detached session (outlives the dashboard, reachable only by focusing it). Those two have different verbs and different lifetimes, so confusing them gets a dev loop killed by reflex or an agent session abandoned.

## Desired behavior

Every live row shows its state, its current activity, and one right-aligned value saying where it runs: the literal word `hosted` for a child process on a pty this dashboard owns, or the pane identifier for a detached session. Never a pane id for a hosted process; never `hosted` for a detached one.

The activity string absorbs all truncation. The where-value is never truncated, because a half-printed pane id reads as a different pane.

The detail pane spells out the consequence rather than repeating the word: a hosted entry says it dies when the dashboard quits, a detached one says it outlives it.

An idle command row is unchanged.

## Key interfaces

- The live-work entry distinguishes a hosted child from a pane-backed entry; the row renderer reads that rather than inferring from a possibly-empty pane field.
- The row renderer's column budget: name, then state, then activity, then the where-value right-aligned.
- The detail pane's location line for both entry shapes.

## Visual acceptance

See the design field.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A hosted running command renders `running`, its activity, and `hosted`.
- [ ] A detached worker renders its state, its activity, and its pane identifier.
- [ ] A hosted row never renders a pane identifier, asserted directly.
- [ ] A detached row never renders the word `hosted`, asserted directly.
- [ ] A long activity truncates with an ellipsis while the where-value stays whole.
- [ ] An idle command row is byte-identical to today's.
- [ ] Each state's word appears as written: `running`, `waiting`, `failed`.
- [ ] Asserted through the dashboard's headless frame renderer at more than one width.

## Out of scope

- The terminal view that reads a hosted process's output. Separate slice.
- Re-grouping the list by hosted-ness. Rejected in the spike — see the design field.
- Any change to how an idle command row renders.

## Blocked by

The dashboard's hosted-pty dispatch.
design:
**Reference frame:** `docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/commands.txt` — the settled Work tab. Also `hosted-quit.txt` for the confirm that reads the same column.

**States** — every one a row must handle, by name:

- `idle` — no live entry. Row is: marker, name, kind, description. Unchanged from today.
- `running` — state word `running`, activity, and the where-column.
- `waiting` — state word `waiting`. The activity is the child's own prompt, verbatim.
- `failed` — state word `failed`, activity is the failure line.
- `exited` — the entry is gone; the row returns to `idle`.

**The where-column** is the decision this frame settles, and it replaces a column that was lying. Two values only:

- `hosted` — a child process on a pty this dashboard owns. Dies when the dashboard quits. Its output opens in-app.
- `<pane id>` (e.g. `pane 3`) — a detached herdr session. Outlives the dashboard. Reachable only by focusing that pane.

A hosted row must never render a pane id, and a detached row must never render `hosted`. Before this change every live row printed `pane N` regardless, which was false for every admin command.

**Copy** — verbatim: `running`, `waiting`, `failed`, `hosted`. Lower case, no punctuation, no colour-only meaning.

**Layout** — state word in a 9-wide column after the 16-wide name column; activity fills the remainder; the where-value is right-aligned against the divider. The activity truncates with `…` before the where-value is touched: the where-value never truncates, because a half-printed pane id reads as a different pane.

**Colour** — semantic roles from `internal/tui/styles.go`, never hex: running green, waiting yellow, failed red, exited/dim grey, `hosted` cyan, a pane id magenta. Every state also differs by its word, so a retheme cannot destroy the meaning.

**Rejected, with reasons** — recorded so this is not re-litigated:
- A leading glyph (`⇱` ours / `⇲` elsewhere) costs one column instead of six but makes the reader learn two symbols for a distinction that changes what a key does.
- Grouping the list into "running here" and "detached panes" cannot work: a hosted process is folded INTO its command's row, so the commands group cannot be titled by running-ness without lying about the idle rows in it.
acceptance_criteria: A hosted running command renders running, its activity, and 'hosted'. A detached worker renders its state, activity and pane identifier. A hosted row never renders a pane identifier. A detached row never renders 'hosted'. A long activity truncates with an ellipsis while the where-value stays whole. An idle command row is byte-identical to today. State words appear verbatim: running, waiting, failed. Asserted through the headless frame renderer at more than one width.
close_reason: Landed as 247dd1f. Live rows now render a where-column: 'hosted' for a child on a dashboard-owned pty, the pane id for a detached session, decided from the livework entry's PTYID/PaneID rather than inferred from an empty pane field. PASS with a discriminating mutation check; build and full go test clean on the merged result.

title: admin check does not reserve every cmd/ verb — a manifest command named archetypes is silently shadowed
description: cmd/manifest.go:39 lists reservedCmdVerbs = branch, prs, populate, help, completion. The verb 'archetypes' (cmd/archetypes.go) appears in neither reservedCmdVerbs nor reservedToolVerbs, so a manifest declaring [commands.archetypes] passes admin check and is then shadowed at dispatch by the tool verb, which wins in dispatchArgs' rootCmd.Commands() loop. Before ADR-0014 this was harmless (a shadowed name fell through to branch shorthand, which also ignored the manifest); now it means a declared command that never runs and never warns. ADR-0011's own comment at cmd/manifest.go:36 already names widening the list as a legitimate follow-up. Fix: derive reservedCmdVerbs from rootCmd.Commands() rather than a literal list, so a new cmd/ verb cannot drift out of the check.

title: Quitting the dashboard confirms before killing hosted processes
description:
## Parent

admin-3rgp

## Category

enhancement

## Summary

Confirm before quitting the dashboard while it is hosting running processes, then kill them.

## Current behavior

Quitting the dashboard exits immediately. Nothing it started is hosted by it today — a long-running Kind dispatched from the dashboard opens a Herdr pane, which outlives the dashboard by design — so there has never been anything to warn about.

Once the dashboard hosts processes on its own pseudo-terminals, quitting kills them silently. A dev server started from the dashboard would die on a reflex keypress with no warning.

## Desired behavior

The dashboard owns the lifetime of what it hosts. This is deliberate: the live-work registry is in-memory and process-scoped by contract, and a hosted process outliving its only watcher is an orphan holding a port that nothing will clean up. Anything meant to outlive the dashboard is dispatched from a plain shell instead, where the lifetime-aware router opens a pane.

So quit becomes a confirmed kill:

- Quitting with no hosted process running exits immediately, exactly as now.
- Quitting with one or more hosted processes running opens a confirm listing them by name and state.
- Accepting kills every listed process, then exits.
- Cancelling returns to the dashboard with everything still running.

Agent workers and pane-backed entries are not listed and are not killed — they run in their own panes and outlive the dashboard on purpose.

## Key interfaces

- The dashboard's quit handling gains a precondition: hosted entries in a running state.
- The confirm follows the repo's existing confirm-overlay pattern — the workflow-confirm overlay and the delete modal are the prior art, and this reuses their shape rather than introducing a new one.
- Accepting invokes each listed entry's kill operation, then proceeds with the existing quit path.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Quitting with no hosted processes running exits immediately, with no confirm.
- [ ] Quitting with hosted processes running opens a confirm listing each by name.
- [ ] The confirm lists only hosted processes — agent workers and pane-backed entries do not appear.
- [ ] Accepting kills every listed process and then exits.
- [ ] Cancelling returns to the dashboard with every process still running and still listed as running.
- [ ] Asserted through the dashboard's headless frame renderer: a frame taken after the quit key with a hosted process running shows the confirm and its process names.

## Out of scope

- Handing a running hosted process off to a Herdr pane instead of killing it. That requires re-parenting a live pty, which this design deliberately does not do.
- Persisting or re-adopting hosted processes across dashboard restarts.
- What happens when the dashboard crashes rather than quits — a crash cannot run a confirm, and the resulting orphans are recovered with the existing port-nuking Kinds.

## Blocked by

The dashboard's hosted-pty dispatch.
acceptance_criteria: Quitting with no hosted processes exits immediately with no confirm. Quitting with hosted processes running opens a confirm listing each by name. The confirm lists only hosted processes; agent workers and pane-backed entries do not appear. Accepting kills every listed process then exits. Cancelling returns to the dashboard with every process still running. Asserted through the headless frame renderer: a frame after the quit key with a hosted process running shows the confirm and its process names.
close_reason: Landed as 5eb6f29. Quitting with hosted processes running raises a confirm listing them by name; accepting kills each then exits, cancelling returns with everything still running. Pane-backed entries and agent workers are not listed. PASS with a discriminating mutation check; build and full go test clean on the merged result.

title: Kill a hosted process from its row
description:
## Parent

admin-3rgp

## Category

enhancement

## Summary

Wire kill and retry for a hosted process so a running Command can be stopped or restarted from its row.

## Current behavior

The live-work registry's kill and retry operations are supplied by the producer that created the entry. Only the pane producers supply them today: kill closes the Herdr pane, retry opens a fresh pane and re-registers under the same entry identity.

A dashboard-hosted process has neither, so its row offers no way to stop or restart it. The only way to end one is to quit the dashboard.

## Desired behavior

A pty-addressed entry supplies both operations.

Kill terminates the child and everything it started, then marks the entry exited. A dev loop typically spawns children of its own — a bundler, a container, a simulator — so signalling only the direct child leaves orphans holding ports, which is the class of mess the port-nuking Kinds exist to clean up after. The whole process group goes.

Kill is idempotent: killing an entry that has already exited is a no-op, not an error.

Retry re-dispatches the same Command on a fresh pty and re-registers under the same entry identity, replacing the entry in place so exactly one row remains. This matches the pane path's existing retry contract, including its overwrite-in-place behavior. Retrying an entry that is still running kills it first.

The arguments the Command was originally dispatched with are retained so a retry runs exactly what ran the first time.

## Key interfaces

- The dashboard's dispatch path supplies kill and retry operations when registering a pty-addressed entry.
- Kill signals the child's process group and transitions the entry to exited.
- Retry re-invokes the same dispatch path with the retained arguments and re-registers under the same identity.
- The registry's operation signatures are unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Kill on a running hosted process terminates it and transitions its entry to exited.
- [ ] Kill terminates children the process spawned, not only the direct child — verified by starting a Command whose body spawns a grandchild and asserting the grandchild is gone.
- [ ] Kill on an already-exited entry is a no-op returning no error.
- [ ] Retry on an exited entry starts a fresh run and leaves exactly one row under the same identity.
- [ ] Retry on a running entry kills it first, then starts a fresh run.
- [ ] A retried run receives the same arguments the original dispatch received.
- [ ] Pane-addressed entries' kill and retry behavior is unchanged.

## Out of scope

- The key bindings that invoke these from a row. The operations are exposed on the entry; the Work tab's key handling for them follows the existing pattern for pane rows and needs no new design.
- Graceful-shutdown negotiation with the child beyond signalling its process group.
- Quit behavior, which is a separate slice.

## Blocked by

The dashboard's hosted-pty dispatch.
acceptance_criteria: Kill on a running hosted process terminates it and transitions its entry to exited. Kill terminates grandchildren, verified with a Command whose body spawns one. Kill on an already-exited entry is a no-op returning no error. Pane-addressed kill is unchanged. No retry affordance is added: the r binding, the footer hint and the worker-detail action were all removed deliberately, because restarting a live thing under the same identity is not something every producer can honour.
close_reason: Landed as 5a81233. Ops.Kill now signals the child's whole process group so grandchildren die with it, and is idempotent on an already-exited entry. Kill only, per the acceptance-criteria field — no retry affordance added; Ops.Retry left in place for admin-3rgp.68 to decide. PASS with a discriminating mutation check; build and full go test clean on the merged result.

title: Terminal ladder for workspace dispatch
description:
## Parent

admin-3rgp

## Category

enhancement

## Summary

Give workspace dispatch a fallback ladder so opening a worktree works on a machine without Herdr.

## Current behavior

Two producers hand a whole repo checkout to a person or an agent: Start Work on an issue/bead, and a workflow's agent-worker dispatch. Both call the Herdr shim's workspace-open directly.

When Herdr is unusable (`HERDR_ENV` unset, `REPO_HERDR=off`, or the CLI missing), that call returns the unavailable sentinel. Start Work has already created the worktree at that point, so the user gets a message reading as a failure — "worktree ready at <path>" with an error attached — and nothing opens. There is no second rung.

## Desired behavior

A single shim operation opens a workspace at a checkout path by trying rungs in order until one succeeds:

1. A Herdr pane (today's behavior, unchanged when Herdr is usable).
2. A new window in the user's terminal emulator.
3. The system terminal.
4. Having exhausted the above, report the path.

Reaching rung 4 is a normal outcome, not an error — the worktree exists and the path is the useful thing to hand back. A rung that is present but *fails* is distinct from a rung that is absent: an absent rung falls through silently, a failing one is worth surfacing, mirroring how the existing Herdr dispatch already separates "unavailable" from "available but the split failed".

Both producers call this operation instead of the Herdr open directly.

## Key interfaces

- A new exported shim operation taking a checkout path (and, for the agent producer, the command line to run in the new workspace) and returning which rung was taken, or an error.
- The existing Herdr availability predicate is unchanged and becomes rung 1's gate.
- The existing Herdr workspace-open stays as rung 1's implementation.
- Producers stop calling the Herdr open directly and call the ladder instead.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With Herdr available, the ladder opens a Herdr pane and reports rung 1 — byte-identical behavior to today.
- [ ] With Herdr unavailable and a terminal emulator present, the ladder opens a window there and reports that rung.
- [ ] With every rung unavailable, the ladder returns the checkout path as a successful outcome, not an error.
- [ ] A rung that is available but fails is reported as an error naming that rung, and does not silently fall through to the next.
- [ ] Start Work with no Herdr opens a real terminal in the new worktree.
- [ ] A workflow's agent workers still open in Herdr panes when Herdr is available.
- [ ] Each rung's selection is covered by a test that stubs rung availability.

## Out of scope

- Any change to how a Command dispatched from the dashboard runs. That is a separate producer with a separate surface.
- Detecting which terminal emulator the user prefers via configuration. Probe order is fixed.
- Windows support — this repo is darwin and linux only per ADR-0012.

## Blocked by

None — can start immediately.
acceptance_criteria: Herdr available: opens a pane, rung 1, identical to today. Herdr absent + emulator present: opens a window there. All rungs absent: returns the checkout path as success, not an error. A present-but-failing rung errors naming that rung and does not fall through. Start Work with no Herdr opens a real terminal in the new worktree. Workflow agent workers still open in Herdr panes when available. Each rung's selection covered by a test stubbing availability.

title: Multi-target picker runs as a stdin prompt outside the TUI
description:
Running a multi-target command from the dashboard drops out of the TUI to a
numbered stdin prompt. Observed in reddit-poker:

    pierce reddit-poker % admin
    build — select target
      1) all  all
      2) ios  ios
    Enter a number, or q to cancel: q

The dashboard already owns a row list, a cursor and a filter, and the resolved
targets are in hand before dispatch — the picker is a second, worse selection
UI for data the TUI is already holding. It should be a pane in the dashboard,
picked with the same keys as every other row.

Scope note: this ticket is ONLY the target selection. Running the chosen action
without tearing down the TUI is a separate open design question and is NOT in
scope here — a picker that selects and then exits to run is still an
improvement and does not depend on that question being settled.
acceptance_criteria: selecting a target for a multi-target command happens inside the dashboard with the existing row/cursor keys, not a stdin prompt
close_reason: Built in f11c4ae: a multi-target command is a disclosure row in the Work tab (arrow, enter toggles, one submenu open at a time); enter on a target dispatches admin <cmd> <target>, so the stdin picker is never reached.

title: Register the `new` verb in the Go binary
description:
cmd/manifest.go:23 lists `new` in reservedToolVerbs, but no cobra command is
registered for it. cmd/root.go's dispatchArgs therefore falls through to the
branch shorthand, so `admin new` is read as branch input instead of scaffolding
a manifest.

The Python entry still has it (admin-run:44 RESERVED_VERBS), so `admin-py new`
works today. That fallback disappears when admin-3rgp.30 deletes the Python.
acceptance_criteria: `admin new` scaffolds an admin.toml the way admin-py does; it is not routed to branch

title: Userscript provisioning has no Go port — the log bridge's browser half must be installed by hand
description:
The log bridge was ported as a server and lost its installer. Surfaced by the
2026-08-31 triage of the pre-rewrite backlog.

## What is there

internal/logbridge (506 lines) is the full server half: a listener bound to
0.0.0.0 over a configurable port range (DefaultPortRangeStart/End 9988-9999 at
logbridge.go:41-42, per-project override resolved at :69-72), the /log and
/health endpoints, batch time-ordering, and discovery files. It is wired into
interactive-shell via internal/kinds/interactiveshell.go:36-64 and
internal/keybindings/keybindings_unix.go:208-210.

## What is missing

The browser half's installer. admin_lib/tampermonkey.py — which wrote the
Tampermonkey managed-storage policy plist so the userscript installed itself
across every Arc/Chrome/Brave profile — has no Go counterpart:
`grep -rn 'tampermonkey' --include='*.go' .` returns nothing. There is no
`admin tampermonkey`, no `admin tampermonkey-status`, and no `admin deploy`
(cmd/root.go:202-207).

The script itself is still committed at tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js, and
per this repo's CLAUDE.md it is NOT installable by hand as-is: its @connect
lines and PROBE_HOSTS carry ${TAILSCALE_HOST_MAC} / ${TAILSCALE_HOST_UNRAID}
placeholders that build_provisioning expanded from the environment before
hashing. With provisioning gone, nothing expands them.

## Who it hurts

Anyone setting up the log bridge on a new machine or profile, and anyone whose
Tailscale addresses change — the expanded bytes were what got hashed, so a
changed address used to re-provision automatically on the next deploy.

## Decisions to carry forward, not re-litigate

- admin-6hjn: do NOT re-implement `installed` as a LevelDB write-ahead-log
  scan. A record Chromium has compacted into an .ldb table is invisible, so
  the field goes false-negative on the browser's next compaction (observed on
  Arc's Work profile 2026-08-25, log 2.1 MB -> 85 bytes). Keep `delivered`
  (managed storage, rewritten every launch) as the one honest signal, or
  relabel `installed` as "written since last compaction".
- admin-wxix: the Go surface already separates tool install (`go install`)
  from archetype deployment (`admin archetypes deploy`, cmd/archetypes.go:25).
  Whatever provisioning verb lands should stay its own step rather than being
  folded into a deploy that quits and relaunches every running browser.

title: test_sign.py designated-requirement test fails when the keychain holds two matching identities
description:
tests/test_sign.py::test_identifier_makes_the_designated_requirement_stable_across_rebuilds fails on this machine, and did so before and after the oa-jsy.2 fix (verified by stashing that change and re-running — identical failure).

What happens:

  AssertionError: a real identity + identifier should anchor to the identifier,
  not the cdhash; got 'cdhash H"17e8f1b00c1be1faa2ac3a014aa89dfd4088e2af" or
  cdhash H"bd79ee21ecacc326b98e66c2d325071d65ce3b55"'

Captured stderr says why:

  multiple code-signing identities match — set [apple].sign_identity to a unique
  substring to disambiguate: Apple Development: Pierce McBride (9XFR2JB2M3),
  Developer ID Application: Pierce McBride (ABCDE12345). Using ad-hoc.

resolve_signing_identity (admin_lib/apple.py:3178-3181) warns and returns None when more than one keychain identity matches the selector. This keychain now holds both an Apple Development and a Developer ID Application certificate, so the test's selector matches two, signing falls back to ad-hoc, and the designated requirement anchors to a cdhash instead of the identifier the test asserts on.

The test asserts a property of a real signing identity but does not pin which one, so it passes or fails on the contents of whoever's keychain runs it. Either give it a unique selector, or build the identity list from a fixture instead of the live keychain.

Rest of the suite: 1115 passed, this one failed (276s).

title: checkUnknownKinds has no regression test
description:
admin-3rgp.50's fix landed as 40 lines in cmd/check.go with ZERO test coverage — the
worker's diff was cmd/check.go only, and cmd/check_test.go already exists, so there was a
natural home for one.

Its mutation evidence was real but MANUAL: it built a mutant binary, ran it against a
scratch project in /tmp, observed the failure, and threw the artifacts away. So the
behaviour was proven once and nothing prevents it regressing.

The orchestrator independently re-verified the behaviour at fdf5941 with a fresh binary
and a manifest declaring kind = "nosuchkind" beside a valid shell action:
  action "build": unknown kind "nosuchkind"   exit 1
No false positive on the valid action. So the fix WORKS — this ticket is about it staying
that way.

The test to add, in cmd/check_test.go beside the existing checks:
- an action with an undeclared kind fails check, and the error names the action and the kind
- a valid kind alongside it does NOT get flagged
- the exit path is the same errors.Join collection the other checks use

Cheap to write; the only reason it is a ticket rather than a footnote is that a validation
check with no test is exactly the thing that silently stops validating.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at e7d00f8. .22 (3ffbc97): visibleTabs now derives the PRs tab from the declared uses_pull_requests key and the tracker tab from the declared tracker key — the old usesPRs() (len(remote.PRs)>0) and hasBeads inference are gone, so the tab set no longer changes under the user; the bd probe now only decides what is INSIDE the Beads tab, never whether it exists. .51 (f086b0c): four regression tests for checkUnknownKinds including the false-positive guard and multi-error collection, mutation run against the SUITE this time, not a hand-built binary. .37 (e7d00f8): docker.deploy and docker.diff are real Lua bodies via a new internal/dockerrun package — admin-3rgp.37 is now COMPLETE, with no kind='python' and no stub left anywhere.

title: admin check accepts an action whose kind does not exist; it only fails at dispatch
description:
MEASURED against the built binary at 5fadaba, with a scratch project whose admin.toml is
just project_name + archetypes = ["docker"]:

  admin check .   ->  "admin.toml: valid — no problems found"   exit 0
  admin build     ->  'command "build": action "build": unknown kind "python"'   exit 1

So a manifest that cannot run passes validation, and the user finds out at dispatch time.
The dispatch error itself is good — it names the command, the action and the kind, and
exits 1 correctly. The problem is purely that check does not catch it first.

WHO THIS HURTS: anyone on the docker or unraid-plugin archetype today (8 actions still
declare kind = "python", tracked on admin-3rgp.37), and in future anyone who typos a kind
name or uses an archetype written against a newer catalog than their binary.

THE FIX: validation already knows the kind catalog — internal/kinds.Declared(name) is the
lookup, and internal/validate is where shape checks live (ADR-0008). Every resolved
action's kind should be checked against the catalog during check, with an error naming the
action and the unknown kind, and ideally the closest valid kind.

Related: admin-3rgp.9 (admin check reports the ADR-0009 anti-patterns) is the natural home
if it is still open; otherwise this stands alone.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at fdf5941. .21 (91ea7ee): tracker and uses_pull_requests are now DECLARED top-level admin.toml keys, merged manifest-wins over archetypes, and the Config tab was rewritten from a raw dotfile viewer with an $EDITOR escape hatch into a read-only resolved readout of seven keys, each naming its origin (archetype name, (manifest), global config, local config, or defaulted); an undeclared tracker renders 'no tracker declared' rather than a guess. Three executed mutations. .50 (5e16558): cmd/check.go checkUnknownKinds validates every resolved action's kind against the catalog via kinds.Declared. Orchestrator re-verified .50 directly with a fresh binary and a manifest declaring kind='nosuchkind' beside a valid shell action: 'action "build": unknown kind "nosuchkind"', exit 1, no false positive on the valid action.

title: Verify the Apple device paths on real hardware: dev_ios, dev_tv, dev_device, deploy_ios, deploy_tv, App Store Connect
description:
admin-3rgp.12's implementation is complete and landed (962d1d0), but a whole class of its
behaviour has never been OBSERVED — only written. The swarm environment had no booted
simulator kept alive, no paired device, and no App Store Connect key, and every worker

title: The Go/Python detector parity harness silently skips when .venv is missing
description:
internal/detect/detect_test.go:394-398 calls t.Skip() when <repo>/.venv/bin/python is absent, so TestParityWithPythonDetectors reports success without comparing anything.

Observed 2026-08-28: a worker in a fresh git worktree (no .venv — it is gitignored and does not ride a checkout) ran the suite, saw green, and returned PASS on a change that inverts detectApple's behaviour. The same code in the primary checkout, where .venv exists, fails immediately: go=[simple] python=[apple]. See admin-3rgp.33.

A parity harness whose whole job is to catch divergence must not report success when it could not run. Skipping is the wrong default for the one test that exists to compare two implementations.
acceptance_criteria: The parity test fails, rather than skips, when it cannot reach a Python interpreter — or it bootstraps one. A run in a fresh worktree with no .venv does not report success without comparing.
close_reason: Fixed on feat/one-tool-go-merge as c31e994, merged ad90bb4. detect_test.go now searches .venv/bin/python, then python3, then python on PATH, version-gating each at >=3.11, and t.Fatalf's naming every path searched plus the ADMIN_SKIP_PYTHON_PARITY opt-out when none qualifies. Re-verified in the primary checkout: 13 parity subtests run green; in a .venv-less worktree the comparison now actually runs; with no python on PATH it fails instead of skipping.

title: Go manifest parser drops three [deploy] validation checks the Python parser has
description:
internal/manifest/manifest.go:322 ports only part of the [deploy] table handling from admin_lib/manifest.py:273-289.

What landed: the unknown-key check (DEPLOY_KEYS).

What was dropped, silently, from the same Python block:
- the required src/dest check
- the exclude-must-be-a-list check
- the delete-must-be-a-bool check

So a Go-parsed manifest with a [deploy] table missing src, or with `exclude = "a"` instead of a list, or `delete = "yes"` instead of a bool, parses clean where the Python parser rejects it. The two frontends disagree on the same file while both are live.

Found by the implementing worker's own review pass during admin-3rgp.2 and reported as a follow-up rather than fixed, since validation is out of scope for that ticket.
acceptance_criteria: The three checks exist in the Go parser and reject the same manifests admin_lib/manifest.py:273-289 rejects, with an error naming the offending key. A table test covers each of the three.
close_reason: Landed 1c19d4b: the three [deploy] checks (required src/dest, exclude-must-be-list, delete-must-be-bool) now match admin_lib/manifest.py:273-289, with a table case each. Mutation check discriminates.

title: Selection-sourced workflows run over a row selection
description:
Let a selection-sourced workflow run over rows selected on the tracker tab.

Multi-select rows, press the workflow key, pick from the workflows whose target source is a
selection, and dispatch over the selection. This is the gesture that replaces creating five to ten
worktrees by hand and giving each the same instruction.

A selection-sourced workflow is never offered anywhere else.

Reference: `docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/issues-selected.txt`.
acceptance_criteria:
- Rows can be multi-selected on the tracker tab and the count is visible.
- The workflow key offers only selection-sourced workflows.
- Dispatching runs the workflow over exactly the selected rows.
- With no rows selected, the workflow key says so rather than dispatching nothing silently.
- Selection-sourced workflows appear nowhere in the Commands tab.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at 04706e3. .27 (ce2ef86): space toggles a tracker row into a selection with a visible checkbox and live count; w opens a picker of declared over='selection' workflows; picking one builds targets and hands off to .26's EXISTING confirm/dispatch path — no second dispatch path. It also found and fixed a real pre-existing footer bug: keybar's pair-trimming protected only the last pair, so growing the keymap silently dropped 'q quit' before the tab hint; regression test added. .9 (4a4a593): checkAntiPatterns reads the project's OWN un-merged admin.toml (archetypes are SUPPOSED to carry implementation per ADR-0009, so they are never flagged), reports multiline-run and sidecar-script as WARNINGS with exit 0 per the ADR's rejection of a hard-fail escape hatch, and excludes kind='lua' because ADR-0010 fixes a lua body's run as inline source. .33 (04706e3): the detector merge now honours an explicit clear via HasProjectName, following the same tri-state convention as HasTracker/HasUsesPullRequests. Together .27 and .9 unblock admin-3rgp.30, the epic's capstone.

title: Query-sourced workflows run bare from the Commands tab
description:
Let a query-sourced workflow run bare from the Commands tab.

Selecting one resolves its query, then shows the resolved target set for confirmation before
anything is dispatched. A query matching nine things must not be able to start nine agents
without the set having been seen.

Confirmation shows what will run, over what, and how many will run at once given the ceiling.

Reference: `docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/dispatch-sheet.txt`.
acceptance_criteria:
- A query-sourced workflow appears in the Commands list and can be activated from it.
- Activating it resolves the query and shows the resolved targets before dispatch.
- Cancelling at the confirmation dispatches nothing.
- Confirming dispatches exactly the shown set, respecting the ceiling.
- A query resolving to nothing says so and dispatches nothing.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at 7669010. .52 (4876fbd): registerManifestCommand now distinguishes 'no admin.toml' (still falls through to branch shorthand) from 'admin.toml exists but fails to parse/resolve' (hard error, no git mutation); ADR-0011 amended to make step 2 three-way. Orchestrator re-ran its own repro against the fix in isolated repos: malformed manifest -> "admin.toml is invalid: ... 'project_name' is required", exit 1, NO branch created; a directory with no admin.toml -> branch shorthand still works exactly as before. .23 (f4de906): the on-enter dispatch logic already existed from .20 with zero tests, so this added five locking it in — note the stored acceptance criteria (per-project-configurable row actions naming workflows) describe a design the epic's amendment superseded. .26 (b686a2a): internal/kinds/workflowquery.go resolves over.query against beads, and internal/tui/workflowconfirm.go resolves-then-confirms before dispatching; selection-sourced workflows are explicitly refused bare ('X is selection-sourced — it cannot run bare'), which keeps .27's boundary intact.

title: on-enter row actions
description:
Make what `Enter` does on a row configurable per row type.

Three keys decide it: what happens on an issue row, on a PR row, and on a branch row. Each names
either a built-in action or a workflow. This is what lets one project review-and-merge while
another reviews-and-leaves-the-branch, with no change to the tool.

An unset key keeps the current default for that row type.
acceptance_criteria:
- Setting the issue-row action to a workflow makes `Enter` on an issue run that workflow over it.
- Setting the PR-row action to a different workflow makes `Enter` on a PR run that one.
- An unset key behaves as it does today.
- A key naming a workflow that does not exist is a validation error, caught by `check`.

Orchestrator re-ran its own repro against the fix in isolated repos: malformed manifest -> "admin.toml is invalid: ... 'project_name' is required", exit 1, NO branch created; a directory with no admin.toml -> branch shorthand still works exactly as before. .23 (f4de906): the on-enter dispatch logic already existed from .20 with zero tests, so this added five locking it in — note the stored acceptance criteria (per-project-configurable row actions naming workflows) describe a design the epic's amendment superseded. .26 (b686a2a): internal/kinds/workflowquery.go resolves over.query against beads, and internal/tui/workflowconfirm.go resolves-then-confirms before dispatching; selection-sourced workflows are explicitly refused bare ('X is selection-sourced — it cannot run bare'), which keeps .27's boundary intact.

title: Tracker and PRs tabs read declared keys, not inference
description:
Drive the tracker tab and the PRs tab from declared manifest keys rather than from what the
tool can infer.

This is a BEHAVIOUR CHANGE, not wiring. repo-dash derives every one of these tabs today, and
"the tracker tab" is three conditional tabs rather than one surface (visibleTabs,
internal/tui/model.go:352):

  PRs     drawn when nwo != "" AND usesPRs(), which is len(remote.PRs) > 0 (model.go:333)
  Issues  drawn when nwo != "" AND NOT hasBeads
  Beads   drawn when hasBeads

Two independent keys replace that, and they are NOT the same question — a review queue is not
an issue tracker, and a repo can use beads for issues while still having pull requests:

  tracker              beads | github | none. Chooses Issues vs Beads, or no tracker tab.
  uses_pull_requests   whether the PRs tab exists at all.

Both keys are added by admin-3rgp.21 (Config tab and the explicit manifest keys), which this
ticket already depends on. The PRD settles the split: user story 11 asks for the manifest to
declare whether the project uses pull requests "so that the tool stops inferring it from branch
protection and being wrong" (docs/PRD.md:39), and lists both keys at docs/PRD.md:105.

The consequence worth stating plainly: today the PRs tab appears only while the repo has open
PRs RIGHT NOW, so a repo with pull requests and none open shows no PRs tab. After this change
the tab's presence follows the declaration, and an empty PRs tab is a legitimate state that
needs an empty state.

Bucketing by who is supposed to act stays as it is, and the rule for what needs your attention
stays the computed one rather than a reading of the review-request list, which the host clears
as soon as you review.

Reference: docs/spikes/admin-tui-desktop/issues.txt.
acceptance_criteria:
- A project declaring tracker = "beads" shows the Beads tab; tracker = "github" shows Issues; tracker = "none" shows no tracker tab. The choice comes from the manifest, not from whether .beads/ exists on disk.
- uses_pull_requests controls the PRs tab independently of tracker: a beads project that declares pull requests shows both Beads and PRs.
- A declared PRs tab with no open PRs renders an empty state rather than disappearing.
- Changing either key changes the tab set with no other edit.
- Rows are grouped by who is expected to act.
close_reason: Landed on feat/one-tool-go-merge at e7d00f8. .22 (3ffbc97): visibleTabs now derives the PRs tab from the declared uses_pull_requests key and the tracker tab from the declared tracker key — the old usesPRs() (len(remote.PRs)>0) and hasBeads inference are gone, so the tab set no longer changes under the user; the bd probe now only decides what is INSIDE the Beads tab, never whether it exists. .51 (f086b0c): four regression tests for checkUnknownKinds including the false-positive guard and multi-error collection, mutation run against the SUITE this time, not a hand-built binary. .37 (e7d00f8): docker.deploy and docker.diff are real Lua bodies via a new internal/dockerrun package — admin-3rgp.37 is now COMPLETE, with no kind='python' and no stub left anywhere.

title: Port interactive-shell, the log bridge and keybindings
description:
Port the remaining long-running kinds: `interactive-shell` and `bridge-listen`, together with the
log-bridge HTTP listener, reload handling and keybindings.

The log bridge listens on a free port from a configurable range, bound so peers on the tailnet can
reach it, and appends posted browser console entries to the same log the action is already
writing. Entries are ordered by their own timestamps within a batch, and each carries the page
host rather than the full URL so query-string tokens stay out of the log. Lines reach the
terminal through the shared pump, so a browser line and a server line are indistinguishable.
acceptance_criteria:
- An `interactive-shell` action starts a listener on a free port from the configured range.
- A posted batch of console entries appears in the log and on the terminal, level-mapped and
  timestamped from the browser's own clock.
- Entries within a batch appear in timestamp order.
- A logged URL records the host only.
- An app that prints its own logger prefix is unwrapped rather than double-stamped.

One additive conflict in factories.go resolved by the orchestrator as the union — three distinct kind names, each registered once. Verified integrated: go build, go vet, go test ./... all green.

title: Port the worktree verbs and the resolver
description:
Port the worktree verbs and the resolver.

`branch <input>` resolves an input to a branch and checks it out in the current working tree.
`worktree <input>` resolves the same input set and creates a separate worktree for it. The
resolver classifies syntactically first with no network, then uses the GitHub CLI to turn an
issue into a slugged branch name and a PR into its head ref.

Dead-branch classification decides which local branches cleanup may delete safely, leaving
everything else as a survivor needing human judgement.

Both verbs take `--prune` for cleanup and open a picker when given no input. A new worktree is
adopted as a Herdr child workspace when Herdr is available, and prints a path otherwise.

Worktree creation carries gitignored files in per the configured populate patterns — including
`admin.toml`, which is never committed and so must be seeded rather than checked out.
acceptance_criteria:
- A branch name, an issue number, a PR number and a GitHub URL each resolve correctly.
- Classification of syntax happens without any network call.
- A dead branch is offered for deletion; a branch with unpushed or uncommitted work is not.
- A new worktree receives the configured populate files, `admin.toml` among them.
- With Herdr unavailable the verb still succeeds and prints the path.

Verified integrated: go build, go vet, go test ./... all green; exactly one OutputPump and one RunWithReload per build tag. .15 is closed for its real scope; the rust/launchd remainder is split out because it is a design question, not a port.

- Killing a held port reports which processes were killed.

title: Guards, requires and the global preflight
description:
Port guards, `requires` and the global preflight.

Built-in guards (`git-clean`, `git-pushed`, `deps-fresh`) produce dynamic diagnostics naming what
to do next. User-defined guards live in `[guards.<name>]` tables as a shell expression plus a
static failure string. Both share one name namespace.

`requires` resolves through both. A multi-target parent's `requires` is the default its children
inherit; a child may replace it, and an empty list is the explicit opt-out.

`deps-fresh` also runs as an always-on preflight before every command, memoized once per
invocation, with the diagnostic verbs exempt so a stale install cannot lock you out of
recovering. It is fail-open: a bug or unusual manifest degrades to a pass.
acceptance_criteria:
- A failing guard blocks the action, prints its diagnostic and exits non-zero.
- Guards run fail-fast in listed order.
- A child target's `requires` overrides the parent's rather than merging with it.
- `requires = []` on a child runs no guards.
- The preflight runs once per invocation regardless of nested dispatch, and is skipped for the
  diagnostic verbs.
- A guard name that resolves to neither a built-in nor a user table is a validation error.
close_reason: Landed as 4a5b95c on feat/one-tool-go-merge (worker commit 06ba0e7). internal/guards ports ADR-0005's four-phase pipeline: ValidateRequires (resolve), Register, RunRequires (dispatch, per-target replace-not-merge with requires=[] as explicit opt-out), RunGlobalPreflight (deps-fresh, memoized, fail-open, logs/kill exempt). Conflict with admin-3rgp.11 in multitarget.go resolved by the orchestrator as the union of two independent per-target inheritance mechanisms; both workers' test suites pass together.

title: Port the detectors to Go
description:
Port the detectors to Go.

Unlike archetypes, detectors are genuinely logic: file-layout heuristics that scan a project root
and propose which archetypes apply. They become Go functions rather than data.

Preserve the existing pairing convention — a detector corresponds by name to the archetype it
proposes.
acceptance_criteria:
- Running detection against a fixture project tree proposes the same archetype set the Python
  detectors proposed for that tree.
- A project matching no detector yields an empty proposal, not an error.
close_reason: Landed 9096151: internal/detect ports all 14 detectors as Go functions with fixture-tree parity tests against the Python detectors. No match yields an empty proposal, not an error.

title: Hook additionalContext output should use jq/python for JSON escaping
description: The `printf` in `session-admin-check.sh` emits a hardcoded literal string, which is safe today but is an anti-pattern. If the message ever becomes dynamic (e.g. includes the project path or regen output), bare string interpolation will produce malformed JSON. Mirror the reference hook pattern: `jq -n --arg ctx "$text"` with a python3 fallback.
close_reason: Closed
