session-admin-check.sh now uses jq (with python3 fallback) to JSON-encode the additionalContext message, preventing injection from special characters.

title: admin logs stamps a replayed file with the time you opened it, not the time each line happened
description:
## What happens

`LogFormatter` gained `reuse_timestamp` in 8a0c65c: when a line already carries its own timestamp, print that (converted to local time) instead of the moment the line arrived. `logtail` wires it for exactly one caller — the log-bridge sink:

```python
# admin_lib/logtail.py:294
set_log_server_sink(LineRenderer(highlight, reuse_timestamp=True).write)
```

The file tail itself does not:

```python
# admin_lib/logtail.py:59-60
def __init__(self, highlight=None, reuse_timestamp=False):
    self._fmt = make_formatter(reuse_timestamp=reuse_timestamp)
```

So `admin logs <target>` on a file written hours ago stamps every line with `datetime.now()`. A 3-hour-old crash reads as having happened the second you scrolled past it, and every line in the file shares one timestamp — the replay is unreadable for anything time-sensitive, which is most of why you open an old log.

The information is there: framed actions write `LOG_FILE` with the source's own timestamps, and bridge lines carry a full ISO stamp.

## Fix

Default `reuse_timestamp=True` for the file/pick kinds, which are replays by definition. The live kinds (`command`, `docker`) are streaming a process now, where arrival time is honest and a source that prints no timestamp still needs one — leave those as they are, or let each kind declare it.

Worth checking `--follow` on a live file: tailing a file that is still being written is a replay for its history and a stream for its tail, and reuse handles both correctly as long as the source stamps its lines.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). RE-POINTED, NOT FIXED. The Python named here is deleted, but so is the whole replay surface: there is no `admin logs` verb in Go (cmd/root.go:202-207 registers branch, worktree, prs, populate, __run-action; check.go and archetypes.go add two more) and no log tailer anywhere in internal/. [logs.*] sections still PARSE (internal/manifest/logs.go, 297 lines) and merge, but nothing consumes a LogSource — actions write log files (internal/luahost/host.go:115-129) and nothing reads them back. The half this bead needs already exists on the writing side: logformat.Options has ReuseTimestamp (internal/logformat/logformat.go:242, honoured at :295) and it is wired for exactly one caller, the log-bridge sink (internal/keybindings/keybindings_unix.go:44) — the identical one-caller situation the bead describes in Python. So when the log reader is ported, build it with ReuseTimestamp: true. Blocked on that port existing.

title: Hashed scope colors don't reach ColumnFormatter, so Apple/Android/docker streams render differently
description:
## What happens

`LogFormatter` now colors every bracketed scope tag by a hash of its own text (`colorize_scopes`, added in 1c08785), so `[api]`, `[supabase]` and `[Messaging]` each get a stable color. A framed `interactive-shell` action and `admin logs` both go through it.

`ColumnFormatter` does not. It has its own copy of the level-coloring loop and stops there:

```python
# admin_lib/log_columns.py:136-143
if self._use_color:
    color = _find_level_color(line)
    if color:
        for pat in _LEVEL_COLORS:
            if pat[0].search(line):
                line = pat[0].sub(lambda m: f"{color}{m.group()}{C.RESET}", line, count=1)
                break
```

So an Apple `log stream`, an Android logcat, or a docker multi-target stream renders level colors but no scope colors, while a plain shell action in the same project renders both. Which coloring you get depends on which formatter the action kind happens to use — not on anything about the log.

## Why it matters

Two formatters own "how a log line looks", and they have now diverged. That is the same shape as the five copies of the output pump (#475): a second body of the same job, silently drifting. Every future rendering change has to be made twice or it only lands for half the projects.

## Fix

`ColumnFormatter._reformat_generic_line` should call the shared `colorize_scopes` after its level pass — or better, both formatters should share one `colorize(line)` entry point in `log_format.py`, with `ColumnFormatter` keeping only the column layout that is genuinely its own.

Note `AppleColumnFormatter` parses fixed native columns, so the scope pass has to run on the assembled message field, not the raw line.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). FIXED BY THE PORT. The second formatter is gone: Go has one renderer, internal/logformat, and it calls ColorizeScopes on every line it renders (logformat.go:303). There is no ColumnFormatter in the Go tree, so an Apple log stream, an Android logcat and a plain shell action cannot render differently — the divergence this bead describes needs two formatters and there is only one.

title: Architecture: tampermonkey-status 'installed' goes false-negative after LevelDB compaction
description:
`admin_lib/tampermonkey.py::profile_status` reads only the LevelDB write-ahead log (`*.log`) of Tampermonkey's `Local Extension Settings`. A record Chromium has compacted into an `.ldb` table is invisible, so `installed (seen in log): …` disappears on the browser's next compaction — Arc's Work profile did exactly this on 2026-08-25 (the log went from 2.1 MB to 85 bytes on relaunch).

Reading `.ldb` tables needs snappy, which ADR-0001 (stdlib only) rules out. Options: drop `installed` and keep `delivered` (managed storage, which Chromium rewrites on every launch) as the one honest signal; or label the field "written since last compaction". Today it prints as if it were a presence check.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). MOOT AS WRITTEN — admin_lib/tampermonkey.py is deleted by admin-3rgp.30 and has no Go port: `grep -rn tampermonkey --include='*.go'` finds nothing, and there is no `admin tampermonkey` or `admin deploy` verb (cmd/root.go:202-207). So profile_status, its LevelDB write-ahead-log read, and the false-negative it reports all cease to exist. NOTE THE GAP THIS LEAVES: the log-bridge SERVER is ported (internal/logbridge, 506 lines) but userscript provisioning is not, so tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js has to be installed by hand. If provisioning is re-ported to Go, do not re-implement `installed` as a WAL scan — this bead's conclusion (keep `delivered`, drop or relabel `installed`) is the answer to carry forward.

title: Architecture: admin deploy couples tool install to a browser restart
description:
`admin.toml` `[commands.deploy]` runs `install` then `tampermonkey`. The second step, when the userscript changed, prompts for sudo and quits/relaunches every running Chromium browser (`admin_lib/tampermonkey.py::provision`).

A stale `~/.admin` and a stale userscript are separate failures with separate blast radii; coupling them means the tool cannot be redeployed without a browser interruption whenever `tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js` moved. Since `d2c5f3f` the step is a no-op when the policy hash is current, which limits the interruption to script changes — but the coupling itself is a design choice worth deciding: keep it (one command keeps both current), or make `admin tampermonkey` its own explicit step and drop it from `deploy`.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). MOOT — the coupling cannot exist because neither half survives. admin_lib/tampermonkey.py has no Go port and there is no `admin deploy` verb (cmd/root.go:202-207); tool install is `go install`, and archetype deployment is its own verb (`admin archetypes deploy`, cmd/archetypes.go:25). The design question — one command keeping both current, versus an explicit separate step — is answered by construction: they are separate. Re-file if userscript provisioning is ported back.

title: test_sign: designated-requirement test fails on main with a cdhash requirement
description:
`tests/test_sign.py::test_identifier_makes_the_designated_requirement_stable_across_rebuilds` fails on `main` (`d2c5f3f`):

```
tests/test_sign.py:111: AssertionError: a real identity + identifier should anchor to the identifier, not the cdhash; got 'cdhash H"b20f945ed55cb39a40348853d08d1dc947406d54" or cdhash H"1f0d38aa64cdf875eb4c508cc5aa4d1301ef6a82"'
```

Last change to the signing path was `4806ac1`. The other two tests in the file pass. Needs a look at whether the identity lookup on this machine falls back to ad-hoc (which yields cdhash requirements) or whether the requirement builder regressed.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). MOOT — this is pytest-suite hygiene for tests/ and admin_lib/, both deleted by admin-3rgp.30. The Go suite (117 *_test.go files) is a fresh suite with none of the machinery named here. tests/test_sign.py is deleted. Go's signing path is internal/kinds/applesign_darwin.go with applesign_darwin_test.go, and apple.sign takes an explicit stable `identifier` so the designated requirement anchors to it (docs/architecture/lua-host-api.md:193). If the cdhash-anchoring symptom reappears against the Go path, file it fresh.

title: The build log admin points you at is the grep-filtered one, so a failure's detail lines are never where you look
description:
`admin build ios` writes **two** logs, and the one it names on stdout is the
one with the diagnosis removed.

## What happens

`admin_lib/apple.py:561` pipes xcodebuild through a console filter:

```python
return f'{cmd} | tee -a "{log_path}" | grep -E "BUILD|error:|warning:" ; exit ${{PIPESTATUS[0]}}'
```

`tee` sits *before* the grep, so `_raw_build_log_path()` —
`tmp/admin-xcode-build.log` — gets everything, stderr included
(`apple.py:549` appends `2>&1`). Measured on iptv-mac just now: **3,619
lines**, starting with the full `Command line invocation:`.

Everything downstream of the grep is what a human sees, and that stream is
what `core.py:293`'s `LOG_FILE` captures into `tmp/build-<target>.<stamp>.log`.
That is also the only path admin ever prints:

```
→ wrote: tmp/build-ios.2026-08-23_180005.log
```

`tmp/admin-xcode-build.log` is never mentioned anywhere in the output.

## Why that matters

`grep -E "BUILD|error:|warning:"` is a per-line filter, and xcodebuild's
failures are multi-line. A bad destination prints:

```
xcodebuild: error: Unable to find a device matching the provided destination specifier:
        { platform:iOS Simulator, OS:latest, name:iPhone 15 Pro }
```

The first line matches `error:` and survives. The second line — the only one
carrying the value you need — matches nothing and is dropped. So the log admin
hands you names a problem and withholds the answer, while a complete copy sits
in a file beside it that nothing tells you about.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone diagnosing a build failure through `admin`, every time the useful
detail is on a continuation line — destination specifiers, "Multiple commands
produce" file lists, provisioning-profile mismatches. Reported on iptv-mac
2026-08-22 (iptv-ivyb), where it cost a manual `xcrun simctl list devices` to
recover a value admin already had on disk.

## Fix shape

Print the raw log's path too, at least on a non-zero rc — `_announce_log_end()`
is the place, and `_raw_build_log_path()` already knows it. Naming the file
that has the answer is cheaper and safer than widening the grep, which would
have to guess at every multi-line shape xcodebuild produces.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — inherited verbatim. The same tee-before-grep pipeline is at internal/luahost/apple_xcode_darwin.go:184: `%s | tee -a %q | grep -E "BUILD|error:|warning:" ; exit ${PIPESTATUS[0]}`. The raw log still gets everything (2>&1 is appended by compose() at :155) and still lands at rawBuildLogPath() = <LogDir>/admin-xcode-build.log. It is exposed as XcodebuildResult.RawLogPath (:176) but the only consumer is DiagnoseBuildFailure (internal/kinds/apple_darwin.go:199, :342), which reads it for two known remediation patterns — a locked keychain and a signed-out Xcode (internal/luahost/apple_darwin.go:238-257) — and warns about those alone. Nothing ever prints the raw path, so the log admin names in the pinned footer is still the grep-filtered one with the diagnosis removed.

title: admin.toml has no answer for secrets, and the only thing keeping them out of git is a machine-local ignore rule
description:
## The problem

Some `admin.toml` manifests embed secrets. The tool offers nothing for this, so each project improvises — mostly `${VAR}` environment-variable expansion, which was designed for portability rather than secrecy and has never been evaluated as a secrets mechanism.

That improvisation is load-bearing in a way it should not be. `admin.toml` is described by `README.md` as the one file a project commits. The only thing currently stopping a manifest with a secret in it from being committed is a **global** git ignore rule on one machine — a rule that exists for an unrelated reason (the tool is private and should not be advertised in public repos). When the tool goes public that rule goes away, and the thing keeping secrets out of git goes away with it, silently.

## Why environment variables may not be the answer

`${VAR}` expansion keeps the literal value out of the file, which is the easy half. What it does not do:

- **Say which vars a manifest needs.** A missing var surfaces as a failed command with a confusing error, not as "you have not set X".
- **Say which vars are secret.** `${BUILD_DIR}` and `${API_TOKEN}` are indistinguishable to the tool, so nothing can warn, redact, or audit.
- **Keep values out of logs.** An expanded command line is echoed and captured; a token in a `run` string ends up in scrollback and in any log the tool tails.
- **Provide the values.** Every project still needs a `.env`, a shell profile, or a keychain read, and the tool has no opinion, so each one differs.

## What to decide

Name the candidates and their tradeoffs before building anything. At minimum worth comparing:

1. **Typed secret references in the manifest** — e.g. a distinct syntax or a `[secrets]` table declaring name, source, and required-ness, so the tool knows what is sensitive and can redact it in logs and refuse to run without it.
2. **Keychain-backed lookup** on macOS, with a documented fallback elsewhere.
3. **A sidecar file** (`admin.local.toml` or similar) that is always ignored and merged over the manifest — mirrors the `Signing.local.xcconfig` pattern several consuming projects already use.
4. **Status quo, but declared** — keep `${VAR}` and add a required-vars declaration plus log redaction, which is the smallest change that fixes the three specific gaps above.

Stdlib-only applies (ADR-0001), so anything needing a third-party SDK is out unless it clears the optional-import carve-out.

## Also in scope: an audit before anything is committed

Independent of the design, the existing manifests need checking. Every `admin.toml` on this machine is currently untracked, so nothing has leaked, but that is an accident of the global ignore rather than a property of the files. Before any manifest is committed anywhere:

- Enumerate the manifests that exist and what each one embeds.
- Flag literal secrets, hostnames, deploy targets, account names, and absolute paths that point at removable or network volumes.
- Decide per finding whether it moves to the new mechanism or stays local.

A `admin check` subcommand that scans a manifest for likely secrets and fails loudly is the natural home for this once the mechanism exists, so the audit is repeatable rather than a one-off read-through.

## Related

- #473 — `admin` roots on the shell's cwd, so a worktree's test run can build the primary checkout instead. Same family: manifest-and-worktree assumptions that hold in the primary checkout and nowhere else.
- The `CLAUDE.md` section explaining why `admin.toml` is globally ignored today points at this issue for the secrets half.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — completely untouched by the rewrite. The Go manifest layer offers exactly what the Python did: ${VAR} / ${VAR:-default} expansion (internal/manifest/envresolve.go, envrefs.go), which is a portability mechanism, not a secrets one. There is no secret type, no reference-to-a-store, no redaction. And the thing keeping a manifest with a secret in it out of git is still one machine-local global ignore rule, as this repo's own CLAUDE.md documents. The rewrite does change one input to the decision: the tool is now a Go binary installed with `go install`, so 'when it goes public' is closer, and the ignore rule's disappearance is the event this bead is about.

title: deploy files: post_sync (and chown) declared in [deploy] never take effect on the live Unraid target
description:
## What happened

etv-station's \`[deploy]\` table declares:

\`\`\`toml
chown     = "${ETV_STATION_UID:-99}:${ETV_STATION_GID:-100}"
post_sync = "chown -R ${ETV_STATION_UID:-99}:${ETV_STATION_GID:-100} ${ETV_STATION_APPDATA}"
\`\`\`

\`admin check\` reports \`ok\` on this manifest. A real \`admin deploy files\` run against the live Unraid host does not apply either: \`etv-next/\`, \`channels/\`, \`plugins/\` still land owned \`1000:20\` (the sending Mac's uid) instead of \`99:100\`, and no \`post_sync: ...\` log line (or the \`POSTSYNC_RAN_AS\` marker used to probe it) appears in the deploy output.

This is the root cause etv-station/#156 is blocked on: a config-only deploy stamps wrong ownership on the appdata dirs, the container can't write \`channelN.json\`, and it crash-loops until someone runs \`chown -R\` by hand.

## Where to look

Both \`chown\` and \`post_sync\` are read from \`[deploy]\` and threaded through correctly on paper:

- \`admin_lib/remote.py:213-215\` resolves \`chown\` from cfg, passed to \`sync(..., chown=chown)\`.
- \`admin_lib/remote.py:231-252\` builds the \`post_sync\` callable from \`cfg.get("post_sync")\` and passes it to \`sync(...)\`.
- \`admin_lib/core.py:920-936\` (remote/rsync branch): \`chown\` becomes \`--chown={chown}\` on the rsync invocation (line 927); \`rc\` comes back from \`run_cmd(...)\` (line 930).
- \`admin_lib/core.py:957-958\`: \`post_sync(dest)\` only runs \`if rc == 0\`.

That last gate is the likely culprit: if the remote rsync doesn't support \`--chown\` (version-dependent) or the flag is silently dropped/rejected on that target, \`rc\` may come back non-zero (skipping post_sync entirely and erroring loud) or the flag may be silently ignored by an older rsync while \`rc\` still returns 0 (in which case post_sync *should* still fire — worth checking with \`-v\` output whether \`run_cmd\` actually returns 0 on the live host, and whether \`docker.py\`'s \`deploy_dispatch\` for the \`files\` target is even the code path being exercised, as opposed to \`admin_lib/interp.py:_make_sync\` — note \`_make_sync\` at interp.py:576-590 builds a generic \`sync\` call that does NOT read \`post_sync\`/\`chown\`/\`host\` from \`cmd.meta\` at all; if \`deploy files\` for a docker-archetype project is somehow routed through that generic path instead of \`deploy_dispatch\`, that would explain the symptom exactly).

## Reproduce

1. On the etv-station repo: \`admin deploy files\` (or \`--dry-run\` first to confirm no crash).
2. On the Unraid host: \`ls -lan /mnt/user/appdata/etv-station/etv-next\` — check owner.
3. Compare against \`ETV_STATION_UID\`/\`GID\` from \`/boot/config/etv-station.env\`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] After \`admin deploy files\` against a real target, the synced directories are owned by \`[deploy].chown\` (or the \`post_sync\` chown, whichever is meant to be authoritative — if both exist, decide which wins and document it).
- [ ] A regression test exercises the actual \`deploy_dispatch\` \`files\` path end-to-end (not just \`sync()\` in isolation) so a future change can't silently stop calling \`post_sync\` again.
- [ ] Root cause (not just a workaround) is identified and named in the fix commit.

Type: AFK
close_reason: Fixed by admin-3rgp.37's docker.deploy/docker.diff port (e7d00f8), rather than ported forward. admin-9bex: internal/dockerrun.BuildDeploySyncPlan is now the ONLY [deploy]-sync implementation, so there is no second path to silently drop post_sync or chown; verified for real with a local sync where post_sync fired and created its marker file, and --chown rendering is mutation-proven. admin-dbmj: diff now reports three axes — declared/live, last-deploy/live, and declared/last-deploy — verified with a simulated manual port change. admin-wxz0: every -e value is masked in both text and --format json output on all three axes, verified with a real secret-rotation scenario. admin-fr0e was deliberately left untouched and not made worse. NOTE: the Python admin_lib still carries these bugs until admin-3rgp.30 deletes it.

title: run_with_keybindings pipes stdout, breaks full-screen TUI commands
description:
\`run_with_keybindings\` in \`admin_lib/keybindings.py:144\` launches the wrapped command with:

\`\`\`python
proc = subprocess.Popen(
    ...,
    stdout=subprocess.PIPE, stderr=subprocess.STDOUT,
    ...
)
\`\`\`

so it can tee output and dispatch keybindings. That gives the child a piped stdout, not a real tty.

Hit this via \`admin epg\` in etv-station, which runs \`tools/epg-browser.py\` (a Textual TUI) through \`interactive-shell\` → \`run_with_keybindings\` (\`admin_lib/interp.py:726\`). Textual sees \`isatty() == False\` on stdout and degrades to non-fullscreen rendering: frames get appended instead of overwriting, so the pane fills with stacked timestamps and overlapping redraws — unusable. Confirmed by sending the pane a repaint (\`ctrl+l\`) and observing no clean redraw, consistent with a degraded non-interactive renderer rather than a hang.

Workaround: run the TUI directly, bypassing the wrapper — \`uv run tools/epg-browser.py\` — which gets a real tty and renders clean.

Real fix: \`run_with_keybindings\` needs to allocate a pty (\`pty.openpty\`/\`pty.fork\`) for the child instead of \`subprocess.PIPE\`, or \`interactive-shell\` needs a mode that skips the pipe/log-tee for full-screen TUI commands.
notes:
The Go binary had the same bug on a different path, and it is now fixed — the fix is the model for this one.

`internal/kinds/shell.go`'s `makeShellPassthrough` had silently dropped the `interactive` knob during the Python-to-Go port; its own doc comment called it a follow-up, but nothing tracked it. So `interactive = true` in a manifest parsed, validated, passed `admin check`, and did nothing: every such action ran through `RunCmd`'s pipe.

The symptom is identical to the one described here and worth recording, because neither half is obvious from the code. A piped child gets no controlling terminal, so it (a) is never sent a window size and never receives SIGWINCH, and (b) fails every isatty probe. A full-screen program therefore falls back to a hardcoded default size and turns colour off — `admin prototype` rendered a 96x30 monochrome island of a program whose window was 150x44. It does not error and it does not hang; it silently renders a small grey fake.

Fixed in b070e2e by `runInteractive`, which execs `/bin/sh -c` with os.Stdin/Stdout/Stderr inherited directly — no pipe, no pty wrapper, no log tee, no frame — and returns the child's exit code. Guarded by TestShellPassthroughInteractiveInheritsStdout, which asserts the child's stdout is the SAME open file as the parent's by swapping a real file in as os.Stdout and reading back what the child wrote. Any reintroduced pipe fails that test.

This issue is the Python half: `run_with_keybindings` needs the same treatment, except it cannot simply inherit, because its whole purpose is teeing output to dispatch keybindings. That is what makes it the harder of the two and why it needs a real pty (pty.openpty / pty.fork) rather than the inherit-directly fix used on the Go side.

title: Five copies of the read-child-output-and-write-it-out loop
description:
## What is duplicated

The same loop — read a chunk from a child process, optionally run it through a formatter, write it to the terminal, append it to the log file — is written out five separate times:

- `admin_lib/core.py` — `_run_cmd_pty`, the pty path of `run_cmd`
- `admin_lib/core.py` — the pipe path of `run_cmd`
- `admin_lib/streams.py` — `stream_subprocess`, the one the module docstring says is the only copy
- `admin_lib/reload.py` — inside `run_with_reload`
- `admin_lib/keybindings.py` — twice inside `run_with_keybindings` (the select loop and the drain-on-exit)

`streams.py` opens by explaining that this pump was once private to `apple.py` and that android grew its own copy rather than find it. That happened again, in three more places.

## Why it matters now

Adding the pinned URL footer meant every one of these had to change from `sys.stdout.write(...)` to `frame.write(...)`, because the footer is repainted after each chunk reaches the terminal. Four separate edits in four files for one behaviour. The next thing that wants to observe child output — a line counter, a filter, a progress meter, anything — pays the same tax, and the failure mode is silent: miss one copy and that one dev loop just doesn't get the feature, with nothing to catch it.

Concretely: `admin dev` under the docker reload loop and `admin dev` under a plain shell action now reach the terminal through two unrelated code paths that happen to agree.

## Fix

Collapse all five onto `streams.stream_subprocess`, which is where the module docstring already says this belongs. The callers differ in real ways — pty vs pipe, whether a formatter is set, whether a partial line is flushed on exit, whether a keypress selector shares the loop — so the shared function needs to cover those as parameters rather than each caller keeping its own copy for the sake of one of them.

Deliberately out of scope: `logtail.py` has a similar-looking write, but it is reading a log file back for `admin logs`, not pumping a child, and its tests inject a stub `sys` at that seam.

## Why it is filed rather than done

It changes the output path of every existing action, so it should land on its own rather than inside a feature change. Split off from the pinned-footer work.

Added admin_lib.streams.OutputPump as the single shared implementation; core.run_cmd (pty + pipe), reload.run_with_reload, keybindings.run_with_keybindings, and streams.stream_subprocess all now build one OutputPump instead of five hand-rolled copies. New tests/test_streams.py exercises the pump's contract directly (line-buffering across chunk splits, flush() on exit, log vs display transforms, collect capture).

title: admin dev cf announces two log files and leaves an empty one behind
description:
## What happens

Running `admin dev cf` in reddit-poker prints two log paths back to back:

```
→ logging to: tmp/dev.2026-08-13_115208.log
→ logging to: tmp/dev-cf.2026-08-13_115208.log
```

Afterwards, `tmp/dev.2026-08-13_115208.log` is 0 bytes. Every line of output went to `tmp/dev-cf.2026-08-13_115208.log`.

| What it did | What it should have done |
|---|---|
| Created and announced two files, wrote to one | Create and announce one file, write to it |

Announcing a path and then writing nothing to it is wrong: the first path printed is the one a person copies, and it stays empty forever.

## Why

`dev` is a command (a step-runner). `_make_step_runner` scopes the log before running any step:

`admin_lib/interp.py:797` — `set_log_context(name)` → creates `tmp/dev.<ts>.log`, prints the announcement.

Its only step is the multi-target action `dev`. Once a target is picked, that action re-scopes:

`admin_lib/interp.py:249` — `set_log_context(name, picked)` → creates `tmp/dev-cf.<ts>.log`, prints a second announcement, and rebinds the module-level `LOG_FILE`. The first file is orphaned.

## Who it hurts

Every command whose steps include a multi-target action. Each run leaves one empty file in `tmp/`, and for the first second the printed path is the wrong one. In reddit-poker that is both `admin dev` flows.

## Fix

Announce once, at the leaf. Either the step-runner defers `set_log_context` until it knows no step will re-scope, or a multi-target action inherits an already-active log context instead of replacing it. The second is narrower.

Structural note: two layers each own "name the log file" with nothing arbitrating between them. The same duplicate announcement is reachable through `@`-ref steps for the same reason, so a fix that only special-cases the step-runner leaves the condition in place.

title: admin roots on the shell's cwd, so a worktree's test run can build the primary checkout instead
description:
## What happened

During a swarm run on `iptv-mac`, four agents each worked in their own git
worktree under `~/.worktrees/iptv-mac/<slug>/`, and each verified its branch by
running the project's test task. One of those runs rooted itself at the
**primary checkout** instead — the one none of them was working in.

The evidence it did:

```
$ ls -lt /Users/pierce/Projects/iptv-mac/tmp/test-apple.*.log
Aug 12 21:21  tmp/test-apple.2026-08-12_212136.log      <- nobody in this checkout started this
```

and, when a later run was attempted from that same primary checkout:

```
Refusing to start — apple test_cmd, started at 21:21:36 (pid 23904)
is already running in this checkout.
```

|  | what happened | what should have happened |
|---|---|---|
| where the build rooted | `/Users/pierce/Projects/iptv-mac` — the primary checkout, on `main` | the worktree holding the branch under test |
| which sources it compiled | whatever `main` had at that moment | the agent's own branch |
| where the log and lock went | the primary checkout's `tmp/` | the worktree's own `tmp/` |

## Why that is wrong

A test run is supposed to answer "does *this* branch pass". Rooted in another
checkout, it answers "does some other branch pass" — and returns a green result
either way, so the answer looks identical whether it was asked the right
question or not. In this run four different branches were in flight at once, so
"the suite passes" from one of them could have described code nobody was
reviewing.

## The line that decides it

`admin_lib/core.py:199`

```python
_project_root = project_root or os.getcwd()
```

The root is the directory you happen to be standing in, and `admin-run` walks
*up* from there looking for an `admin.toml` (`admin-run:63-66`). Neither step
consults git.

That interacts badly with one more fact: `admin.toml` is globally gitignored, so
**no git worktree ever contains one**. `git worktree add` copies tracked files
only. So inside `~/.worktrees/iptv-mac/fix-something/` there is no `admin.toml`,
the walk-up goes to `~/.worktrees/iptv-mac/` → `~/.worktrees/` → `~/` and finds
nothing. `admin` is unusable there unless someone hand-copies an untracked file
into every worktree. And if the caller's shell was still sitting in the primary
checkout — which is the default for an agent that was told to work in a
worktree but ran a bare `admin test apple` — it silently succeeds against the
wrong tree instead of failing.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone running parallel worktrees: the `/orchestrate` swarm, `git worktree`
users generally, and issue #472's parallel-build spike, which assumes each
worktree builds its own sources. It fires silently — there is no error, just a
pass or fail about the wrong code. In this run it cost ~40 minutes: the
misrooted run also hung (see below), and diagnosing which checkout owned the
lock took `ps`, `lsof` and reading the log by hand, because the refusal names a
pid and a time but never a directory.

## What is *not* broken

The `flock` design in `admin_lib/apple.py:143-185` is sound and its docstring is
accurate: killing the holder released the lock immediately, with no stale pid
file to clean up. The 40-minute block was a genuinely live process, not a stale
lock. Worth saying because "the lock got stuck" is the wrong diagnosis and would
send a fix in the wrong direction.

Separately observed and probably its own issue: that run hung at
`ExecuteExternalTool .../actool --version` and produced no further log output
for 40 minutes until killed.

## Fix — to brainstorm, not decided

Three candidates, roughly in order of how much they remove the condition rather
than guard it:

1. **Root on git, not on cwd.** Resolve the project root with
   `git rev-parse --show-toplevel`, which returns the *worktree's* root inside a
   worktree. Then the lock and the logs follow the checkout that owns the
   sources, which is what `_xcode_lock_path()`'s docstring already claims
   happens ("two worktrees/clones building different branches never
   contend"). Needs an answer for how a gitignored `admin.toml` reaches a
   worktree — perhaps look it up from the common git dir, or fall back to the
   primary checkout's manifest while keeping the *root* at the worktree.
2. **Refuse on disagreement.** Keep cwd-based discovery, but error out when the
   discovered root and `git rev-parse --show-toplevel` differ. Turns a silent
   wrong answer into a loud one. A guard, not a fix — but a cheap one, and it
   makes candidate 1 safe to land incrementally.
3. **Name the root everywhere.** Print the resolved project root in the lock
   refusal and at the top of each run's log. This is worth doing regardless of
   1 and 2 — it is the thing whose absence cost the diagnosis time — but on its
   own it only makes the bug easier to spot after it has already happened.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — and the surface changed enough to be worth re-checking before fixing. Manifest resolution roots on the process working directory: registerManifestCommand calls os.Getwd() and hands that to resolveProjectManifest (cmd/root.go:130-135), same for __run-action (:182-191). So a run started in a worktree still resolves from that worktree's cwd — the question this bead raises is whether the build it then launches roots itself the same way. Re-verify against the Go paths: luahost.Host.ProjectRoot (internal/luahost/host.go:77-86) and the Xcode lock, which is per-checkout by construction (lockPath = h.LogDir/<name>, internal/luahost/apple_darwin.go:399) — that lock is what produced the 'already running in this checkout' message quoted in the report.

title: Spike: parallel worktrees each rebuild the whole project — share the cache, or queue the builds
description:
## Category

spike — investigate and recommend, do not implement from this ticket

## Summary

When several worktrees of one project build at the same time, each one compiles the whole dependency
tree into its own `target/`. The machine thrashes, checks that take seconds alone take minutes, and
at least one agent has reported a compiler error in a file it never touched. Find out whether the
builds can share work, and if they cannot, whether they should be queued.

## What was measured, on one repo, today

`etv-station`, an ordinary Rust workspace, with three worktrees open at once:

```
53G    Projects/etv-station/target
3.9G   .worktrees/etv-station/fix-clock-seeded-tests/target      (mid-build)
4.2G   .worktrees/etv-station/reconcile-plexdb-ids/target        (mid-build)
234M   .worktrees/etv-station/repoint-deployed-channels/target   (just started)
```

Disk sits at **91% used, 82 GiB free**. The two mid-build worktrees were each compiling the same
third-party crates — `zerocopy`, `read-fonts` — from scratch, at the same moment, having each
already been compiled in the 53G directory next door.

Three concrete harms, all observed rather than predicted:

1. **A `cargo clippy` that takes seconds on a quiet machine ran 49 seconds without finishing** while
   two siblings built. An agent waiting on it woke three times, found it unfinished, and stopped
   again each time — burning a wake cycle per poll and making no progress.
2. **A worker reported `cargo clippy` failing at `config/validate.rs:1971`, a file its branch never
   touched.** That was dismissed as a build race — and separately, a *real* lint failure in that same
   file went unnoticed for a week because the documented lint command was narrower than CI's. Races
   and real failures became indistinguishable, which is the expensive part.
3. **Disk.** One project, one language, four checkouts, ~61 GB of build output for what is one
   source tree.

## Why this is not one project's problem

The shape is: **a build tool caches per output directory, and a worktree is a new output directory.**
Everything with a compile cache has it.

- Rust — `target/`, per worktree
- Node — `node_modules/` plus a bundler cache (`.next`, `.turbo`, `.vite`), per worktree
- Xcode — DerivedData, keyed by workspace path; admin-project-tool#471 and #466 already deal with
  side-by-side Apple worktrees
- Go — a shared module cache, but per-directory build output
- Docker — layer cache shared by daemon, which is the one that mostly gets this right

Any project run with parallel agents in worktrees hits it, so the fix belongs wherever worktrees are
created and builds are invoked, not in each project.

## What to find out

**Can the work be shared, so parallel stays parallel?**

- A single `CARGO_TARGET_DIR` across every worktree of a project. Cargo takes a file lock on the
  target directory, so this shares artifacts — but it also **serialises** builds, turning parallel
  agents into a queue whether or not that was intended. Worth knowing whether the lock is per-target
  or finer, and what two branches thrashing one cache costs in rebuilds.
- A compilation cache — `sccache` for Rust/C/C++, keyed on inputs rather than output path, so N
  worktrees compiling identical dependencies compile them once. Parallel is preserved. What is the
  hit rate across branches that differ only in a few crates?
- Per-language equivalents worth naming rather than reinventing: `sccache`, `ccache`, Turborepo's
  remote cache, Gradle build cache, Bazel/Buck. The question is not "is there a cache" but "does a
  cache keyed on inputs beat sharing an output directory."

**If sharing doesn't work, what does queueing look like?**

- A cross-worktree build lock, so `admin check` / `admin build` waits rather than thrashing. Where
  would it live — a lockfile under the project root, something the tool holds?
- Does an agent waiting on a lock behave better than an agent waiting on a slow build? It burns
  fewer cores, but it still burns wake cycles unless the wait is inside the command.
- Capping concurrency at the point worktrees are created is the crude version and may be enough.
  Worth pricing against the alternatives rather than dismissed.

**What good looks like, either way**

- Two worktrees running `cargo clippy` at once finish in about the time one takes, or one waits
  and says so.
- A failure reported by a build is a real failure. No more phantom errors in untouched files.
- Disk for N worktrees of one project is closer to 1× than N×.

## Deliverable

A recommendation with numbers behind it: which mechanism, what it costs, what it breaks, and whether
it is per-language or general. If the answer is "shared cache for Rust, queue for Xcode, nothing for
Node", that is a fine answer — but say why, per ecosystem.

Not in scope: implementing it. This ticket ends at a decision.

## Blocked by

None.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — a spike about the machine, untouched by the rewrite. Parallel worktrees each compiling a whole dependency tree into their own target/ is a property of cargo and of how the swarm dispatches, not of admin's implementation language. One adjacent fact worth carrying into the spike: admin already serializes same-checkout Xcode builds with a per-checkout flock (internal/luahost/apple_darwin.go:398-423), which is the 'queue the builds' half of this question implemented for exactly one toolchain — evidence for whether the queueing approach generalises.

title: Every apple project needs one pbxproj edit before admin dev builds side-by-side again
description:
`admin dev ios` and `admin dev mac` used to give the Debug build a different bundle ID by telling Xcode "the bundle ID is X". As of `4e07efd` (issue #331) admin no longer states any target's bundle ID — it passes a suffix, and each target appends it to its own ID. That fixed app extensions colliding with their parent app, and it means each Xcode project now has to say where the suffix goes.

## What happens until the edit is made

Nothing errors. The dev build simply gets the same bundle ID as the release build, so it installs *over* it instead of beside it — one icon where there used to be two.

| Before the edit | After the edit |
|---|---|
| dev build installs over the release build, same identity | dev build installs beside it as `com.foo.app.dev` |

## The edit

In each target's build settings in the Xcode project, change the bundle identifier from a fixed string to one that appends admin's variable:

```
PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.foo.app$(ADMIN_DEV_BUNDLE_SUFFIX)
```

An app extension appends its own part after the variable, which is the whole point of the change:

```
PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER = com.foo.app$(ADMIN_DEV_BUNDLE_SUFFIX).widgets
```

Release builds pass no suffix, the variable expands to nothing, and the shipped bundle ID is unchanged.

## Projects that need it

Every project whose `admin.toml` declares the `apple` archetype:

- `~/Projects/apple-coding-tool`
- `~/Projects/apple-notepad` — also the one with a widget extension, so it is the real test of #331
- `~/Projects/macterm`
- `~/Projects/iptv-mac`
- `~/Projects/stash-ios`

## How to know it worked

In `apple-notepad`, after the edit:

```
admin dev ios
```

Then read the bundle identifier out of both built bundles — the app should be `com.piercemakes.scratchpad.ios.dev` and the widget `com.piercemakes.scratchpad.ios.dev.widgets`. Before #331 both read `com.piercemakes.scratchpad.ios.dev`, and the install failed with `Mismatched bundle IDs`.

For the other four, `admin dev mac` or `admin dev ios` should install a second copy alongside the release one rather than replacing it.

## What not to do

Do not put `PRODUCT_BUNDLE_IDENTIFIER=` back into a manifest's `dev_build_settings` to work around a project that has not been edited yet — admin now hard-errors on that, deliberately, because that string is exactly what broke extensions.

## Why this is not automated

The edit is inside each project's `.xcodeproj`, in a different repository per project, and confirming it worked means building and installing a real app. Filed as one issue rather than five so the sweep is visible in one place; each project can be done independently.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — the port kept the suffix design, so the per-project pbxproj edit is still required. internal/kinds/apple_darwin.go:17-21 confirms the convention layer survived and that ADMIN_DEV_BUNDLE_SUFFIX 'is wired into every dev-loop build in appledevloop_darwin.go'. admin still does not state any target's bundle ID; it passes a suffix each target must append. Until each Xcode project says where the suffix goes, the dev build installs over the release build — silently, exactly as described.

title: install.sh writes the PATH line to ~/.profile when run through admin deploy, so zsh never sees it
description:
`install.sh` decides which startup file to add `~/.admin` to by asking "what program launched me?". When a person runs it by hand that answer is their shell, and it is right. When `admin deploy` runs it, the answer is `Python`, and it writes to a file zsh never reads.

## Real values from this machine

`install.sh:155` asks the operating system for the name of its parent process:

```sh
comm="$(ps -p $PPID -o comm= 2>/dev/null)"
```

Two ways of starting it, two different answers:

| How it was started | What that line returns | File it then writes to |
|---|---|---|
| `bash install.sh` typed in a terminal | `/bin/zsh` | `~/.zprofile` — correct |
| `admin deploy` (which runs `bash install.sh`) | `.../Python.framework/.../Python` | `~/.profile` — wrong |

Reproduced just now:

```
$ python3 -c "import subprocess; subprocess.call('bash -c \"ps -p \$PPID -o comm=\"', shell=True)"
/opt/homebrew/.../Python.app/Contents/MacOS/Python
```

`admin.toml` line 37 is `run = "bash install.sh"`, and admin runs that through Python's `subprocess`, so the parent really is Python.

## What it does next to what it should do

| It does | It should do |
|---|---|
| sees `Python`, falls through the `zsh` and `bash` cases to the catch-all, writes the PATH line to `~/.profile` | see `zsh` and write to `~/.zprofile` |

`shell_rc` at `install.sh:166-183` has three cases: `zsh`, `bash`, and everything else. `Python` matches everything else.

## Why that is wrong

zsh does not read `~/.profile`. So the line that puts `~/.admin` on your PATH gets written into a file that is never opened, and the `admin` command still isn't found in a new terminal — while the installer reports success. Meanwhile `~/.profile` slowly collects duplicate entries nobody reads.

## Who it hurts and when

Anyone whose first install goes through `admin deploy` rather than a hand-typed `bash install.sh`, on a Mac with the default zsh. It fires on every such run. It does not bite this repo's own maintainer today only because `~/.admin` is already on PATH from an earlier direct run.

## The line that causes it

`install.sh:149-163`, `_active_shell()` — specifically the `ps -p $PPID` call on line 155.

## Why this needs a decision rather than a quick patch

Every candidate fix trades something:

1. Read `$SHELL` first and use the parent-process name only as a fallback — `$SHELL` is the user's login shell, which is what "which rc file will future terminals read" actually means. Risk: `$SHELL` is stale if someone changed shells without re-logging-in.
2. Walk up the process tree past non-shell parents until a known shell name appears. Handles nesting, but has no natural stopping point.
3. Have `admin deploy` pass `--shell "$SHELL"` explicitly, since `install.sh` already accepts a `--shell` override at line 150. Smallest change, but only fixes the one caller.

Related: `uninstall.sh` (added for #65) carries a copy of `_active_shell` because `install.sh` has no sourceable library form — so whatever is chosen has to land in both, or the two files need a shared piece. That duplication is itself worth deciding about.

Found while implementing #65: the uninstall worker started to wire `admin uninstall` into `admin.toml`, noticed it would hit this same detection through the same Python wrapper, and reverted the wiring rather than shipping a second copy of the failure. `uninstall.sh` is standalone (`./uninstall.sh`) until this is settled.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). MOOT — install.sh is deleted by admin-3rgp.30: `go install` is the only documented installation path, and the binary needs no PATH-writing shell script, no shell detection and no rc file. The ps -p $PPID shell-detection heuristic that wrote to ~/.profile under `admin deploy` does not survive.

title: interactive shell-passthrough prints a resolved command but runs an unresolved one
description:
An action declared `kind = "shell-passthrough"` with `interactive = true` tells you it is about to run one thing and then runs a different thing.

## What happens, with real values

Say a project has this action, and the machine's LAN address is `192.168.1.50`:

```toml
[actions.serve]
kind        = "shell-passthrough"
interactive = true
run         = "python3 -m http.server --bind ${LAN_IP}"
```

Run `admin serve`:

| What admin prints | What actually runs |
|---|---|
| `running: python3 -m http.server --bind 192.168.1.50` | `python3 -m http.server --bind` |

The server binds to nothing and the command errors on a missing argument, while the log insists the address was there.

## Why that is wrong

The line admin shows you is supposed to be the command it runs. Here the two are produced from different text, so the log is a claim about something that never happened — and the first thing anyone does with a failing command is copy the printed line and run it by hand, where it works fine, which sends the search in the wrong direction.

## The line that causes it

`admin_lib/interp.py:179` builds the message from the resolved text:

```python
info("running: " + resolve_env(cmdline))
```

`admin_lib/interp.py:186` then hands the *unresolved* text to the shell:

```python
rc = subprocess.call(cmdline, shell=True)
```

The non-interactive branch on line 188 calls `run_cmd(cmdline)`, and `run_cmd` resolves the text itself at `admin_lib/core.py:687` — so only the interactive branch skips resolution.

## Which variables actually break

Only the computed ones. `COMPUTED_VARS` in `admin_lib/core.py:463` holds `LAN_IP`, whose value admin calculates rather than reads from the environment. An ordinary `${HOME}` survives because the shell expands it too; `${LAN_IP}` means nothing to the shell, so it expands to an empty string.

## Who it hurts and when

Anyone running an interactive passthrough action whose command contains `${LAN_IP}` — a dev server binding to the LAN address, a QR code pointed at it. It fires every time such an action runs, and it fails quietly: the log looks right.

## Fix

Resolve once and use the same text for both — build `resolved = resolve_env(cmdline)`, log that, and pass that to `subprocess.call`.

Found while landing #55, which made the log line resolved and thereby exposed the gap; the unresolved execution predates that change.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). FIXED BY THE PORT. One string is now both printed and run: internal/kinds/shell.go computes `resolved` once at :72 and uses that same variable for the 'running: ' line at :80 and for h.RunCmd at :81. The split this bead describes came from the `interactive` knob taking a different code path, and that knob no longer exists on shell-passthrough (documented at shell.go:51-58). Note the removal: an action that relied on `interactive = true` needs kind="interactive-shell" instead.

title: remote_container_diff's _pair_args still guesses flag-vs-value by leading dash
description:
`admin diff` compares the container running on the target against what your `admin.toml` says it should be. To do that it has to pair each command-line flag with its value. It pairs them by guessing: if the next word does not start with a dash, treat it as this flag's value. A value that legitimately starts with a dash therefore gets misread as a flag of its own, and the pair it belonged to is reported wrong.

## What happens, with real values

Given a container argument list containing `--workdir` followed by `-app`:

| What the pairing produces | What it should produce |
|---|---|
| `--workdir` and `-app` as two separate flags, neither with a value | `--workdir -app` as one flag-and-value pair |

The comparison then reports a difference that isn't there, or misses one that is, depending on which side carries the dash-prefixed value.

## The line that causes it

`admin_lib/docker.py:1548`, inside the `_pair_args` closure in `remote_container_diff`:

```python
if i + 1 < len(flat) and not flat[i + 1].startswith("-"):
```

The closure runs from `admin_lib/docker.py:1543-1554`.

## This is reachable, not dead code

The original filing said `_pair_args` looked like dead code with no caller. That was wrong, and the reason it looked that way is worth knowing: `archetypes/docker.py:80` wires the `diff` command's action to `remote_container_diff` from inside a `run = "..."` Python string. An action body written as a string is invisible to a grep for callers, so a live function reads as unreachable. Any project on the docker archetype reaches this through `admin diff`.

## What to do

Replace the closure's own pairing loop with a call to `_argv_pair_at(argv, i)`, the shared helper at `admin_lib/docker.py:1126`. It decides flag-vs-value by arity against `_BOOLEAN_FLAGS` rather than by a leading dash, and `_argv_to_pair_set` and `_live_argv_for_drift` already both use it. This is the third and last copy of the rule in this file.

Do not add a fourth copy of the boolean-flag set — the whole reason this issue exists is that one rule was written in three places and fixing one left two broken.

## Acceptance check

A regression test in `tests/test_docker.py` covering `remote_container_diff`'s pairing with a dash-prefixed value, red before the change and green after, in the same shape as `test_live_argv_for_drift_strips_dash_prefixed_image_workdir`. Full suite green (`.venv/bin/pytest`, 861 at time of writing).

## History

Split out of the original #468, whose part 1 — routing `_live_argv_for_drift` through the shared helper — landed in `1433b0a` (merged `f9f0409`). Part 1's own origin is #387, which fixed the first copy in `_argv_to_pair_set`.

Type: AFK
