The body rewrite and ordering comments since then were made against a closed issue. That is a flaw in how the work was tracked, not in the work — recording it here so the history reads straight.

title: [apple] launch_args reaches dev mac but not dev ios or dev tv
description:
#442 added the `[apple] launch_args` key and wired it into `dev_mac`. It does not reach the other platforms, which reads as an oversight rather than a decision.

## What is there today

`dev_ios` has had a `launch_args` parameter since before #442 (`admin_lib/apple.py:2641`, forwarded through `dev_simulator` at `:2584` and into `install_and_launch_sim`). Nothing populates it from config: `archetypes/apple.py`'s `dev` command calls `dev_ios(cfg, log_level=log_level, clean=force_clean)` with no launch args at all. So the parameter exists, the plumbing exists, and the only missing piece is reading the key.

This is the same shape #442 was filed about — one platform can do a thing and the sibling silently cannot — with the asymmetry now pointing the other way.

## What has to be decided

Whether `[apple] launch_args` is one key for every platform, or whether iOS and tvOS want their own (`ios_launch_args`, `tv_launch_args`). The existing `[apple]` table already splits some keys per platform (`mac_scheme`, `ios_device`) and shares others (`subsystem`), so both are consistent with what is there.

Shared-key is the smaller answer and probably right: an argument like `--defaults-suite=` is about the run, not the platform.

## Acceptance

`[apple] launch_args` set in a manifest reaches the launched app on `admin dev mac`, `admin dev ios` and `admin dev tv` — or, if per-platform keys are chosen instead, each documented in `docs/archetypes/apple.md` next to the `launch_args` row #442 added.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). FIXED BY THE PORT. appleDevSimulator — the one body behind both `dev ios` and `dev tv` — reads [apple].launch_args at internal/kinds/appledevloop_darwin.go:197-200, the identical three lines appleDevMac uses at :61-64 (flag wins, else config). It reaches install_and_launch_sim as UIApplication launch arguments (docs/architecture/lua-host-api.md:201).

title: [apple] launch_args should be able to name the worktree it came from
description:
Split out of #442, which added `[apple] launch_args` but deliberately left this part unspecified.

## The case that motivates it

From #442, in iptv-mac: the app accepts `--defaults-suite=<name>` so a throwaway run's saved servers stay out of the real ones. Parallel build agents each launch the app and overwrite each other's saved state, because every checkout passes the same literal string. Three of four agents in one run were affected.

A static `launch_args` in `admin.toml` cannot fix that — every worktree reads the same manifest and therefore the same value. What is needed is a value that differs per checkout without anyone editing the file.

## What has to be decided before this can be built

The syntax. Two shapes, and nobody has picked one:

1. **A token expanded inside each string** — `launch_args = ["--defaults-suite=${WORKTREE}"]`, where `${WORKTREE}` resolves to the current checkout's directory name. Fits the existing `${VAR}` / `${VAR:-default}` convention the manifest already uses everywhere, and needs no new key. But it adds a second source of substitution values alongside the environment, so `admin env` would have to know about it or it becomes invisible.
2. **A separate key** that declares the templating explicitly, leaving `launch_args` literal.

Option 1 looks right — it reuses machinery that exists rather than adding a parallel one — but the `admin env` question is real and unanswered.

## Acceptance

Two worktrees of the same project, same `admin.toml`, both running `admin dev mac`, pass different values for the templated argument, matching their own directory names, with no per-checkout edit.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — undecided, and the port made no choice for you. launch_args is read as a flat list of strings from the [apple] table and passed through verbatim (internal/kinds/appledevloop_darwin.go:61-64 for mac, :197-200 for ios/tv). Nothing expands a per-checkout token inside those strings. Note that the Go path DOES already run each string through nothing at all — so if you pick option 1 (a ${WORKTREE} token), the machinery to hang it on is manifest.ResolveComputed + the ComputedVars map (internal/manifest/envresolve.go:46-48), which today holds exactly one entry, LAN_IP. Adding WORKTREE there is a two-line change once the syntax is decided.

title: Xcode build-lock refusal can name the wrong holder in a microsecond window
description:
Cosmetic follow-up to #450. The refusal itself is always correct — only the message's specificity can degrade.

## What happens

In `_acquire_xcode_lock()` (`admin_lib/apple.py`), the process that wins the lock writes its description in two separate syscalls:

```python
fh.truncate()
fh.write(description)
```

A second process that loses the `flock` race and reads the file between those two calls sees an empty string, so instead of

```
Refusing to start — xcodebuild build -scheme "TestScheme" ..., started at 14:49:47 (pid 3196) is already running in this checkout.
```

it prints the generic fallback: another Xcode build is running, without saying which.

## Why it barely matters, and why it is still worth recording

The refusal fires correctly either way — nothing runs concurrently, no build is corrupted. What is lost is the part of #450's acceptance that made the message useful: naming the running build so you know what you are waiting on. The window is the gap between two adjacent syscalls, so hitting it needs two builds starting within microseconds of each other.

## Fix

Write the description to a temp file and `os.rename()` it into place, so a reader sees either the old contents or the new ones and never a half-written file.

Found by the #450 self-review; deliberately not fixed in that pass.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — inherited to the syscall. internal/luahost/apple_darwin.go:418-421 still writes the holder description in two steps: `f.Truncate(0)` / `f.Seek(0,0)` then `fmt.Fprintf(f, ...)`. A process that loses the flock race reads the file at :409 and, on an empty read, falls back to the generic message via firstNonEmpty(..., "another Xcode build") at :412. Same microsecond window, same degraded message, same correct refusal.

title: A real tailnet IP is committed in three files, including the userscript documented as carrying no prod URLs
description:
Found while fixing #438 — which is itself about a prod URL with a raw tailnet IP appearing where it shouldn't. The same address is committed in this repo.

## Where it is

| file | occurrences | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `tests/test_docker.py` | 7 | test fixture values |
| `admin_lib/docker.py` | 1 | inside a docstring |
| `tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js` | 2 | line 15 `// @connect`, line 50 in the host list, commented `// second machine (tailnet)` |

## Why the userscript one is the worst of the three

`CLAUDE.md` states the design plainly:

> The userscript is project-agnostic — no prod URLs baked in. It decides which pages to forward at runtime […] any other host is opt-in via a single Tampermonkey menu command […] so a new project needs one menu click, never a script edit.

The script does not match that description. A specific machine's tailnet address is hardcoded in two places, one of them a `@connect` grant. Anyone who installs this userscript gets a browser permission entry naming that machine — and the documented reason the runtime opt-in exists is precisely so that isn't necessary.

The `tests/` and docstring occurrences are the ordinary version of the same rule: real hostnames, IPs, and deploy targets belong in `.env`, not in committed files. The repo is private today, so nothing is currently exposed — but "it's private" is not the reason the rule exists, and a repo's visibility can change with one click.

## Fix

- `tests/test_docker.py` and the `admin_lib/docker.py` docstring: swap for a placeholder. #438's own new test fixture already uses `http://prod.example.test:8419` — follow that.
- `tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js`: remove the hardcoded host from `PROBE_HOSTS` and the `@connect` line, so the script actually is what `CLAUDE.md` says it is. If a `@connect` grant is genuinely required for tailnet hosts, that needs its own answer — a wildcard grant, or documenting that the user adds their own line locally — rather than shipping one machine's address to everyone.

## Acceptance

`grep -r '100\.' ` over the tracked tree returns no real host addresses, and the userscript's behaviour matches `CLAUDE.md`'s description of it: no prod URL baked in, hosts opted into at runtime.

comments.author: github-import
comments.text:
[migrated from GitHub #464] @McBrideMusings at 2026-08-10T22:23:08Z:

Correcting my own count — it is worse than the issue body says.

There are **two** machine addresses hardcoded, not one, and each appears twice:

```
tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js:14   // @connect      100.64.0.11
tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js:15   // @connect      100.64.0.10
tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js:48       "100.64.0.11",   // primary dev machine (tailnet)
tampermonkey/log-bridge.user.js:50       "100.64.0.10", // second machine (tailnet)
```

The comment above them names them outright: "primary dev machine" and "second machine".

I also conflated two different lists in the body. They are not the same mechanism:

- **`LOCAL_HOST_RES`** decides which *page hostnames* get forwarded. It is already generic — `10.0.0.0/8`, `192.168.0.0/16`, `172.16.0.0/12`, and the full Tailscale CGNAT range `100.64.0.0/10`. Nothing to fix here.
- **`PROBE_HOSTS`** decides which *machines to probe* for a running listener. This is where the two addresses live, and it is the part that contradicts "no prod URLs baked in".

So the fix is narrower than I wrote, but the `@connect` problem is real and doubled: installing this userscript grants the browser permission to contact two named machines, and both names ship to anyone who installs it.

Worth noting the two lists solve related problems in opposite styles — one derives from a CIDR range, the other enumerates addresses. Deriving `PROBE_HOSTS` the same way is not directly possible (you cannot probe a /10), so this needs a real answer: read the hosts from a local config outside the tracked file, or have the script discover the listener some other way.

title: Sweep for flag rejections that don't name the accepted set
description:
#445 fixed one instance — `--log` rejecting an unknown level without saying which four are accepted. Its closing note asked for the pattern to be applied wherever it appears; that sweep was deliberately not done in that pass, so it lives here.

## The shape to look for

A value validated against a fixed, known set, rejected with a message that says the value is wrong but not what would have been right. The user learns nothing from the rejection and the next guess is no better informed than the first.

## Known so far

**Real instance, not yet fixed:** `admin_lib/core.py:1263` — `err(f"Unknown {cmd_name} target: {target}")`, inside the multi-target dispatch helper. `handlers` is a fixed dict right at the call site, so the message can name `", ".join(sorted(handlers))` exactly the way #445 did.

**Already correct, listed so a future sweep doesn't re-flag them:** `admin_lib/docker.py:1992`, `:1781`, `:1784` — all name their sets.

**Not yet checked:** `admin_lib/manifest.py`, `admin_lib/validate.py`, `admin_lib/interp.py`. They were held by concurrent workers when #445 ran.

## How to fix each one

Follow #445's shape (`ff4ca34`), not a hand-typed list in the error string: build the message from the same collection the dispatch reads, so adding a new accepted value makes it appear in the rejection with no second edit. The repo already has this pattern in `_LOG_LEVEL_PREDICATES` (`apple.py:303`) and `TARGET_CONSUMING_KINDS` (`kinds.py:115`).

## Acceptance

No rejection of a value from a fixed set anywhere in `admin_lib/` prints the bad value without also printing the accepted ones, and no accepted-set list is typed out separately from the collection that defines it.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — inherited, and the sweep target moved to internal/kinds/multitarget.go:216: `return fmt.Errorf("action %q: unknown target %q", name, picked)`. The valid set is right there — `order` and `targets` are both in scope at that line — so this is the same one-line fix #445 made. Worth noting the pattern IS already correct elsewhere in the Go tree: internal/guards/guards.go:219 and :245 both reject an unknown guard with `Known: %s`, which is exactly the shape to copy.

title: [deploy].chown has no local-copy equivalent — admin running on-host as a mismatched uid still hits #440
description:
## What

`[deploy].chown` (added in #440) is passed straight through as `rsync --chown=UID:GID`, which only exists on the remote-rsync branch of `admin_lib/core.py`'s `sync()`. When `[deploy]` has no `host` (or `host` resolves to the current machine), `sync()` takes the local `shutil.copytree` branch instead, which has no ownership-reassignment step at all — it now logs a warning (`chown=X has no effect on a local copy — files stay owned by whoever runs the sync`, `admin_lib/core.py`) rather than silently doing nothing, but it still doesn't apply the chown.

## Who it hits

A project that runs `admin deploy files` **directly on the machine that also runs the container** — e.g. `admin` invoked as `root` on an Unraid box itself, rather than pushed from a laptop over SSH — with a `[docker_run].user` that differs from the account running `admin`. That's exactly #440's failure mode (container can't write into a directory owned by the wrong uid), just reached through the local branch instead of the remote one.

## Why it's a different fix than #440

`rsync --chown` has no local equivalent to reuse. Applying an arbitrary-uid chown to a local copy needs `os.chown`/`os.walk` (or a `chown -R` subprocess), and reassigning to a uid other than your own needs root — a real permission constraint, not just missing code. That's genuinely different plumbing from the rsync flag #440 added, which is why it was left out of that fix rather than folded in.

## Suggested shape

In `admin_lib/core.py`'s `sync()` local branch, when `chown` is set and the process has the privilege to do it (or just attempt it and report the `PermissionError` clearly), walk the copied tree and `os.chown` each entry to the parsed uid:gid, replacing today's warn-and-no-op. Needs a decision on what to do when the process *can't* chown (non-root, target uid isn't the caller's own) — warn as today, or fail loudly — before landing.

Surfaced while working #440 (`fix-deploy-chown` branch, commit 50f2ee41a5cb5e0b543741c4eaa2099554717e6e) — self-review flagged the silent no-op, which is now a warning; this issue is the follow-up for making the local branch actually do something instead of just naming the gap.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL, DIFFERENT SHAPE — the port did not fix the asymmetry, it removed the working half. internal/kinds/sync.go:25-28 states it plainly: 'dry_run, post_sync and chown are not exposed — none of the 14 archetypes' current sync actions use them'. So the remote-rsync branch no longer passes --chown either, and NEITHER branch reassigns ownership now. The local-copy branch is a pure-Go tree copy (runSync) and the remote branch shells out to `rsync -avz --delete` with no --chown (:72). Anyone hitting the #440 failure mode — admin running on-host as a uid that differs from [docker_run].user — has no mechanism at all, where before they at least had the remote path. Re-scope accordingly: this is now 'add chown to the sync kind', both branches, not 'add the missing local equivalent'.

title: admin diff prints secrets in plaintext, same as #436
description:
## What happens

`admin diff` (wired to `remote_container_diff` in `admin_lib/docker.py`) compares the live container's `docker run` args against the snapshot from the last deploy and prints the result — but unlike the sites fixed in #436, this path was never touched by that fix.

Concrete example: a project has `TAUTULLI_API_KEY` in `[docker_run.env]`. Someone rotates the key and redeploys. The next `admin diff` (or a stale `admin diff` run before the redeploy, comparing an old snapshot against a container that already has the new key) prints both the unified-diff lines and a "Reconstructed docker run" line with the real key value in plaintext:

```
-  -e TAUTULLI_API_KEY=oldkeyvalue
+  -e TAUTULLI_API_KEY=newkeyvalue

Reconstructed docker run (current config):
  docker run -d --name etv-station ... -e TAUTULLI_API_KEY=newkeyvalue ...
```

## Why that's wrong

Same reasoning as #436: the value lives in a gitignored `.env` specifically to keep it out of anything read, copied, pasted, or shared, and `admin diff` is exactly the kind of output someone pastes into a chat or a ticket when asking "why does this say drift."

## Where

`admin_lib/docker.py`, `remote_container_diff` — a separate implementation from the `[docker_run]` drift-on-deploy report (`_compute_drift` / `_format_drift_report`) that #436 fixed. It builds its own diff via `difflib.unified_diff` over `_pair_args(...)`, plus a `reconstructed_run` value (both the text and `--format json` output carry it), so #436's masking (`is_secret_env_name` / `MASK_VALUE` in `admin_lib/core.py`) needs to be applied here too, at both the diff-line level and the reconstructed-command level.

## Fix

Apply the same name-based masking (`*_TOKEN`, `*_KEY`, `*_SECRET`, `*_PASSWORD`) used in #436 to `remote_container_diff`'s printed diff lines, the `--format json` output, and the "Reconstructed docker run" line.
close_reason: Fixed by admin-3rgp.37's docker.deploy/docker.diff port (e7d00f8), rather than ported forward. admin-9bex: internal/dockerrun.BuildDeploySyncPlan is now the ONLY [deploy]-sync implementation, so there is no second path to silently drop post_sync or chown; verified for real with a local sync where post_sync fired and created its marker file, and --chown rendering is mutation-proven. admin-dbmj: diff now reports three axes — declared/live, last-deploy/live, and declared/last-deploy — verified with a simulated manual port change. admin-wxz0: every -e value is masked in both text and --format json output on all three axes, verified with a real secret-rotation scenario. admin-fr0e was deliberately left untouched and not made worse. NOTE: the Python admin_lib still carries these bugs until admin-3rgp.30 deletes it.

title: Why did a 9-second xcodebuild report BUILD SUCCEEDED and write no .app?
description:
Split out of #448, whose closing note asked this and which the #448 fix does not answer.

## What was observed

```
21:31:09.202  export TARGET_BUILD_DIR=.../DerivedData/iptv-mac-fgrnssly.../Build/Products/Debug
21:31:09.202  ** BUILD SUCCEEDED **
```

9 seconds after start, after two source files had been edited, with nothing recompiled — and per the report, no `.app` in `TARGET_BUILD_DIR` at all.

## Why it still matters after #448

#448 made this loud instead of silent: `admin dev mac` now exits with `BUILD SUCCEEDED but no app at <path>` rather than launching a stale substitute from another worktree. So it can no longer produce a wrong answer. But a build that reports success and produces nothing is still a build that will now fail every `admin dev mac` run instead, and nobody knows why it happens.

## What this needs

A live repro against a real Xcode project — this is not answerable by reading `admin_lib/apple.py`. Candidates worth checking: an incremental build whose products were cleaned out from under it, a scheme building a target whose product lands elsewhere, or `TARGET_BUILD_DIR` from `-showBuildSettings` disagreeing with where an incremental build actually wrote.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — unaffected by the rewrite, and the loud-failure guard it depends on survived. appleDevMac exits with 'BUILD SUCCEEDED but no app at <path>' when TargetBuildDir reports a directory with no .app in it (internal/kinds/appledevloop_darwin.go:107-111), plus a second guard for xcodebuild reporting no TARGET_BUILD_DIR at all (:103-106). So a 9-second successful build that writes nothing still fails every dev mac run, loudly, and still nobody knows why. Needs the live repro against a real Xcode project this bead already says it needs.

title: No automated test for dev_loop_macos failing loudly when the built app is missing
description:
The #448 fix gave `dev_loop_macos()` two behaviours: launch the app at `TARGET_BUILD_DIR`, and — when nothing is there — print `BUILD SUCCEEDED but no app at <path>` and exit 1 instead of searching DerivedData for a substitute.

The second one is the half that stops the original bug from coming back, and it has no pytest coverage. It was proven live during the #448 pass by driving the real function against a scratch DerivedData layout with `xcodebuild` and `open` shadowed on PATH, but that driver was ad-hoc and is gone.

`tests/test_apple.py`'s existing `_load_apple` harness execs `apple.py` with `subprocess` stubbed, which cannot reach `dev_loop_macos()` end to end — a real test needs the PATH-shadowing setup the driver script used.

## Fix

Add an integration test modelled on that driver: scratch DerivedData with a stale sibling carrying a newer mtime, `xcodebuild`/`open` shadowed, assert the correct path is launched, and assert the missing-app case exits non-zero without launching anything.

Found while implementing #448.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — the behaviour survived, the test still does not exist. appleDevMac hard-fails with 'BUILD SUCCEEDED but no app at <path>' rather than searching DerivedData for a substitute (internal/kinds/appledevloop_darwin.go:107-111), plus a second guard for no TARGET_BUILD_DIR at all (:103-106). Neither is covered: internal/kinds/apple_darwin_test.go does not exercise either message. The PATH-shadowing driver this bead describes is much easier to build in Go — the exec calls go through runOpen and h.XcodebuildFiltered, both replaceable in a test — so re-scope to a Go test against those two guards.

title: target_build_dir() and xcodebuild_filtered() build the same xcodebuild argv twice
description:
Both functions in `admin_lib/apple.py` assemble the same xcodebuild invocation — project/workspace flag, scheme, configuration, destination, `extra_settings`, `-allowProvisioningUpdates` — from scratch, independently.

`target_build_dir()` was added by the #448 fix and has to produce an argv matching what `xcodebuild_filtered()` actually built with, or it reports the build settings of a *different* build than the one that ran, which is the whole failure #448 was about. Nothing enforces that they match. A future change to one — a new flag, a changed destination string, a signing argument — silently misses the other, and the symptom is `TARGET_BUILD_DIR` pointing somewhere the build did not write.

## Fix

One `_xcodebuild_base_args(...)` helper both call, so the argv can only be built one way.

Deferred out of the #448 pass because it touches `xcodebuild_filtered()`, outside that fix's diff.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — inherited, both halves. TargetBuildDir assembles its argv at internal/luahost/apple_xcode_darwin.go:65-81 and XcodebuildFiltered assembles its own at :132-157, independently. They share only projectFlag() (:47-56) and allowProvisioning() (:40-45); scheme, configuration, destination, ExtraSettings and the -allowProvisioningUpdates + AppStoreConnectAuthFlags tail are written out twice. The coupling this bead warns about is now load-bearing in Go exactly as it was in Python: appleDevMac calls XcodebuildFiltered and then TargetBuildDir with a hand-copied options literal (internal/kinds/appledevloop_darwin.go:82-102) and hard-fails if the reported directory has no .app. A flag added to one and not the other fails every dev mac run. Same fix: one base-args builder both call.

title: admin dev ios/tv/device still pick the just-built app by globbing DerivedData for the newest mtime
description:
#448 fixed this for `admin dev mac` only, because that is what the issue named. The same defect is still live on three other commands.

## What happens

`find_app()` globs every `<scheme>-*` directory under DerivedData — one per git worktree the scheme has ever been built from, including worktrees that no longer exist — and returns whichever `.app` has the newest modification time. That is not the app the build just produced; it is whatever was written most recently on the whole machine.

In #448 this launched an app built 45 minutes earlier from a deleted worktree, right after `BUILD SUCCEEDED`. Every scripted check against it answered from source written half an hour before, and an `osascript` error that looked like a broken scripting term was really just an app that predated the term.

## Where it still is, after #448

- `dev_loop_simulator()` — `admin dev ios`, `admin dev tv` — post-build call site, `admin_lib/apple.py:1528`
- `dev_loop_device()` — `admin dev device` — post-build call site, `admin_lib/apple.py:1647`

`dev_loop_device()`'s *other* `find_app()` call, in the `skip_build` cache-reuse path, is not this bug — there is no fresh build to anchor to, so searching is the right thing.

## Fix

Same as #448: `target_build_dir()` asks `xcodebuild -showBuildSettings` for the exact directory that build used, and the launch joins it with the app basename. No app there is a failure to report, not a cue to go looking.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone with more than one checkout of an iOS or tvOS project — worktrees, or two clones. For parallel agent runs that is the normal case, not the exception.

Found while implementing #448.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL for ios/tv — inherited; mac is fixed. `dev mac` no longer globs: appleDevMac asks xcodebuild for TARGET_BUILD_DIR and hard-fails if the .app is not there (internal/kinds/appledevloop_darwin.go:99-111). appleDevSimulator — the body behind BOTH `dev ios` and `dev tv` — still calls luahost.FindApp(appPattern) at :247 and :277, and FindApp is a glob returning the newest match by mtime (internal/luahost/apple_darwin.go:326-345). appPattern comes from appleDerivedGlob (internal/kinds/apple_darwin.go:163), the same one-directory-per-worktree DerivedData glob. The fix is the one already proven on mac: TargetBuildDir with the simulator destination. Note Go added a partial mitigation — it warns when the built app's bundle ID differs from the expected one (:294-298) — but that is a symptom check, not the fix.

title: Three copies of --help handling, and the generic one that was built for it has never been wired up
description:
## What exists today

`admin_lib/core.py` already contains a generic `--help` interceptor, wired into `boot()`:

```
core.py:789   _subcommand_help = {}
core.py:834   def subcommand_help(name):          # decorator that registers into it
core.py:1302  if ("-h" in args or "--help" in args) and cmd_name in _subcommand_help:
core.py:1303      _subcommand_help[cmd_name]()
```

A repo-wide grep finds **zero** uses of `@subcommand_help`. The dict is never populated, so the check at `:1302` can never fire. It is a handler with no route — built for the shape the tool should have had, and never connected.

## What that has already cost

- **#441** (`admin deploy --help` ran a real production deploy) was just fixed by adding `--help` handling *inside* `deploy_dispatch` in `admin_lib/docker.py` — a second implementation of exactly what the empty registry was built to do.
- **#446** (`admin docs --help` starts the VitePress server and blocks until the caller times out) is still open, and fixing it the same way would be a third. #446's own text predicts this: *"a fix at the dispatch layer probably covers more than docs."*

Every new subcommand that shells out to a long-running process will need someone to remember this again. The registry sat empty for that same reason — it needed a human to remember to register, and nobody ever did.

## What has to be decided

1. **Wire the existing registry.** Register a help function per command; `boot()` already checks it. Fixes #446 generically. Still needs remembering for each new command — which is why it is empty today.
2. **Delete the registry, keep per-command checks.** What #441 landed becomes the pattern, #446 gets its own copy. Cheapest now; the condition stays.
3. **Intercept `-h`/`--help` in `boot()` for every command, with no registration at all.** The runner already knows every command's name, `desc`, and steps from the resolved manifest — it can print usage without being told. Nothing to register, nothing to forget. The ad-hoc check inside `deploy_dispatch` gets deleted.

Option 3 is the only one that removes the condition rather than guarding it; 1 and 2 both leave a step a person has to remember.

## Acceptance, whichever is chosen

`--help` and `-h` print usage and exit 0 for **every** command in a project's manifest, including ones whose action body is a long-running process, and no command's action body runs as a side effect of asking for help. `admin deploy --help` and `admin docs --help` are the two known cases.

Blocks #446.

title: needs human input: #449 — icon backup/restore bug does not reproduce against current HEAD
description:
While implementing #449 ("admin icons restore puts back an already-bannered icon instead of the committed one"), I could not reproduce the reported bug against current main.

admin_lib/apple.py already has a self-heal step (`restore_stranded_dev_icons`, added in commit 48c7848, predating #449) that runs at the start of every `build_icon_hooks()._pre()` — it restores any stranded backup from an interrupted prior run and deletes the stale backup dir BEFORE taking a fresh backup, so a second un-restored `admin dev mac` run can never persist an already-bannered icon into the backup.

I reproduced the issue's exact repro (two dev-mac-style runs with no intervening restore, simulating a process that died before its cleanup ran, then `admin icons restore`) against the real backup/self-heal/restore functions for both the appiconset PNG path and the Xcode 26 Icon Composer .icon path — both landed byte-identical to the committed originals.

I added two regression tests to tests/test_apple.py (branch `fix-icons-restore-backup`, commit bfa5995) proving this, but made no source change since none was needed.

This needs a human decision: either close #449 as already-fixed/stale (it was moved from the iptv-mac tracker and may describe behavior against an older admin_lib deployed to that project's `~/.admin`, not current admin-project-tool), or investigate further against the actual iptv-mac reproduction if there's a scenario I didn't cover.

I have no tracker-write access to comment on or close #449 directly.

The bug could not be reproduced against the Python because restore_stranded_dev_icons self-healed it, and that Python is deleted by admin-3rgp.30. In Go the dev-icon-swap hooks are not wired at all — internal/kinds/apple_darwin.go:22-25 lists 'Dev-icon-swap hooks (build_icon_hooks: backup/swap-banner/restore around each build)' as a deliberate, documented gap — so there is nothing running to reproduce against either. title: Add regression tests for run_with_reload's bounded fast-exit retry
description:
## What's missing

`admin_lib/reload.py`'s `run_with_reload()` fast-exit branch (around line 319-334) now actually retries the backend, capped at 3 consecutive fast exits, and resets the counter when a manual reload (`r`/SIGUSR1) interrupts a healthy run (line 321-326). None of this is covered by an automated test in `tests/test_docker.py`, which currently only exercises `run_with_reload`'s SIGINT/SIGTERM-forwarding behavior.

## Why it matters

This is the fix for #439 ("waiting before retry" prints, then admin gives up without retrying) — the exact code path that regressed silently before. Without a test, a future refactor of the `while True:` loop can reintroduce the same bug (falling through to `return rc` instead of `continue`) with nothing to catch it.

## What to add

Using the existing `_make_reload_driver` / `_child_script` pattern in `tests/test_docker.py`:

1. A child that always exits fast (e.g. `sys.exit(1)` immediately) — assert `run_with_reload` prints 3 retry/give-up messages, launches the child exactly 3 times, and returns the child's real exit code.
2. A child that exits slowly (>2s) — assert no retry message and immediate return, unchanged from before this fix.
3. A sequence exercising the reset-on-manual-reload path: a fast exit (count=1), then a launch that runs long enough to receive a manual reload signal, then another fast exit — assert the counter did NOT carry over from the pre-reload fast exit (i.e. it took 3 *new* fast exits after the reload to give up, not 2).

## Provenance

Surfaced while implementing #439 (branch `fix-dev-retry-loop`) — scoped out of that pass because the task confined the change to `admin_lib/reload.py` only, to avoid touching a shared test file while sibling workers were running concurrently. Verified manually instead via an ad-hoc synthetic-child harness; see the verify verdict for that pass.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). FIXED BY THE PORT. internal/reload/reload_unix_test.go:143-268 covers the bounded fast-exit retry end to end: wantLaunches == 3 asserts maxFastExitAttempts bounds the loop, and the test carries explicit mutation evidence (':255 — change maxFastExitAttempts from 3 to 1 and this test fails'). That is the regression guard this asked for.

title: admin dev tv reaches a simulator but never a real Apple TV
description:
Split off #451 on 2026-08-10, once the simulator half was working, because the two halves are checkable in completely different ways and only one of them could be proved on this machine.

## What #451 landed

`admin build tv` and `admin dev tv` drive a tvOS **simulator**: `resolve_simulator("tv")` picks an Apple TV, the dev loop builds to `platform=tvOS Simulator,id=<udid>`, installs, launches and streams the log. All of it verified end to end against a real build.

## What it does not do

Put a build on the Apple TV sitting under the television. That is a different path in every respect:

    simulator                        physical Apple TV
    -------------------------------  ------------------------------------
    xcrun simctl install / launch    xcrun devicectl, over the network
    a udid from simctl list          a device paired to Xcode first
    log stream via simctl spawn      devicectl --console owns the launch
    no signing needed                needs a real team, like an iOS device

`dev_device` in `admin_lib/apple.py` already does exactly this shape for an iPhone — find the device, install, launch with `--console`, stream. An Apple TV is reached the same way once paired, so this is most likely the same generalisation #451 did for the simulator path: give `dev_device` a platform key rather than writing a second function.

## Why it was not done at the same time

It cannot be verified without the device paired and switched on, and #451's whole value was unblocking three tickets in another project that need *something* on the box. Landing an unverifiable device path alongside a verified simulator path would have made the working half unprovable too.

## What this unblocks

The three hands-on tickets in iptv-mac's tvOS epic — watching a channel decode, watching what the box does with audio, using the thing with a real remote. All three need a build on real hardware and none of them can start without this.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — the split still holds and the physical half is still unbuilt. The Go port covers the simulator half for tv (appleDevSimulator handles both ios and tv via appleSimSDK, internal/kinds/appledevloop_darwin.go:180-194) and covers physical DEVICES for iOS (appleDevDevice at :340, apple.find_connected_device / install_on_device / launch_on_device, docs/architecture/lua-host-api.md:204-207). What is missing is the same thing as before: a real Apple TV as a devicectl target. Note the adjacent constraint — docs/architecture/lua-host-api.md:244-246 lists dev_device/deploy_ios/deploy_tv as not exercised end to end for lack of a paired device, which is admin-3rgp.47, the ticket blocking the Python deletion.

title: admin icons regenerate can make flat PNGs, and a tvOS icon is not flat PNGs
description:
## What it generates today

`admin icons regenerate` renders a glyph SVG into every size an app icon needs
and writes the PNGs into the asset directories named in `[apple.icons]`. It knows
two of them:

    admin_lib/apple.py:1860    key_map = {"mac": "mac_asset_dir", "ios": "ios_asset_dir"}

and it detects what to write by reading the sizes of the PNGs already sitting in
each `.appiconset` (`admin_lib/apple.py:2684`, and the empty-set bootstrap at
2720).

## Why tvOS does not fit that

An Apple TV icon is not a square PNG. It is a stack of layers the system slides
apart as the icon takes focus, plus a wide top-shelf image for when the app is in
the top row. tvOS will not accept a single flat image as an app icon, so the
current generator cannot produce a valid one no matter which directory it is
pointed at — this is a new output shape, not a third entry in `key_map`.

## What has to be added

- `tv_asset_dir` in `[apple.icons]`, beside `mac_asset_dir` and `ios_asset_dir`.
- A tvOS branch that writes a layered icon rather than a flat one: at minimum a
  background layer and the glyph on its own layer, so the parallax has something
  to separate. The existing glyph render is reusable; the packaging is not.
- The top-shelf image, which is a different aspect ratio to everything the
  generator currently produces and needs its own composition rather than the
  glyph centred on a square.

## And the DEV banner

The banner swap is the other half of this. It overlays a ribbon on the committed
icon before a Debug build and restores it after, and it has two code paths
already — the `.appiconset` PNG swap and the macOS `.icon` path
(`admin_lib/apple.py:1912`, 1945-1998), because the Liquid Glass `.icns` is not
an appiconset of flat PNGs. A layered tvOS icon is a third shape with the same
question: which layer does the ribbon go on, and does `admin icons restore` put
it back correctly after an interrupted run.

## Who it hurts, and when

Any project with a tvOS target, from the first build — the target does not ship
without a valid icon. Right now that is iptv-mac, which has a ticket blocked on
this.
close_reason: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). FIXED BY THE PORT. `apple.generate_tv_icons(brandassets_dir, {...})` generates a complete tvOS .brandassets catalog — both App Icon imagestacks' Front/Middle/Back layers, both Top Shelf image sets, and every Contents.json (docs/architecture/lua-host-api.md:218; implementation in internal/luahost/apple_icons_generate_darwin.go). Back is always opaque because tvOS rejects a transparent bottom layer; Middle is a transparent spacer. The layered output shape this bead said the flat-PNG generator could never produce is exactly what it now produces.

The tvOS target in iptv-mac needs a layered icon and a top-shelf image now, and that ticket (iptv-855.4) is hand-building the catalog once instead of waiting for this. The reason is that the art is a placeholder: the glyph standing in today is waiting on that project's naming-and-icon decision, so teaching the generator to emit a layered stack would be building a machine for artwork that is about to be thrown out.

title: The apple archetype knows two Apple platforms, and tvOS is a third
description:
## What the archetype can be told today

`[apple]` in a project's `admin.toml` names exactly two schemes, and the code
reads exactly those two keys:

    admin_lib/apple.py:230    cfg.get("ios_scheme") or cfg.get("mac_scheme")
    archetypes/apple.py:228   cfg.get("mac_scheme") or cfg.get("ios_scheme")

There is no third key, so there is no way to tell `admin` that a project has an
Apple TV scheme. `admin dev tv` and `admin build tv` do not exist, and there is
nothing to add to `admin.toml` that would make them exist.

## What the project asking for it looks like

iptv-mac is adding a tvOS target (`iptv-tv`) alongside its existing `iptv-mac`
and `iptv-ios` ones. Its whole dev loop today is `admin dev mac`, and the tvOS
equivalent is currently an `xcodebuild` line with a hand-copied simulator udid
in the `-destination`.

## What has to be added

A `tv_scheme` key, and the two paths that read it:

- **`build_tv`** — the sibling of `build_ios` (`admin_lib/apple.py:2622`). The
  destination logic at 2634-2640 already handles the ambiguous-simulator problem
  by resolving a name to a udid; tvOS needs the same with
  `platform=tvOS Simulator`.
- **`dev_tv`** — the sibling of `dev_ios` (`admin_lib/apple.py:2426`): boot a
  simulator, install, launch, stream the log. The simulator helpers at 313-443
  are `simctl` calls that are not iOS-specific — `simctl list devices` returns
  Apple TV devices from the same output — so most of this is teaching the
  runtime filter about tvOS rather than writing a second set of helpers.

## Two things worth settling while doing it

- **A physical Apple TV as a destination.** Unlike a phone, a real Apple TV is
  reached over the network and is the only place several kinds of tvOS bug show
  up at all — no simulator has the device's decoder or a Siri Remote. If `dev tv`
  can only ever reach a simulator it will not be enough.
- **The dev-app rename.** `dev_macos_postprocess` (`admin_lib/apple.py:151`)
  renames the built `.app` so the Dock says which copy it is. An Apple TV has no
  Dock and no Finder, so the equivalent question is whether a tvOS dev build
  distinguishes itself by bundle id alone, and whether that is enough to tell two
  copies apart on the home screen.

## Who it hurts, and when

Any project with a tvOS target, on every build. Right now that is iptv-mac,
where two tickets are blocked on this one.

All three need a way to put a build on the device, and this issue is that way.

The alternative considered and rejected: add `tv_scheme = "iptv-tv"` to that repo's `admin.toml` now and reach the device with a raw `xcodebuild -destination` line until this lands. That produces a config key nothing reads and a ticket that reads finished with no working command behind it.

What changed: the four values that made the simulator path iOS-only are now one SIM_PLATFORMS row per platform — the device-name filter, the xcodebuild destination, the DerivedData SDK suffix, and the config-key prefix. resolve_simulator, ensure_booted_simulator, dev_loop_simulator (was dev_loop_ios), dev_simulator and build_simulator take a platform key; dev_ios/build_ios and dev_tv/build_tv are one-line entry points over them.

title: Two admin build tasks can fight over the Xcode build lock and nothing stops them
description:
## What happened

Twice in one session, two Xcode builds ran against the same project at the same time:

```
21:57  xcodebuild ... -scheme iptv-mac -destination platform=macOS test
21:57  xcodebuild ... -scheme iptv-ios -destination 'generic/platform=iOS Simulator' build
```

and again later with a macOS test run alongside a Release build. They contend for the Xcode build lock, so a check that takes about 70 seconds alone stretches out with no sign of why — the log just goes quiet.

That is part of why two agent workers ran past the end of their turn: each had started a test suite that was taking far longer than it should, and neither had any way to see it was queued behind someone else's build.

## Why that is wrong

Nothing in `admin` prevents it. `admin test apple`, `admin dev mac` and `admin build` can all be started while another is running, and the second one looks like it is working — it prints output, it eventually succeeds. The only symptom is duration, which is exactly the signal nobody watches.

## Fix

Take a lock around the Xcode invocations in the apple archetype — a lockfile held for the duration, with the second caller either waiting and saying so ("waiting for the build started at 21:57") or refusing outright. Refusing is probably better for an agent: a clear failure beats a silent five-minute wait.

Related: #447 (raw Xcode build log uses one fixed /tmp path, so parallel checkouts overwrite each other's) — same root condition, that nothing in the apple archetype expects a second concurrent run.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone running more than one admin build task at once, deliberately or not — including any parallel-agent run, where it is the normal case rather than the exception.

## Acceptance

Starting a second admin build task while one is running either refuses with a message naming the running build, or waits and says it is waiting. Neither silently queues.

Moved from the iptv-mac tracker (bead `iptv-0dl`) — the lock belongs in the apple archetype, not in that repo.

comments.author: github-import
comments.text:
[migrated from GitHub #450] @McBrideMusings at 2026-08-10T18:52:53Z:

Landed on `main` (merge of `fix-xcode-build-lock`, `f22414a`).

Every `xcodebuild` invocation now takes an exclusive `flock(2)` lock, and a second caller refuses instead of queueing:

```
Refusing to start — xcodebuild build -scheme "TestScheme" -destination "platform=macOS",
started at 14:49:47 (pid 3196) is already running in this checkout.
```

**Scoped per checkout, not per machine** — the lock path comes from `get_log_dir()`, the same scoping #447 gave the raw build log. Two worktrees building different branches never contend; two builds in the same checkout do. Getting that backwards would have made parallel agent runs worse rather than better, so it was verified explicitly.

**Also closed the hole this issue's own example sat in:** `admin test apple` ran a raw `xcodebuild … test` shell string through `run_cmd()` directly, bypassing `xcodebuild_filtered` entirely — which is exactly why your two 21:57 invocations could overlap. It now goes through a shared `run_locked_xcode()` helper and contends with `build` and `dev` like everything else.

Verified with genuinely simultaneous OS processes against a stubbed `xcodebuild`:

- **same checkout:** second build refused in 1.04s while the first was mid-build; the first still succeeded.
- **crashed holder:** holder `SIGKILL`ed a second into its build, next build succeeded immediately — `flock`'s open-file-description semantics reclaim it, so there is no pid file and nothing to delete by hand.
- **two checkouts:** both finished in ~4.05s rather than ~8s, so neither blocked the other.

A self-review caught one real thing before commit: a bare `except OSError` around the non-blocking acquire would have reported a genuine I/O failure (permission denied, flaky mount) as "another build is running". Narrowed to `BlockingIOError`, with other errors propagating.

`target_build_dir()` is deliberately left unlocked — it is a `-showBuildSettings` metadata query, not a build, and only runs after the lock is already released.

Suite on the merged result: 847 passed. One microsecond-scale cosmetic race in the refusal *message* (not the refusal) is recorded in #465.

title: admin icons restore puts back an already-bannered icon instead of the committed one
description:
## What happened

`admin dev mac` overlays a DEV banner on the committed app icons before building and restores them afterwards. Run it twice without an intervening restore and the backup it restores from is itself already bannered — so `admin icons restore` puts the banner back rather than removing it.

| what you run | what you get |
|---|---|
| `admin dev mac` (first time) | committed icon backed up, banner applied |
| `admin dev mac` (again) | the BANNERED icon is backed up |
| `admin icons restore` | the bannered icon comes back |

## Why that is wrong

The one command whose job is "put the icons back the way they were" leaves them wrong, and quietly. The working fix, found by hand, was to skip the tool entirely: `git checkout --` on the icon files.

## Fix

Do not overwrite an existing backup. If a backup is already present when the banner is applied, that means a previous run did not restore, and the existing backup is the good one — keep it. Or drop the backup entirely and restore from git, which is where the committed originals already live.

## Who it hurts

Anyone who runs `admin dev mac` twice, which is normal during a session.

## Acceptance

Running `admin dev mac` twice in a row and then `admin icons restore` leaves the icons byte-identical to the committed ones.

Moved from the iptv-mac tracker (bead `iptv-zcf`) — the banner/restore logic lives in `admin_lib/icons.py`, not in that repo.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL, CURRENTLY UNREACHABLE — keep it open as the requirement for whoever wires the hooks. The dev-icon-swap hooks are not wired in Go: internal/kinds/apple_darwin.go:22-25 lists 'Dev-icon-swap hooks (build_icon_hooks: backup/swap-banner/restore around each build)' as a deliberate documented gap, and nothing calls BackupIcons/SwapDevIconsBanner/RestoreIcons outside the Lua bindings. When they are wired, this bug comes back by default: internal/luahost/apple_icons_darwin.go:70-84 overwrites a pre-existing backup unconditionally (MkdirAll + copyPNGs, no 'does a backup already exist' check), and the Python self-heal that masked it — restore_stranded_dev_icons — has no Go counterpart (grep 'Stranded' in internal/ finds nothing). So the fix this bead specifies stands unchanged: do not overwrite an existing backup; a backup already present means a previous run did not restore. Same applies to BackupTVIcons (:141), whose doc comment says outright that it replaces any prior backup.

comments.author: github-import
comments.text:
[migrated from GitHub #449] @McBrideMusings at 2026-08-10T18:04:00Z:

This does not reproduce against current `main`, and the reason looks like a stale install rather than a live defect.

`admin_lib/apple.py:2155` defines `restore_stranded_dev_icons`, which runs at the start of the pre-build hook: it restores any stranded backup and deletes it *before* a fresh `backup_icons()` / `swap_dev_icon_composer()` runs. So a second un-restored `admin dev mac` cannot bank an already-bannered icon — the banner is peeled off first. It is wired at five call sites (`apple.py:2095, 2599, 2640, 2720, 2752`) and covers both the appiconset PNG path and the Xcode 26 Icon Composer `.icon` path.

It landed in `48c7848` on **2026-05-01**. This issue was filed **2026-08-09**, three months later, and was moved here from the iptv-mac tracker — so the behavior observed there was most likely an older `admin_lib` sitting in that machine's `~/.admin/`, not this repo's code.

Regression tests for the exact scenario are now on `main`: two un-restored dev runs followed by a restore, driven against the real unmocked backup/self-heal/restore functions for both icon paths, asserting the final files are byte-identical to the committed fixtures. Both pass. Full suite 796.

Leaving this open for your call — closing your own bug report as "not a bug, your install was stale" is your decision, not mine. See also #455, which the worker filed asking the same question. If you agree, both can close.

title: admin dev mac says BUILD SUCCEEDED and then launches a different app than it built
description:
## What happened, with the real values

Ran `admin dev mac` in an apple-archetype project at 21:31:00 after editing two source files.

```
21:31:09.202  export TARGET_BUILD_DIR=.../DerivedData/iptv-mac-fgrnssly.../Build/Products/Debug
21:31:09.202  ** BUILD SUCCEEDED **
21:31:09      Launching .../DerivedData/iptv-mac-cclftyfv.../Build/Products/Debug/iptv-mac Dev.app
```

Two things wrong in those three lines:

| what it said | what was true |
|---|---|
| BUILD SUCCEEDED | 9 seconds after start; nothing recompiled |
| Launching ... cclftyfv | it had just built into fgrnssly, not cclftyfv |

`cclftyfv` is the DerivedData of a git worktree that had already been deleted. The app it launched was built 45 minutes earlier and carried the old source.

## Why that is wrong

Every scripted check run against that app was answering from source written half an hour earlier. An `osascript` query came back:

```
39:53: syntax error: A identifier can't go after this identifier. (-2740)
```

which reads exactly like a newly added scripting term being broken. It was not — the term was fine, the app predated it. A tool reporting success while handing back a stale answer.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone verifying a change in a running Mac app — every `admin dev mac` on a machine where more than one DerivedData directory for the project exists, which is any machine that has ever used a git worktree. Cost roughly 20 minutes and three wrong diagnoses in one session.

## Fix

Launch the app at the path the build just produced. `admin dev mac` already has `TARGET_BUILD_DIR` in hand; it should open `"$TARGET_BUILD_DIR/<app name>.app"` rather than searching DerivedData and taking whatever it finds. If the built app is not at that path, that is a failure to report, not a cue to look elsewhere.

Worth checking at the same time why the build took 9 seconds and produced no `.app` in `TARGET_BUILD_DIR` at all.

## Acceptance

After editing a source file, `admin dev mac` launches an app containing that edit, or fails loudly. Deleting an old DerivedData directory changes nothing about which app runs.

title: Raw Xcode build log uses one fixed /tmp path, so parallel checkouts overwrite each other's
description:
## Summary

The raw Xcode build log is written to one fixed path shared by every checkout on the machine. Two builds running at once overwrite each other's, so reading the log after your own build can hand you someone else's output with nothing to indicate it.

## What happens

`admin_lib/apple.py:95`:

    _RAW_BUILD_LOG = "/tmp/admin-xcode-build.log"

and `:147`:

    f'{build_cmd} | tee {_RAW_BUILD_LOG} | grep -E "BUILD|error:|warning:" ; exit ${{PIPESTATUS[0]}}'

Building in one worktree and then reading that file produced the build output of a *different* worktree (`issue-15`), which had built moments earlier. Nothing in the file says which checkout, branch or scheme produced it.

| what was read | what it was |
|---|---|
| "the log from the build I just ran" | a sibling worktree's build, written after mine |

## Why this is wrong

A raw log is read precisely when the filtered output was not enough — something failed and the detail matters. That is the worst moment to be handed a different build's output, because it looks like evidence. In the case above it nearly produced a wrong diagnosis of a failure that was not in that log at all.

There is no way to detect it after the fact. The file has no header identifying its source, so a stale or foreign log is indistinguishable from a correct one.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone building the same project from more than one checkout — worktrees, or two clones. It fires whenever two builds overlap, which for parallel agent runs is the normal case rather than the exception.

## Fix

Key the path on the checkout rather than using one global name: derive it from the repo or worktree path, or put it under the project's own `tmp/` where the rest of that build's output already goes. Writing the project path and a timestamp into the first line of the log is worth doing either way, so a log that is somehow still wrong says so.

The first line of every log is now `# <project root> @ <timestamp>`, so a log that is somehow still wrong says whose it is.

Verified under actual concurrency, not sequential calls: two real OS processes running at the same time, each pointed at its own temp project with no pre-existing `tmp/`, against a stubbed `xcodebuild` on PATH and the real `tee -a` / `grep` / `PIPESTATUS` pipeline. Each wrote its own log, neither saw the other's. `diagnose_build_failure()` then correctly diagnosed a real `errSecInternalComponent` failure in project B's log while staying silent for project A's clean one — proving it reads the log keyed to the active project rather than whichever file happens to exist.

title: admin docs --help starts the server instead of printing usage
description:
## What happens

`admin docs --help` does not print a usage string. It starts the VitePress dev server and blocks until the caller times out.

Other subcommands behave correctly — `admin dev -h` prints help and exits.

## Why it is worth fixing

`--help` is the first thing anyone reaches for when they do not know a subcommand's shape, so the failure mode is a hung command and a wasted timeout rather than a wrong answer. For an agent driving the runner from a tool shell, that is a blocked call with no output to learn from — and it teaches avoidance of `--help` generally, which costs more than the one incident.

## Likely cause

`docs` appears to pass its arguments straight through to the underlying command rather than letting the runner's own parser see `--help`/`-h` first. Any subcommand that shells out to a long-running process will have the same shape, so a fix at the dispatch layer probably covers more than `docs`.

## Reproduce

```
admin docs --help
```

Expected: usage text, exit 0. Actual: VitePress starts and the command blocks.

Observed 2026-07-27 against `apple-notepad`'s `admin.toml`, but the behaviour belongs to the runner, not that repo's config.
notes: Go-rewrite triage (admin-3rgp landed). STILL REAL — inherited, and the dispatch-layer cause this bead predicted is now explicit in the code. Every manifest command is registered with `DisableFlagParsing: true` (cmd/root.go:158, with the comment 'flags belong to the underlying steps, not to cobra'), so cobra never intercepts --help for a project command — the flag is handed straight to the action. `admin docs --help` therefore still starts the VitePress server (kind="docs", internal/kinds/docs.go) and blocks. Cobra DOES handle --help correctly for the tool verbs (branch, worktree, prs, check, archetypes), so this is now a clean split rather than three ad-hoc copies: one place to fix, the manifest-command registration at cmd/root.go:155-163. This is also what admin-pzbj's generic-registry idea becomes under cobra.

title: 'Unknown log level' does not say which levels are known
description:
## Summary

`admin dev mac --log` takes one of four words. The only way to learn which four is to guess wrong and read the rejection.

## What happens

    $ admin dev mac --log info
    Unknown log level: info

`info` is the obvious guess — it is a log level in most things that have log levels. The accepted set is `app`, `debug`, `system`, `verbose` (`admin_lib/apple.py:259`), and none of them is `info`.

| what was guessed | what is accepted |
|---|---|
| `info` | `app`, `debug`, `system`, `verbose` |

## Why this is wrong

The error says the value is unknown but not what is known, so it rejects the guess without narrowing the next one. With four accepted values and no list, the only reliable path is reading the source.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone passing `--log` for the first time, on a flag whose whole purpose is to be reached for while debugging something else.

## Fix

Print the accepted values in the rejection: `Unknown log level: info (expected one of: app, debug, system, verbose)`. Same for `--help`, if it mentions the flag at all.

Generally: any flag validated against a fixed set should name the set when it rejects. This is the one that came up, but the fix is worth applying wherever that pattern appears.

So the accepted set is never typed out twice and cannot drift from what is actually handled — same shape as `TARGET_CONSUMING_KINDS` in `2119ca2` earlier today. title: 'admin build' with no target blames the TTY instead of naming the missing argument
description:
## Summary

`admin build` needs a target. Nothing says so until you run it without one, and the message it gives then talks about terminals rather than about the missing argument.

## What happens

    $ admin build
    no target given and stdout is not a TTY

The working command is `admin build mac`. Nothing printed before that point mentions `mac` or `ios`, or that a choice is required.

| what the message says | what is actually wrong |
|---|---|
| stdout is not a TTY | no target was given |

The TTY half is true — interactively it would have prompted — but it is the reason the fallback did not fire, not the reason the command failed. Read as a diagnosis it points at the terminal, which is fine, instead of at the command line, which is not.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone running `admin build` for the first time in a project with more than one target, and anything running non-interactively, where the prompt can never appear and the message is all there is.

## Fix

When no target is given and there is no TTY, list the targets that were available: `no target given (expected one of: mac, ios)`. The prompt-needs-a-TTY detail can stay, but after the thing that is actually missing.

Worth checking whether `admin build --help` names the targets. If it does not, that is the same gap one step earlier.

`admin build` with no target and no TTY now says:

```

The target names are read from the `targets`/`order` arguments `pick_target` already receives — the resolved manifest's sub-targets — not a hardcoded list. Whoever takes #456 should close this too.

title: Missing 'kind = multi-target' turns every sub-target into an empty command that reports success
description:
## Summary

Leave `kind = "multi-target"` off a parent action that has sub-tables, and every sub-target silently becomes an empty command. It prints a success line and exits 0 without running anything, and `admin check` reports the manifest as fine.

## What happens

Given a manifest with `[actions.dev]` and `[actions.dev.mac]`, but no `kind` on the parent:

    $ admin dev mac
    running:
    dev complete
    $ echo $?
    0

Note the `running:` line with nothing after it. That is the whole command — an empty string. No binary ran.

    $ admin check
    ok (9 commands, 18 actions)

| what it printed | what it did |
|---|---|
| `running:` then `dev complete`, exit 0 | ran an empty string |

## Why this is wrong

Exit 0 and the word "complete" mean the thing was done. Nothing was done. This is worse than an error, because an error stops you and this does not: it cost two separate "it works" claims, both wrong, before the tee'd log was grepped for the name of the binary that was supposed to run and it was not there.

`admin check` reporting `ok` is the second half. The one command whose job is to tell you the manifest is sound counts the action and approves it.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone adding a multi-target command and forgetting the one key that makes it multi-target. It fires on every invocation, and it always reports success.

## Fix

Two places, and both are worth doing:

- `admin check` should fail on an action table that has sub-tables but no `kind`, since that combination cannot be anything but a mistake.
- Whatever runs the command should refuse to report success for an empty command string — an empty command is not a command that succeeded.

The second one is the general guard: it catches every other way an action can end up empty, not just this one.

comments.author: github-import
comments.text:
[migrated from GitHub #443] @McBrideMusings at 2026-08-10T18:09:00Z:

Landed on `main` (merge of `fix-multitarget-missing-kind`, plus a follow-on commit — see below).

Both halves, as the issue asked:

**`admin check` now rejects it.** An action with sub-tables (or a flat `targets = {...}`) whose `kind` is not one that actually reads those targets fails with `has target(s) ['mac'] but kind is 'shell' — targets only run under kind = "apple-dev-loop" or "multi-target"`, exit 1. Previously: `ok`, exit 0.

**The runtime refuses to claim success.** A shell action or multi-target child whose command string is blank or whitespace-only prints `refusing to run an empty command` and exits non-zero, instead of `running:` / `<name> complete` / exit 0. It is per-target, so one blank child fails while its real sibling still runs.

Driven against scratch manifests, not just tests — the issue's exact repro, the flat-`targets` form, and a correct multi-target manifest to confirm no false positive. Suite: 801 passed.

**Follow-on commit `2119ca2`.** The fix originally carried `_TARGET_CONSUMING_KINDS = {"multi-target", "apple-dev-loop"}` in `validate.py` — a second hand-maintained list of kind names, which is the exact drift `admin_lib/kinds.Kind` exists to prevent ("KINDS is the single source of truth", and the record's own docstring says the metadata and the factory can't drift because both key off it). A new targets-consuming kind could have been added to the catalog and to `register_factory` and still been rejected by the validator, with nothing to catch it. `Kind` now carries a `consumes_targets` flag, `multi-target` and `apple-dev-loop` set it, and `TARGET_CONSUMING_KINDS` joins the derived views next to `KNOWN_KINDS` / `CONFIGLESS_KINDS` / `KIND_MODULES`. The rejection message names the derived set rather than repeating it in prose.

title: admin dev mac cannot pass launch arguments to the app, but admin dev ios can
description:
## Category

enhancement

## Summary

`admin dev ios` can hand arguments to the app it launches. `admin dev mac` cannot. So any Mac app that reads a launch flag has no way to be given one by the dev loop.

## What happens

The iOS path takes a `launch_args` list and forwards it:

    admin_lib/apple.py:421   def install_and_launch_sim(device_id, app_path, bundle_id, launch_args=None):
    admin_lib/apple.py:429       if launch_args:
    admin_lib/apple.py:430           cmd.extend(launch_args)
    admin_lib/apple.py:2426  def dev_ios(cfg, *, log_level="app", clean=False, output_config=None, launch_args=None):

The macOS path has no equivalent. It launches with a fixed command and nothing else:

    admin_lib/apple.py:1358  subprocess.run(["open", "-n", app_path], check=True)

`open` does support this — `open -n <app> --args foo bar` — the call just never passes it, and `dev_mac` has no parameter to carry it.

| what `admin dev mac` can do | what `admin dev ios` can do |
|---|---|
| launch the app | launch the app, and tell it something on the way in |

## Why that matters

A Mac app that changes behaviour based on a launch flag — pointing at a throwaway preferences store, turning on a debug mode, choosing a fixture — can only be given that flag by a human typing `open -n ... --args` by hand. Every automated path silently launches without it, and the app runs in its default mode while the person who set up the flag believes it is in use.

Concretely, in iptv-mac: the app accepts `--defaults-suite=<name>` to keep a throwaway run's saved servers out of the real ones. Parallel build agents each launch the app and overwrite each other's saved state, because there is no way to put that flag on the command line from a task. Three of four agents in one run were affected.

## Who it hurts, and when

Anyone whose Mac app takes a launch argument, on every `admin dev mac`. It is silent — the app starts, so nothing looks wrong.

## Fix

Give `dev_mac` a `launch_args` parameter the way `dev_ios` already has one, append it to the `open` call as `--args ...`, and read the default from a new `[apple]` key in `admin.toml` so each project states its own. Worth having the value support the current worktree's directory name, since "give this run a name unique to the checkout it came from" is the case that keeps coming up.

comments.text:
[migrated from GitHub #442] @McBrideMusings at 2026-08-10T18:55:01Z:

Landed on `main` (merge of `fix-dev-mac-launch-args`, `5988052`, plus the doc entry).

`dev_mac` and `dev_loop_macos` both take a `launch_args` parameter now, mirroring the one `dev_ios` already had. The launch becomes `open -n <app> --args <...>` when it is set and is unchanged when it is not. The default is read from a new `[apple] launch_args` key (a list of strings), so each project states its own.

Proved at the command-construction level — four tests asserting the literal argv handed to `open`, with and without the key. **Not observed:** a real launch, or the app actually reading the argument. This machine can't drive a GUI, and there's no headless way to launch a macOS app and inspect its process arguments without a window. So what's proven is that the right argv is built, not that macOS delivers it — though `open -n <app> --args` is the documented mechanism and the iOS path already relies on the same shape.

- **The worktree-name templating** you suggested at the end. It's the motivating case (iptv-mac's `--defaults-suite` colliding across parallel agents), but nobody has specified the syntax — a `${WORKTREE}` token expanded inside each string, or a separate key. Filed as #466.

title: deploy treats any unrecognized flag as 'deploy image', so 'deploy --help' rebuilds and recreates the container
description:
## What happened

Ran `admin deploy --help` in etv-station to read the deploy subcommand's flags. No help text appeared. It started a real production deploy — a full `linux/amd64` Docker image build — and I killed it about sixty seconds in, still in the build phase. Had it finished, it would have pushed the image to the Unraid host, stopped the running container, removed it, and recreated it.

| what it did | what it should have done |
|---|---|
| built and began deploying to production | printed the deploy subcommand's usage and exited |

## Why that's wrong

`--help` is the one flag a person types when they are *not* sure what a command does. It is the safest thing you can ask for. Here it is indistinguishable from typing the most destructive available option.

## The line

`admin_lib/docker.py:1687`

```python
if args and not args[0].startswith("-"):
    # A typo'd sub-target must not fall through to a default. `admin deploy
    # fiels` silently rebuilding and recreating the container is the one
    # failure here with real blast radius, so unknown words are fatal.
    if args[0] not in ("image", "files", "all"):
        err(f"Unknown deploy target: {args[0]!r} (expected image, files, or all)")
        return 1
```

The guard is already here, and its comment names this exact hazard. But it only inspects arguments that do **not** begin with `-`. Anything starting with a dash skips the check entirely, `target` stays `None`, and execution reaches line 1698:

```python
if target is None:
    if deploy_cfg and sys.stdout.isatty():
        target = pick_target(menu, "what to deploy?")
    else:
        target = "image"
```

Only `--dry-run` and `--force` are ever read (lines 1695-1696). Every other flag is silently discarded.

So `admin deploy fiels` is correctly refused, while `admin deploy --help`, `admin deploy -h`, and `admin deploy --dryrun` all deploy to production. The typo guard protects the word form and leaves the flag form wide open.

## Who it hurts

Anyone reaching for help on a deploy command, and anyone who mistypes a flag. Worse without a terminal attached: with a TTY the menu at least asks "what to deploy?" and gives you a chance to escape. Under a script, a CI job, or a coding agent, `isatty()` is false, so it goes straight to `image` with no prompt at all — which is how it got me.

## Fix

Reject unrecognized flags the same way unrecognized words are already rejected, and handle `--help` / `-h` by printing the usage that `deploy_dispatch`'s docstring already contains:

```
Usage: admin deploy [image|files|all] [--dry-run] [--force]

  image  rebuild the image and recreate the container (default)
  files  sync the [deploy] mirror directory only
  all    sync the mirror directory, then the image
```

The check belongs on every argument, not just the first, so `admin deploy files --hlep` fails loudly instead of quietly dropping the flag.

title: deploy files chowns the target dirs to the local user, breaking any container that runs as a different uid
description:
## What happened

Deploying a new channel to the etv-station container on Unraid. `admin deploy files` synced three files, reported success, and took production down for four minutes.

Before the sync, on the Unraid host:

```
drwxr-xr-x 1 nobody users  /mnt/user/appdata/etv-station/channels
drwxr-xr-x 1 nobody users  /mnt/user/appdata/etv-station/etv-next
```

After:

```
drwxr-xr-x 1 pierce games  /mnt/user/appdata/etv-station/channels
drwxr-xr-x 1 pierce games  /mnt/user/appdata/etv-station/etv-next
drwxr-xr-x 1 pierce games  /mnt/user/appdata/etv-station/plugins
```

`pierce:games` is my laptop's ownership, carried across the wire. The container runs as `99:100` (`nobody:users`), set from `[docker_run] user`. On every start it rewrites `channel1.json` through `channel60.json` inside `etv-next/` — and a directory owned by somebody else at mode 755 does not allow that. It crashed on startup, ten times in a row:

```
render-etv-next: /config/etv-next/channel1.json: Permission denied (os error 13)
[entrypoint] failed to render ETV-next config from /config/station.yaml
```

| what it did | what it should have done |
|---|---|
| stamped the laptop's owner onto every directory it touched | left the target's ownership alone, or set it to the uid the container runs as |

## Why that's wrong

The tool knows exactly which user the container runs as — it is written in the same `admin.toml`, ten lines above the `[deploy]` table, and the deploy path already uses it to `chown` the bind-mount directories it provisions. It then hands the config directory to a different owner and starts a container that cannot write there.

## The line

`admin_lib/core.py:749`

```python
f"rsync -avz{delete_flag}{dry_flag} {exclude_flags} {src_dir}/ {dest}/".strip()
```

`-a` includes "preserve owner" and "preserve group". Over SSH as root, the receiver honours both, so the source's ownership wins. `[deploy]` has no key to change this — `_DEPLOY_KEYS` in `admin_lib/remote.py:180` accepts only `src`, `dest`, `host`, `exclude`, `delete`.

## Who it hurts

Any project whose `[deploy]` mirror is read by a container running as a non-root user — which is every Unraid deploy, since `99:100` is the standard there. Four minutes of dead air on a TV station; for something with users attached it is a full outage.

## When it fires

Only when rsync touches a **directory** — creating a new one, or updating one whose contents changed. That is why it stayed hidden: dozens of earlier deploys edited existing files and never disturbed a directory entry. It first bit on the deploy that added a new `plugins/` folder. So it is rare, silent, and lands on exactly the deploys that change the most.

## Fix

Add a `chown` key to `[deploy]` and pass it through as `rsync --chown=UID:GID`:

```toml
[deploy]
src   = "deploy/appdata"
dest  = "${ETV_STATION_APPDATA}"
chown = "${ETV_STATION_UID:-99}:${ETV_STATION_GID:-100}"
```

`--no-owner --no-group` alone does not fix it: everything would land root-owned, and uid 99 still cannot create files in a root-owned 755 directory. The receiving side needs to be told which user actually runs the app.

Worth considering: default `chown` to `[docker_run] user` when the project has one, since that is the answer in every case I can construct.

[migrated from GitHub #440] @McBrideMusings at 2026-08-10T18:29:58Z:

Landed on `main` (merge of `fix-deploy-chown`, `50f2ee4`, plus the design-doc entry in `c9e2eed`).
